prompt: A team wraps every `client.messages.create` call in a decorator that retries up to 5 times with exponential backoff on any exception. The Anthropic SDK client is left at its default settings. During a burst of 429s, logs show many more attempts per logical request than the decorator should allow, and recovery is slower than expected. What is the best fix?

options.text: Restrict the decorator to connection errors only, because the SDK never retries 429 responses itself, so rate limits must stay with application-level retry logic.
Keep retries in only one layer, because the SDK already retries transient failures and a second layer multiplies attempts; rely on the SDK, or turn its retries down.
Raise the decorator's cap to 10 attempts so it outlasts the SDK's own retries, since the outermost retry layer should always hold the largest budget in the call stack.
Remove the decorator's backoff and retry immediately, since the SDK's internal backoff already spaces the calls and an outer delay only adds latency on top of it.

explanation: The Anthropic client libraries already retry transient failures, rate limits included, with progressive delays up to a configurable number of attempts. Wrapping them in an application retry loop multiplies the attempts (outer attempts times SDK attempts) instead of capping them, which deepens a rate limit, so the rule is to decide where retries live and never let two layers retry the same failure without knowing about each other. Analogy: a waiter re-sends a stuck order to a swamped kitchen three times, while the manager, unaware, tells the waiter to try five times; the kitchen ends up with fifteen copies of one ticket at its busiest moment. Raising the decorator's cap so it outlasts the SDK is tempting, but a larger outer cap makes the multiplication worse, because the problem is two uncoordinated layers, not an undersized cap.

distractor_explanations.A: The SDK does retry transient failures, including rate limits. This change rests on a false premise and keeps two layers retrying other errors.
distractor_explanations.C: A larger outer cap makes the multiplication worse. The problem is two uncoordinated retry layers, not an undersized cap.
distractor_explanations.D: Immediate outer retries count against the same limit and deepen it. The course warns that instant retries make rate limits worse.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Hard Tier)
prompt: A developer sends a signed contract to the Messages API as base64 and receives a 400 validation error. Which content block is correctly structured for a PDF?

options.text: `{"type": "image", "source": {"type": "base64", "media_type": "application/pdf", "data": "<b64>"}, "title": "msa.pdf"}`
`{"type": "file", "source": {"type": "base64", "media_type": "application/pdf", "data": "<b64>"}, "filename": "signed-msa.pdf"}`
`{"type": "document", "name": "msa.pdf", "source": {"type": "pdf", "media_type": "application/pdf", "data": "<b64>"}}`
`{"type": "document", "source": {"type": "base64", "media_type": "application/pdf", "data": "<b64>"}, "title": "msa.pdf"}`

explanation: PDFs are sent in a `document` block, whose `source` follows the same pattern as images: base64 with a `media_type` of `application/pdf`, a URL, or a Files API `file_id`. A document block has no required `name` field; `title` (a readable name) and `context` (extra metadata) are optional, and there is no `file` block type at all. Analogy: at the post office, letters and parcels can carry identical postage, but they go into different slots; a contract dropped down the parcel chute because its stamps look the same is still bounced, just as a PDF in an `image` block fails even with a correct base64 source. The image-block option is the tempting one because its source structure matches exactly, but PDFs must use the document type.

distractor_explanations.A: PDFs are sent in a document block, not an image block, even though the source structure looks the same.
distractor_explanations.B: There is no file content block type. PDFs use the document type, with an optional `title` rather than a `filename`.
distractor_explanations.C: Inline bytes use a source of type base64, not pdf, and `name` is not a document block field; the optional readable name is `title`.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Hard Tier)
prompt: A customer has called Claude for two years through Amazon Bedrock's `InvokeModel` API with ARN-versioned model identifiers. Their new agent code is written against the Messages API and relies on broad feature parity with the first-party API. Inference and data must stay inside their configured AWS boundary. Which integration and model reference fit?

options.text: Claude in Amazon Bedrock, which serves the Messages API at `/anthropic/v1/messages` with broad parity, keeps data inside AWS, and pins the `anthropic.`-prefixed model ID.
Claude Platform on AWS, because it is billed through the customer's AWS account and uses Anthropic's own model IDs and lifecycle, giving the closest parity with the first-party API.
Claude on Amazon Bedrock (legacy) through `Converse`, which is Bedrock's Messages-compatible interface and the recommended route for new agent code on AWS.
Claude in Amazon Bedrock, pinned with the same model ID string the first-party API uses (for example `claude-opus-4-8`) so the agent code ports without changes.

explanation: The course separates three AWS routes. Claude in Amazon Bedrock offers the Messages API at `/anthropic/v1/messages` with broad feature parity, keeps data inside the customer's AWS boundary, and pins with the `anthropic.`-prefixed model ID. Claude on Amazon Bedrock (legacy) uses InvokeModel or Converse with ARN-versioned identifiers, and Claude Platform on AWS uses Anthropic model IDs but runs inference outside the AWS boundary. Analogy: a hotel chain offers three stays: its modern hotel inside your gated resort, booked with the resort's own room codes; the resort's old booking desk with legacy forms; or its hotel just outside the gate, billed to your resort account but physically beyond the wall. Claude Platform on AWS is tempting for its Anthropic IDs and AWS billing, but its inference runs outside the AWS boundary, breaking the residency constraint.

distractor_explanations.B: Claude Platform on AWS runs inference on Anthropic-operated infrastructure outside the AWS boundary, which breaks the stated residency constraint.
distractor_explanations.C: `Converse` and `InvokeModel` are the legacy integration with ARN-versioned identifiers. The Messages API integration is Claude in Amazon Bedrock.
distractor_explanations.D: Using Anthropic's own ID format is how Claude Platform on AWS pins models. Claude in Amazon Bedrock pins the `anthropic.`-prefixed full model ID.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Hard Tier)
prompt: A regulated EU insurer has standardized on Microsoft Foundry and wants two Claude models there: one listed as Hosted on Azure and one listed as Hosted on Anthropic. Their requirement is that inference stays on EU infrastructure under their Azure agreement. What should the developer conclude?

options.text: Both models qualify, because any Claude model consumed through Foundry inherits the customer's Azure data-residency terms regardless of where its inference actually runs.
Only the Azure-hosted model qualifies, because it runs inference end to end on Azure; the Anthropic-hosted one fails EU residency. Confirm the split with Microsoft.
Neither model qualifies, because Claude on any third-party platform always runs on Anthropic infrastructure, so the insurer must move the workload to Bedrock or Vertex AI.
Both qualify as long as the Foundry resource is created in an EU region, as the resource's region then pins the inference location for every model it hosts.

explanation: Microsoft Foundry offers Claude in two hosting forms. Hosted on Azure models run inference end to end on Azure infrastructure, while Hosted on Anthropic models run on Anthropic-operated infrastructure and do not satisfy EU regional residency, so residency depends on the hosting form of each specific model, and the course says to confirm the current split with Microsoft before committing a regulated workload. Analogy: a local travel agency sells two tours in the same brochure; one runs on the agency's own coaches inside the country, the other is handed to a foreign operator, so booking both at the same local office does not keep both inside the border. Assuming both qualify because the Foundry resource sits in an EU region is tempting, but the resource region does not override a model's hosting form.

distractor_explanations.A: Foundry hosting is set per model, and Anthropic-hosted Foundry models do not run inference on Azure infrastructure.
distractor_explanations.C: Hosted-on-Azure models run inference end to end on Azure, so rejecting both is wrong.
distractor_explanations.D: The resource region does not override a model's hosting form; Anthropic-hosted models still fail EU regional residency.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Hard Tier)
prompt: A federal contractor must run a Claude workload at FedRAMP High, and procurement has shortlisted five routes. Which TWO are authorized routes according to the course? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Claude for Government (C4G), which holds a direct FedRAMP High authorization through Palantir Federal Cloud Service – Supporting Services.
Claude via Amazon Bedrock GovCloud, which is approved for FedRAMP High and DoD IL4/5 workloads run by US federal agencies.
The first-party Claude API under a Zero Data Retention agreement, which takes stored data out of the authorization's scope.
Claude Enterprise bought through AWS Marketplace, since it is provisioned and billed inside the agency's existing AWS account and inherits its controls.
Claude Platform on AWS in a US region, since inference billed through AWS inherits the account's FedRAMP authorization.

explanation: The course lists three authorized routes as of publication: Claude for Government (C4G), with a direct FedRAMP High authorization through Palantir FedCloud (PFCS-SS); Claude via Amazon Bedrock GovCloud, approved for FedRAMP High and DoD IL4/5; and Claude via Vertex AI Assured Workloads. Claude Enterprise on AWS Marketplace is explicitly not FedRAMP authorized, and teams should verify current status at trust.anthropic.com before configuring anything. Analogy: a restricted building site admits only contractors holding a specific safety licence; a crew is not licensed just because it was hired through the site owner's usual supplier catalogue, and a crew promising to throw away its notes afterwards still has no licence. Claude Enterprise via AWS Marketplace is the tempting pick because it is billed inside the agency's AWS account, but the course states it is not FedRAMP authorized.

distractor_explanations.C: ZDR is a retention arrangement, not a FedRAMP authorization. The commercial endpoint is not an authorized route.
distractor_explanations.D: The course states that Claude Enterprise on AWS Marketplace is not FedRAMP authorized.
distractor_explanations.E: Claude Platform on AWS runs inference on Anthropic-operated infrastructure outside the AWS boundary, and it is not listed as an authorized route.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Hard Tier)
prompt: A release reviewer audits model references in three services: Service X uses `"sonnet"`, Service Y uses `"claude-haiku-4-5"`, and Service Z uses `"claude-haiku-4-5-20251001"`. Policy says no service may use a reference that can resolve to a new snapshot without a code change. Under the course's versioning guidance, which services violate the policy?

options.text: Only X, because an identifier that names both a model family and a version number, such as `claude-haiku-4-5`, already resolves to one fixed snapshot.
X and Y, because `sonnet` is an alias and `claude-haiku-4-5` is a pre-4.6 ID missing its date suffix, so it can move; only Z is a pinned snapshot.
All three, because pinning is configured in the platform console rather than in the model string, so every string reference tracks the latest snapshot.
Only Z, because date-suffixed identifiers refer to retired snapshots that the API silently redirects to the family's current version.

explanation: Aliases such as `opus` or `sonnet` move over time and can resolve to different versions on different platforms. For models before 4.6, a pinned reference needs the ID plus a date suffix (for example `claude-haiku-4-5-20251001`), while for Claude 4.6 and later the model ID alone pins a snapshot; pinning makes an upstream update a deliberate change, and the convention should be confirmed at build time. Analogy: asking a mechanic for 'the latest brake pads' or just 'the 4.5 pads' lets the parts counter hand over whichever revision is current, whereas quoting the full part number with its production date gets the identical pad every time. Treating `claude-haiku-4-5` as fixed because it names a family and version is tempting, but for pre-4.6 models pinning requires the date suffix, so without it the ID behaves as an alias.

distractor_explanations.A: For models before 4.6, pinning requires the date suffix. Without it, the identifier behaves as an alias.
distractor_explanations.C: A pinned full model ID in the request is what fixes the snapshot. The course shows the date-suffixed ID as the pinned form.
distractor_explanations.D: For pre-4.6 models the date-suffixed ID is the pinned form, which is exactly the course's example of fixing the version.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Hard Tier)
prompt: A law firm's application calls the first-party Claude API from inside its own environment, authenticated through SSO via a firm-approved LLM gateway. For privilege audits, compliance asks where the record of prompts, responses, and tool-call payloads will come from. What is the accurate answer?

options.text: A PostToolUse hook in the firm's Claude Code settings captures the full conversation, including prompts and responses from the application's own API calls.
Anthropic's compliance tooling records prompts, responses, and tool payloads for every direct API request, so the firm only needs to request a periodic export for audits.
The application must log conversations itself and route them to an approved destination; Anthropic does not capture that content by default on direct API traffic.
Turning on Zero Data Retention produces an auditable retention record for each request, which gives compliance the per-request evidence that privilege audits require.

explanation: On direct API traffic, Anthropic does not capture Compliance Conversation content (prompts, responses, and tool call payloads) by default, so the organization must log it in its own application layer and send it to an approved destination. The course's surviving privilege pattern is direct API calls from the firm's own application, authenticated via SSO and routed through an approved gateway with full request and response logging. Analogy: a courier delivers your sealed envelopes without photocopying what is inside them; if your office needs a record of every letter it sent, your own mailroom keeps that log before handing the envelopes over. Assuming Anthropic's compliance tooling records everything and only needs an export request is tempting, but the course states this content is not captured by default on direct API traffic.

distractor_explanations.A: Claude Code hooks govern Claude Code sessions. They do not record traffic from a separate application calling the API.
distractor_explanations.B: The course states that this conversation content is not captured by Anthropic by default on direct API traffic.
distractor_explanations.D: ZDR minimizes what is retained; it does not produce the firm's audit record. Logging belongs in the application layer.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Hard Tier)
prompt: A digital-health startup has a BAA with Anthropic covering a dedicated HIPAA-enabled organization. To move fast, the team plans to (1) iterate on prompts containing PHI in the Console Workbench and (2) upload patient PDFs once through the Files API beta and reference them by `file_id` in production. What should the developer flag?

options.text: Only the Workbench step, because the Files API is part of the core API surface and is covered automatically once the organization has been HIPAA-enabled.
Both, because the BAA does not extend to Console or Workbench use or to beta features such as the Files API, so PHI must stay on covered API features.
Neither, because once the organization is HIPAA-enabled the BAA extends to every surface that organization can reach, Console and beta endpoints included.
Only the Files API step; the Workbench runs inside the HIPAA-enabled organization, so any PHI entered there falls under the same BAA coverage.

explanation: Anthropic arranges first-party BAA coverage through a dedicated HIPAA-enabled organization, but the course is explicit that the BAA does not cover Console, Workbench, beta features, or consumer plans, and that not all API features are covered. PHI workflows therefore have to avoid both the Workbench and beta features like the Files API unless current eligibility documentation says otherwise. Analogy: a hotel's insurance covers guests in the rooms and the restaurant, but not the rooftop still under construction or the staff test kitchen; being a registered guest does not extend cover to every area your key card happens to open. Flagging only the Workbench step is tempting because the Files API feels like core API surface, but it is in beta, and the BAA excludes beta features.

distractor_explanations.A: The BAA excludes beta features, and the Files API is in beta.
distractor_explanations.C: The BAA's scope is not "everything the organization can reach." Console, Workbench, and beta features are explicitly excluded, so the developer must verify eligibility per feature.
distractor_explanations.D: The course explicitly lists Console and Workbench as outside BAA coverage.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Hard Tier)
prompt: During a customer engagement, a developer fixes a pagination bug in a widely used open-source MCP server and also writes a general retry helper around it. They want to contribute the fix. Which plan matches the course's contribution guidance?

options.text: Open the PR right away with the fix and a test, and raise licensing with the customer only if the maintainer asks about provenance during the review.
Open a PR on the server's repository with the fix, the retry helper, and a refactor of the pagination module, so maintainers can see the full context of the improvement.
Clear the right to contribute the engagement code, then open a focused PR on the server's own repository with only the fix, an example, a test, and stated assumptions.
Submit the fix and the retry helper together to the Claude Cookbook as one example, since the Cookbook is the central channel for contributions to the Claude ecosystem.

explanation: Contributions go through the channel built for their shape: open-source MCP servers and tools have their own repositories, while the Cookbook takes focused reference examples. Maintainers accept what they can verify, meaning code that does one thing, an example that shows it running, a test that proves it, and stated assumptions, and licensing and attribution for engagement code are a gate that comes before any technical review. Analogy: a school science fair takes one project per entry, with a demonstration and results, and first requires a signed permission slip; a student who arrives without the slip, or tapes three unrelated projects onto one board, is turned away before the judges look. Opening the PR now and raising licensing only if asked is tempting, but an engagement licensing constraint can block the merge regardless of code quality.

distractor_explanations.A: Rights and attribution come before technical review. An engagement licensing constraint can block the merge regardless of code quality.
distractor_explanations.B: A sprawling contribution forces the reviewer to reconstruct intent. The code should do one thing.
distractor_explanations.D: The Cookbook is for focused reference implementations. A fix to an MCP server belongs in that server's own repository, and bundling the helper makes the change harder to verify.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Hard Tier)
prompt: A service-account credential for an internal ticketing API is used by four services and two CI pipelines. Security wants a design that limits exposure and makes rotation cheap. Which TWO practices does the course recommend? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Store the credential in each service's `.claude/settings.local.json`, because that file is git-ignored and therefore keeps the value out of repository history entirely.
Rotate only when the credential expires or a consumer reports a 401, to avoid breaking the consumers that have the value hardcoded in their configuration.
Scope the credential narrowly and keep a record of which services use it, so a leak reaches less and rotation surfaces no forgotten consumers.
Keep the credential in a managed secret store that serves it to authorized callers at runtime and records reads, so one rotation reaches every consumer.
Base64-encode the credential inside each service's committed configuration file so the raw value is never readable in plain text during code review.

explanation: The course's three practices are separation, storage, and rotation: keep values out of the configuration that references them, use a secret store when a credential is shared or must be audited so one rotation reaches every consumer, and rotate on a schedule and after suspected exposure. Scoping each credential narrowly and recording which services use it make rotation cheaper. Analogy: a hotel keeps one master key in a front-desk safe that logs every sign-out, instead of cutting copies for each department; when the lock changes, only the key in the safe is swapped, and the sign-out list means no department is left locked out. Storing the value in each service's git-ignored `settings.local.json` is tempting, but it still puts the secret on disk and multiplies the copies.

distractor_explanations.A: A per-machine settings file still stores the secret on disk and multiplies the copies. The course puts shared secrets in a secret store and keeps them out of configuration files.
distractor_explanations.B: Rotate on a schedule and immediately after any suspected exposure. Consumers that read the value by reference rotate without code changes.
distractor_explanations.E: Encoding is not protection. A committed value lives in history and must be treated as compromised.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Hard Tier)
prompt: A product team runs a long-lived agent on Claude Managed Agents and references it by agent ID across many sessions. They want new sessions to use an updated compliance-review skill, so a developer adds the skill to the payload that starts each session. New sessions do not use it. What is the correct change?

options.text: Update the agent definition itself, because Managed Agents attach skills when the versioned agent resource is defined, not when a session starts.
Commit the SKILL.md to the repository's `.claude/skills` directory, so the managed sandbox discovers it from the filesystem when each new session starts.
Set `settingSources` to include `project` in the session configuration so the hosted loop loads skills from the project's filesystem sources.
Send the `code-execution-2025-08-25` and `skills-2025-10-02` beta headers with the session request, which is what turns on per-session skills.

explanation: With Claude Managed Agents, you define the agent once as a versioned API resource that names the model, system prompt, tools, MCP servers, and skills, and Anthropic loads the skill server-side when the agent runs. Skills are attached when the agent resource is defined, not at session time, so you change which skills are available by updating the agent definition. Analogy: a building site works from the approved blueprint on file; a note handed to the crew at the gate one morning does not change what gets built, and the only way to add a room is to revise the blueprint itself. Committing a SKILL.md to the `.claude/skills` directory is tempting, but Managed Agents load skills server-side from the agent resource, with no filesystem discovery on the caller's side.

distractor_explanations.B: Managed Agents load skills server-side from the agent resource. There is no filesystem discovery step on the caller's side.
distractor_explanations.C: `settingSources` is an Agent SDK setting that controls filesystem loading in your own process. It does not apply to an Anthropic-hosted agent resource.
distractor_explanations.D: Those headers belong to the Messages API skills path. Managed Agents attach skills in the agent definition.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Hard Tier)
prompt: A backend service wants a review-checklist skill to run as part of a Messages API request. The request is rejected because the skills configuration is not recognized. Which beta headers does the course specify for this path?

options.text: `skills-2025-10-02` alone; the skills header enables both skill loading and the runtime environment the skill executes in.
`managed-agents-2026-04-01` and `skills-2025-10-02`, because skills are an agent capability that executes in the managed sandbox.
`mcp-client-2025-11-20` and `skills-2025-10-02`; skills are delivered to the Messages API through the MCP connector toolset.
`code-execution-2025-08-25` and `skills-2025-10-02`, because skills invoked through the API run inside the code execution container.

explanation: Skills on the Messages API are in beta and need two headers, `code-execution-2025-08-25` and `skills-2025-10-02`, because they run inside the code execution container rather than in the calling application's environment. Beta headers are versioned and change as features mature, so check current values before relying on them in production. Analogy: boarding an international flight takes two documents, a visa for the destination (the skills header) and a boarding pass for the plane that carries you (the code execution header); the skill only runs once it is aboard the container, so a visa without a boarding pass leaves you at the gate. Sending `skills-2025-10-02` alone is tempting, but the course requires both headers, because the code execution container needs its own.

distractor_explanations.A: The course requires two headers. Skills on the API run inside the code execution container, which needs its own header.
distractor_explanations.B: The managed-agents header is for Claude Managed Agents endpoints, not for running a skill inside a Messages API request.
distractor_explanations.C: The mcp-client header enables the MCP connector's `mcp_toolset`. Skills do not travel through MCP.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Hard Tier)
prompt: A team is porting code from an older Claude model to one of the newest generation. The old request used `thinking: {"type": "enabled", "budget_tokens": 2048}` with `max_tokens: 4096`, and it worked. On the new model the same request returns a 400. Which change matches the course?

options.text: Move `budget_tokens` into `output_config` alongside the effort level, because the newest models consolidated all thinking controls under that one parameter.
Remove the `thinking` parameter and raise `max_tokens`, because the newest models always reason at maximum depth and only the output length needs configuring.
Raise `max_tokens` well above `budget_tokens`, because the 400 indicates the thinking budget consumed too large a share of the output limit on the new model.
Switch to adaptive thinking and tune depth with the effort setting, since `budget_tokens` is deprecated on these models and returns a 400 on any request using it.

explanation: On current models, reasoning is adaptive: the model decides when and how much to think, and you tune depth with an effort setting rather than a fixed token budget. The course states that `budget_tokens` is deprecated and returns a 400 on the newest model generations, and per-model thinking defaults vary, so confirm them at build time. Analogy: an old exam gave every student exactly twenty minutes of scratch time per question; the new exam board scraps the fixed timer and instead tells students how thorough to be, so a form still requesting a set number of scratch minutes is rejected at the door. Raising `max_tokens` well above `budget_tokens` is tempting because that was the old constraint, but on the newest generations the `budget_tokens` control itself is rejected.

distractor_explanations.A: Effort is a separate control; `budget_tokens` is not relocated anywhere. It is deprecated, so sending it under another parameter still sends a rejected control.
distractor_explanations.B: Defaults differ by model, and depth is tuned with effort. Dropping thinking configuration does not give calibrated reasoning.
distractor_explanations.C: That was an older-model constraint. On the newest generations the `budget_tokens` control itself is rejected.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Hard Tier)
prompt: An agent caches a 30,000-token system prompt and tool set using the default cache lifetime. Between steps it waits for an external approval that usually takes 10–15 minutes. Billing shows a cache write on almost every step and almost no cache reads. Which change best fits the course's caching guidance?

options.text: Set the breakpoint's `ttl` to `1h`; one-hour writes cost 2x instead of 1.25x, but the entry survives the gaps, so later steps read at about 0.1x.
Keep the default lifetime, because each cache read resets the five-minute clock, so the prefix stays warm across the approval wait without any changes.
Switch to automatic caching mode, which manages breakpoints for you and extends the cache lifetime as the conversation grows across steps.
Add more breakpoints, up to the limit of four, so that at least one of the cached segments survives the gap between steps and the next request can read from it.

explanation: The default cache lifetime is five minutes from the last read, which suits requests arriving every few minutes; the course points to the one-hour lifetime (`ttl: 1h`) for workloads with longer gaps, such as an agent that pauses between steps. Writes cost 1.25x (5-minute) or 2x (1-hour) base input and reads about 0.1x, so when the entry expires before the next request you pay the write premium again with no read benefit. Analogy: a hotel holds your room for five minutes after you last check in at the desk; if your meetings run fifteen minutes, the room is released every time and you pay the booking fee again, whereas paying a little more for a one-hour hold keeps it waiting. Keeping the default because reads reset the clock is tempting, but reads only reset it when they arrive, and with 10–15 minute gaps none do.

distractor_explanations.B: Reads reset the clock only when they happen. With 10–15 minute gaps, no read arrives in time and the entry expires.
distractor_explanations.C: Automatic mode manages where breakpoints go, not how long entries live. It does not keep the cache alive across long gaps.
distractor_explanations.D: More breakpoints do not extend lifetime. Every segment on the default lifetime expires five minutes after its last read.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Hard Tier)
prompt: A team puts one `cache_control` breakpoint on the last system block. Every request's usage shows a large `cache_creation_input_tokens` value and `cache_read_input_tokens: 0`. The system prompt text is a fixed constant. Tool definitions are assembled at startup by iterating over plugin modules found on the filesystem, and discovery order varies between worker processes. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: Cache reads are only reported from the second request carrying the same session identifier, and the team never sends one, so every read is recorded as a write.
A breakpoint on the system prompt caches only the system prompt itself, so tool order is irrelevant and the system prompt must be below the per-model minimum length.
The cached prefix includes the tools, since requests are processed tools, then system, then messages; any change in tool order between workers alters that prefix.
Each worker process keeps its own isolated cache, so hits only occur when the same process serves the follow-up; pinning each session to one worker would fix it.

explanation: Requests are processed in a fixed order of tools, system prompt, and messages, and a breakpoint caches everything up to and including the marked block. The match is on an exact prefix, so a single difference before the breakpoint, such as tool definitions in a different order, invalidates it and forces a new write; sorting the tool definitions deterministically restores cache reads. Analogy: a bank fast-tracks a recurring payment form only when every line from the top down to the signature matches the stored copy exactly; if two clerks list the same payees in a different order, the form looks new and is processed from scratch every time. Blaming a too-short system prompt is tempting, but a breakpoint caches the whole prefix up to that block, and tools come before the system prompt.

distractor_explanations.A: There is no session identifier for caching. A hit depends on an exact prefix match within the cache lifetime.
distractor_explanations.B: A breakpoint caches everything up to and including that block, and tools come before the system prompt in processing order.
distractor_explanations.D: The cache matches on identical prefix content, not on which client process sent it.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Hard Tier)
prompt: A quality-inspection pipeline sends a 1,400 × 700 pixel photo with each request, and the team is estimating context cost. Which TWO statements are accurate? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Image cost depends on encoded file size, so recompressing the JPEG to half as many bytes roughly halves the visual-token count for each request.
Any image above the model's maximum native resolution is rejected with a 400, so the pipeline must resize every photo before it can be sent.
Referencing the photo by Files API `file_id` shrinks the request payload, but the image still uses its visual tokens on every request.
Each image carries a flat per-image token charge regardless of resolution, so only the number of images per request changes the cost.
Assuming it is within the model's resolution limits, it costs about ⌈1400/28⌉ × ⌈700/28⌉ = 50 × 25 = 1,250 visual tokens per request.

explanation: Claude views images in 28×28-pixel patches, so an image costs ⌈width/28⌉ × ⌈height/28⌉ visual tokens; images above a model's resolution limits are downscaled first, and those limits differ by tier. The Files API removes repeated payload by referencing a `file_id`, but it does not change how many visual tokens the image uses in context. Analogy: a tiler prices a floor by how many square tiles it takes to cover it, so a floor fifty tiles long and twenty-five wide always needs 1,250 tiles; the price depends on the floor's dimensions, not on how heavy the delivery was, and storing the tiles on site saves the delivery trip but not the tiling. Recompressing the JPEG to fewer bytes is tempting, but visual tokens are calculated from pixel dimensions, not from byte size.

distractor_explanations.A: Visual tokens are calculated from pixel dimensions in 28×28 patches, not from byte size.
distractor_explanations.B: Oversized images are downscaled before processing, and the formula then runs on the scaled dimensions.
distractor_explanations.D: Cost scales with dimensions; a high-resolution original can cost many times as much as a thumbnail.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Hard Tier)
prompt: A due-diligence tool answers broad questions by fanning out across many independent company filings. An orchestrator-worker design clearly beats a single agent on the team's eval, but the token bill is well over budget. Every agent currently runs on the top model tier. Which change best follows the course?

options.text: Keep the fan-out, but run the lead on the capable model and the subagents on a cheaper tier, then confirm on the eval that quality holds.
Collapse to a single agent with a larger context window; the multi-agent token multiplier is not justified when one agent can read the filings in sequence.
Stream each subagent's output to the lead so synthesis can start early, which avoids paying for the remainder of each subagent's response.
Double the number of subagents so each one reads fewer filings, which shortens each individual context and therefore lowers the total token count.

explanation: Anthropic's reported orchestrator-worker results show a substantial quality gain on parallelizable research at roughly 15x the tokens of a normal chat. When a task really does split into independent parts, the course keeps the pattern and reduces the multiplier by using a more capable model as the lead and cheaper models for the subagents, then verifying on the eval. Analogy: a building site keeps an experienced foreman to plan the job and check the work, but the crews laying bricks on separate walls do not all need to be paid chief-engineer rates, and the walls still have to pass inspection afterwards. Collapsing to a single agent is tempting because it removes the multiplier, but this task genuinely splits and the eval shows fan-out winning, so the lever is model choice per role.

distractor_explanations.B: This task genuinely splits into independent parts, and the eval shows fan-out winning, so the multiplier is justified. The lever is model choice per role.
distractor_explanations.C: Streaming changes perceived latency, not how many tokens are generated or billed.
distractor_explanations.D: Each additional subagent spends its own tokens against its own context, so more workers raise the multiplier.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Hard Tier)
prompt: A user-facing summarizer's design document sets a floor: p95 latency under 4 seconds, at most 3 retries per dependency, and an eval score no lower than the pinned baseline. A proposal to move from Sonnet to Haiku more than halves the cost; on the eval it scores two points below baseline, and p95 latency improves. What should the team do?

options.text: Ship it, because latency improved and the saving is large, and a two-point drop is within normal judge noise for summarization tasks.
Reject it as proposed, because it drops the eval below the pinned baseline that defines the floor, and look for savings that keep the score at or above it.
Lower the baseline to the new score so the gate passes, since the baseline should reflect the cheapest configuration the team intends to run in production.
Ship it to all traffic behind a feature flag and revisit if users complain, since real-world feedback is more reliable than an offline eval score.

explanation: The course says to define the reliability floor first, meaning the retry budget, the latency ceiling, and a pinned eval baseline, and then tune cost above it, never below. A cheaper model is acceptable if it fits inside the floor; here the eval gate fails, so the proposal is rejected regardless of the savings or the latency improvement. Analogy: a relay squad has a qualifying time; a runner who is cheaper to bring and quicker off the blocks but finishes two tenths over the mark does not make the team, and the officials do not move the qualifying time to fit him. Lowering the baseline to the new score is tempting because the gate then passes, but moving the floor to fit a cheaper model defeats its purpose: reliability is the fixed constraint, and cost is optimized underneath it.

distractor_explanations.A: The pinned baseline exists to make the floor checkable. A change that fails the gate does not ship, and judge noise is handled through calibration, not by waiving the gate.
distractor_explanations.C: Moving the floor to fit a cheaper model defeats its purpose. Reliability is the fixed constraint, and cost is optimized underneath it.
distractor_explanations.D: That lets the louder cost pressure win and discovers the floor only after crossing it, which is the order the course warns against.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Hard Tier)
prompt: A chat feature uses Sonnet because an eval shows Haiku missing the quality bar. Each prompt is short (about 300 tokens) and unique per user. Users complain about a blank screen for roughly three seconds before a long answer appears all at once. Which lever addresses the complaint without changing quality or cost?

options.text: Add a prompt-caching breakpoint on the system prompt, so the model skips reprocessing it and the time to first token falls on every request.
Stream the response so the first tokens reach the user as they are generated; total time and cost stay the same, but the perceived wait drops.
Generate the first sentence with Haiku and the remainder with Sonnet, so the user sees text sooner without fully changing the model.
Move the feature to the Message Batches API, which lowers per-token cost and processes large numbers of requests faster in aggregate.

explanation: Streaming changes how latency is perceived: the first token reaches the user as soon as it is ready instead of after the full response, even when total generation time and cost are identical. With the model fixed by the eval and no stable prefix to cache, streaming is the lever that fixes the blank-screen complaint. Analogy: a restaurant that brings each course out as soon as it is plated, instead of holding the whole meal until dessert is ready, gets food in front of the diner sooner without the kitchen cooking any faster or the bill changing. Adding a caching breakpoint is tempting because caching can cut time to first token, but these prompts are short and unique per user, so there is no stable prefix above the caching minimum to reuse.

distractor_explanations.A: The prompt is short and unique per user, so there is no stable prefix above the caching minimum to reuse.
distractor_explanations.C: Generating part of the answer on a model that misses the bar changes quality and adds orchestration; streaming solves perceived latency directly.
distractor_explanations.D: Batching trades latency for cost and can take up to 24 hours, which is wrong for a user waiting live.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Hard Tier)
prompt: A support-ticket labeler runs on the top model tier with high reasoning effort and returns one of five labels. Users wait synchronously on each label. An eval shows a cheaper tier holding the quality bar without extended thinking. Which TWO changes reduce cost without breaking the workload's constraints? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Step down to the cheaper tier for this call, because the eval shows the quality change is acceptable for this particular task.
Enable streaming, because streamed responses are billed only for the tokens the client actually reads before closing the connection.
Call `count_tokens` before each request; requests that were pre-counted by the endpoint are billed at a reduced input-token rate.
Turn off extended thinking (or lower effort) for this call; reasoning is wasted on classification, and thinking tokens bill at the output rate.
Submit the labeling requests through the Message Batches API, which cuts the per-token price roughly in half for the same model and prompt.

explanation: Reasoning earns its cost on hard, multi-step problems and is wasted on lookups and classification, and thinking tokens cost the same as output tokens. Moving down a tier is correct when an eval shows the quality drop is acceptable for that task. Batching is ruled out because a user is waiting, and neither streaming nor token counting changes what is billed. Analogy: marking a five-option multiple-choice quiz does not need the head examiner writing pages of notes on every answer; a teaching assistant with the answer key can do it once a sample check shows their marks match, and paying examiner rates for unneeded notes is waste. Sending the labels through the Message Batches API is tempting for its roughly half price, but users wait synchronously and batch latency can reach 24 hours.

distractor_explanations.B: Streaming changes perceived latency, not billing. Every generated token is billed.
distractor_explanations.C: `count_tokens` measures the request without running inference; it does not discount the request that follows.
distractor_explanations.E: Users wait synchronously, and batch latency can reach 24 hours, so this breaks the workload's main constraint.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Hard Tier)
prompt: On one of the newest models with adaptive thinking on, an analyst notices that responses contain no readable reasoning, yet `usage.output_tokens` is several times larger than the visible answer. Finance asks whether they are paying for reasoning they cannot see. What is accurate?

options.text: Yes, but only when `budget_tokens` is set explicitly; adaptive thinking is not billed because the model decides the amount of reasoning itself.
Yes. The reasoning is still generated and billed at the output rate, because display settings never change billing, even though thinking is omitted by default.
No. When thinking content is omitted from the response, the model skips the reasoning pass entirely, so the extra output tokens must be hidden tool-call arguments.
No. Thinking tokens are billed at the input rate as context fed back into the model, so the output count covers only the visible answer and its formatting.

explanation: The course makes two relevant points: thinking tokens cost the same as output tokens, and on the newest models thinking content is omitted from responses by default, so you request summarized display when you need to show it. Display is separate from generation; hidden reasoning is still reasoning you pay for, which is why effort should be matched to the task. Analogy: a mechanic spends an hour diagnosing your car and hands back only a one-line note saying what was fixed; you never saw the diagnostic work, but the labour still appears on the invoice. Concluding that omitted thinking means the model skipped reasoning is tempting, but omission affects only what is displayed, not whether the model reasoned, so the extra output tokens are the reasoning itself.

distractor_explanations.A: `budget_tokens` is deprecated on the newest models, and adaptive thinking still produces billed thinking tokens.
distractor_explanations.C: Omission affects what is displayed, not whether the model reasoned. The extra tokens are the reasoning.
distractor_explanations.D: The course states that thinking tokens cost the same as output tokens.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Hard Tier)
prompt: A travel-rebooking assistant handles disruptions whose details vary unpredictably (strikes, weather, missed connections, partial refunds), and the right sequence of lookups and seat holds cannot be enumerated in advance. Issuing a ticket is irreversible and charges the customer. Which design matches the course?

options.text: A fixed workflow that enumerates every disruption type as its own branch, giving irreversible actions the step-level guardrails only workflows can provide.
An agent loop with the full booking toolset and a system-prompt instruction to confirm with the customer before it issues any ticket on their behalf.
An agent loop with a constrained toolset for the open-ended rebooking, plus a human checkpoint that pauses before every run of the irreversible ticket-issuance tool.
An agent loop that issues tickets autonomously, with a human reviewing all issued tickets in a daily audit so mistakes are caught and refunded.

explanation: Choose an agent when you can specify the goal and the tools but not the path, and a workflow when you can enumerate the steps. Whichever you choose, a tool that can take an irreversible action needs a human-in-the-loop checkpoint before it runs, placed in the loop at design time rather than left to a prompt instruction or a later audit. Analogy: a bank teller may freely look up accounts and draft whatever arrangement an unusual case needs, but the vault will not release cash until a manager turns a second key; a poster reminding tellers to double-check, or an audit the next morning, cannot stop a wrong payout. A full toolset plus a system-prompt instruction to confirm is tempting, but a prompt instruction is not an enforced checkpoint; the gate belongs before the irreversible tool executes.

distractor_explanations.A: The path cannot be enumerated, so a workflow breaks the first time an input falls outside its branches. Guardrails can be added to an agent through a checkpoint.
distractor_explanations.B: A prompt instruction is not an enforced checkpoint. The gate belongs in the loop, before the irreversible tool executes.
distractor_explanations.D: Reviewing after an irreversible charge is too late; the checkpoint has to come before the destructive call.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Hard Tier)
prompt: An agent loop exits when the assistant's text contains the word `DONE`, which the system prompt asks Claude to write when the task is complete. On some inputs the loop never sees `DONE` and keeps requesting tool calls until the job is killed hours later. Which fix best follows the course?

options.text: Add `DONE` as a stop sequence so the API halts generation the moment the keyword appears, which guarantees the loop sees it and exits cleanly.
Raise `max_tokens` so that each turn has enough room to finish the whole task and reach the `DONE` keyword before the response is cut off.
Strengthen the system prompt so it states in capitals that Claude must always finish with `DONE`, and repeat that instruction in every user turn of the loop.
Drive the loop from `stop_reason` (continue on `tool_use`, stop on `end_turn`) and add an iteration and token budget, so stopping never relies on a keyword.

explanation: The course's loop checklist requires an exit condition that does not depend on Claude volunteering to stop, because without one the agent keeps requesting tools beyond what the task needs. The loop should continue while `stop_reason` is `tool_use`, stop on `end_turn`, and enforce a hard cap on iterations or budget as a guard against runaways. Analogy: a football match ends on the referee's whistle, backed by a fixed limit on added time, not when a player shouts that the team is done; if no player ever shouts, a match that waited for one would run all night. Adding `DONE` as a stop sequence is tempting because generation halts the instant the keyword appears, but it still relies on the model producing the keyword, so when it never appears the loop is just as unbounded.

distractor_explanations.A: A stop sequence still relies on the model producing the keyword. When it never appears, the loop is just as unbounded.
distractor_explanations.B: `max_tokens` limits one response's length. It neither caps iterations nor guarantees the keyword appears.
distractor_explanations.C: The course says the stopping criterion must not depend on Claude volunteering to stop, however firmly it is asked.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Hard Tier)
prompt: A team is comparing the three wiring paths for a production agent. Which TWO statements are accurate? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Claude Managed Agents sessions become eligible for Zero Data Retention when each session is deleted at the end of its run.
With the Agent SDK, the loop and context management run inside your own process, but your code still executes the tools the agent calls.
With Managed Agents, you define the agent once as a resource, reference it by ID, and stream results back over server-sent events.
The Agent SDK loads CLAUDE.md and project skills by default, so its filesystem configuration behaves exactly like the Claude Code CLI.
With a raw Messages API loop, the API supplies parallel tool handling and context management, leaving only the exit conditions to your own code.

explanation: The three wiring paths differ in how much of the runtime you own. In a raw Messages API loop you write everything: the loop, tool execution, context management, retries, and exit conditions. The Agent SDK runs the loop and context handling in your process while your code executes tools, with filesystem settings governed by `settingSources`. Claude Managed Agents run the loop and sandbox for you, from an agent resource referenced by ID, streaming results over server-sent events, but their server-side sessions are not currently ZDR or HIPAA BAA eligible. Analogy: cooking from scratch is the raw loop, a meal kit that plans the steps and portions while you still do the cooking is the SDK, and ordering from a restaurant that cooks and delivers is Managed Agents. Assuming the API supplies parallel tool handling and context management in a raw loop is tempting, but there you own everything.

distractor_explanations.A: Sessions are stateful and stored server-side, which is why Managed Agents are not currently eligible for ZDR or a HIPAA BAA.
distractor_explanations.D: Filesystem loading is controlled by `settingSources`, and the course says to set it explicitly rather than rely on a default.
distractor_explanations.E: In a raw loop you own everything: the loop, tool execution, context management, retries, and exit conditions.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Hard Tier)
prompt: A team prototyped an agent on the Agent SDK using code-level configuration and CLAUDE.md-based instructions. For production they want hours-long sessions and a managed sandbox, so they plan to move to Claude Managed Agents. The workload has no PHI and no ZDR requirement. What should they expect?

options.text: A re-expression step: the definition carries over conceptually but is rebuilt as a versioned API resource and called with the required beta header.
A rewrite of every tool, because Managed Agents can only call tools that are exposed through MCP servers hosted and operated by Anthropic.
No changes: Managed Agents read the same filesystem configuration through `settingSources`, so pointing the SDK at the hosted endpoint is enough.
A direct export: the SDK serializes its configuration, including CLAUDE.md, into a Managed Agents definition that then runs unchanged on the hosted loop.

explanation: A common progression is prototyping on the Agent SDK and moving to Managed Agents for production. The core agent definition carries over conceptually, but the format changes: the SDK uses code and filesystem configuration, while Managed Agents define the agent as a versioned API resource, so expect a re-expression step, and remember the product is in public beta behind the `managed-agents-2026-04-01` header. Analogy: a house designed on a builder's notepad sketches can be built for real, but the council will only accept it once it is redrawn in the registered-plan format; the design survives, the paperwork is rewritten. A direct export of the SDK configuration, CLAUDE.md included, is tempting, but the course says to expect a re-expression step rather than a direct export, because the two configuration formats differ.

distractor_explanations.B: The agent resource names its tools and MCP servers; the course does not limit Managed Agents to Anthropic-hosted MCP tools.
distractor_explanations.C: Managed Agents define the agent as an API resource, with no filesystem discovery; `settingSources` is an SDK setting.
distractor_explanations.D: The course says to expect a re-expression step, not a direct export, because the two configuration formats differ.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Hard Tier)
prompt: A claims-assistance agent runs as several stateless instances behind a load balancer. Consecutive turns from the same adjuster can land on different instances, and adjusters come back to the same claim over several days. Which memory scope fits?

options.text: Summarized memory kept in each instance's process memory and rebuilt whenever an instance restarts, so detail is lost only when a restart happens.
No persistent memory; load-balanced instances should be stateless by design, and adjusters can restate their claim context at the start of each day.
In-context memory, because the full conversation is resent on every request, so whichever instance receives a turn can rebuild state from the messages array.
External storage, written to a database and read back at session start or on demand, because the state must outlive sessions and be shared across instances.

explanation: The course's memory table says external storage is for state that must survive across sessions, move between users, or be shared across multiple agent instances, at the cost of retrieval latency and read/write logic. In-context state disappears when the session ends, and stateless loses exactly the continuity this agent needs. Analogy: a hotel with many front-desk clerks on rotating shifts keeps each guest's preferences in the central reservation system, not in one clerk's head, so whichever clerk greets a returning guest days later can look them up in seconds. In-context memory is tempting because the conversation is resent on every request, but the messages array lives in a session that ends, so it does not survive across days or move reliably between instances behind a load balancer.

distractor_explanations.A: Process-local memory is not shared across instances behind a load balancer. Summarized memory is persisted and injected at session start.
distractor_explanations.B: Stateless suits self-contained jobs. Here, follow-ups depend on earlier sessions.
distractor_explanations.C: The messages array lives in a session that ends. In-context state does not survive across days or move reliably between instances.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Hard Tier)
prompt: In Claude Code, a parent session has permission to run a deployment script and has loaded a custom `release-notes` skill. It delegates release-note drafting to a custom subagent defined in `.claude/agents` whose frontmatter lists no skills. What does the subagent start with?

options.text: No parent conversation history and no `release-notes` skill unless its own configuration lists it, but it does inherit the parent's permission context.
The loaded skills, because skills are session-wide, but not the conversation history; it also inherits the parent session's permission context.
A clean context with no skills and no inherited permissions, so it can run only the tools its own definition explicitly allows without prompting.
The parent's conversation history and loaded skills, but with permissions reset to the default mode so it has to prompt for each tool call it makes.

explanation: A subagent starts from a clean slate: it does not inherit the main conversation history, accumulated files, or skills, and a custom subagent that needs a skill must list it in its frontmatter. The course notes one thing that does carry over: the parent's permission context, which is not reset at delegation. Analogy: a substitute teacher arrives without the class's past lessons or the regular teacher's personal lesson plans, unless those are placed in the substitute's own folder, yet their key card opens the same rooms the regular teacher's did. Assuming skills are session-wide and therefore inherited is tempting, but subagents do not automatically inherit skills; the `release-notes` skill has to be listed explicitly in the subagent's configuration before it is available.

distractor_explanations.B: Subagents do not automatically inherit skills; the skill has to be listed explicitly in the subagent's configuration.
distractor_explanations.C: Subagents inherit the parent's permission context; only history and skills start clean.
distractor_explanations.D: This is reversed: subagents start without history or skills, and the permission context is not reset at delegation.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Hard Tier)
prompt: An infrastructure agent can read metrics, propose a remediation plan, scale services, and delete stale resources. Following the course's insertion-point guidance, where should human-in-the-loop checkpoints go? (Select TWO.)

options.text: After every metrics read, so an operator can confirm the data the agent saw before it starts reasoning over that data.
Once at session start, where the operator pre-approves every action the session will take in a single confirmation step.
Immediately after the delete tool returns, so the operator can verify exactly what was removed while the change is still fresh.
Before the delete tool executes, because removing resources is irreversible and a wrong call cannot be undone after it runs.
After the planning step and before execution begins, because a wrong plan fails even if every step executes correctly.

explanation: The course places HITL checkpoints by worst-case cost. Before a destructive tool call addresses high, irreversible risk; after a planning step addresses medium risk from a wrong plan; and on unexpected output (error flags, empty or out-of-range results) catches failures that retries won't fix. Gating harmless reads or reviewing after the fact misses the point of the checkpoint. Analogy: on a demolition site the safety officer signs off before the charges are fired, and the site manager reviews the demolition plan before crews begin, but nobody needs sign-off to glance at the survey drawings, and inspecting the rubble afterwards cannot rebuild the wrong building. Reviewing immediately after the delete tool returns is tempting because the change is fresh, but review after an irreversible action is too late; the checkpoint has to precede the destructive call.

distractor_explanations.A: Reads are low-stakes and reversible. Gating them adds latency without addressing the high-risk actions.
distractor_explanations.B: A single upfront approval cannot gate an action the agent has not proposed yet.
distractor_explanations.C: Reviewing after an irreversible action is too late; the checkpoint has to precede the destructive call.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Hard Tier)
prompt: A team can afford to try an orchestrator-worker design on exactly one of four workloads. Which workload best matches the conditions under which the course says the token multiplier pays off?

options.text: Compiling a competitive landscape from 30 unrelated vendor sites, where each site can be researched without waiting on any other.
Migrating a monolith's authentication module, where each refactoring step depends on the interfaces changed in the step before it.
Answering a single factual question against a stable product manual that many different users ask in slightly different words.
Classifying 200,000 short, independent support messages overnight into five labels, where every message can be handled in parallel.

explanation: An orchestrator-worker run costs roughly 15x the tokens of a single chat in Anthropic's reported case, because every subagent spends tokens in its own context. That pays off only when a task splits into independent parts that benefit from parallel exploration, such as research across separate sources, and it is wasted on tightly coupled work, simple lookups, and bulk single-call jobs that belong in a batch. Analogy: a travel guide's editor flies thirty reporters to thirty different cities at once because no city's report depends on another, then a lead writer stitches the guide together; flying a team out to answer one timetable question wastes the airfares. Classifying 200,000 messages is tempting because each one is independent, but those are high-volume, non-urgent single calls, which is a Message Batches job, not an agentic fan-out.

distractor_explanations.B: Tightly coupled coding work leaves subagents waiting on one another. The course says a single agent with good context wins there.
distractor_explanations.C: A one-pass retrieval answers a lookup. Fanning out would pay the multiplier for contexts the task never needed.
distractor_explanations.D: These are independent, high-volume, non-urgent single calls, which is a Message Batches job, not an agentic fan-out.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Hard Tier)
prompt: A contract-review assistant's system prompt reads `You are a helpful assistant for contracts.` Sessions rarely exceed 6,000 tokens. The assistant answers correctly in early turns, but later in sessions it starts giving tax advice and using a casual tone, neither of which the product allows. The output format stays correct throughout. Which missing piece does the course's diagnosis table point to?

options.text: Pruning and compaction, because the standing instructions are being crowded out by accumulated turns as each session grows longer.
Few-shot examples of correct contract reviews, so the model can see the exact shape and tone of a good answer and match it on every turn.
An output constraint naming the allowed fields and the stopping point, since the responses are going beyond what the user actually asked for.
A more specific system prompt that fixes role, scope, and tone as a contract for every response, since the drift is in content, not shape.

explanation: The course's diagnosis table maps each failure type to the missing technique. Content that drifts in scope or tone, getting worse deeper into a conversation, means the system prompt is missing or too vague to hold role, scope, and format steady across turns; wrong shape points to an output constraint, invented structure to few-shot examples, and edge-case breaks to a constraint for the variant. Analogy: a new hotel concierge told only to help the guests starts well, then drifts into giving tax tips and chatting casually, because nobody gave them a job description stating what they cover and how they speak, even though their booking forms stay perfectly filled in. An output constraint is tempting because the answers stray beyond the brief, but output constraints control form, and the form is correct here.

distractor_explanations.A: At under 6,000 tokens the context is not under pressure. The instructions never defined scope and tone in the first place.
distractor_explanations.B: Few-shot examples fix invented structure. The problem here is behavioral drift in content, not structure.
distractor_explanations.C: Output constraints control form, and the form is correct here. Scope and tone drift point to the system prompt.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Hard Tier)
prompt: A classifier prompt contains instructions, then three worked examples written as plain paragraphs (`Ticket: ... Label: ...`), then the real ticket. Sometimes Claude returns labels for the example tickets as well as the real one, or treats an example's wording as part of the instructions. What is the targeted fix?

options.text: Wrap each example in consistent tags such as `<sample_input>` and `<ideal_output>`, and the real ticket in its own tag, so that every boundary is unambiguous.
Move the three examples into the system prompt and keep the real ticket in the user turn, since role separation tells Claude which text is only an example.
Use the official tag names from Anthropic's reserved XML vocabulary, since Claude only treats text as bounded when it uses documented tag names.
Remove the examples and add a paragraph describing each label in more detail, because the examples are being misread as additional tasks to classify.

explanation: XML tags make the boundary unambiguous when a prompt mixes instructions, examples, and inputs. The course recommends wrapping few-shot examples in a consistent structure such as `<sample_input>` and `<ideal_output>`, with the real input in its own tag, so Claude does not read the examples as part of the task; descriptive tag names chosen for your content work best, and no reserved vocabulary is needed. Analogy: an exam paper that prints its worked examples in a shaded box labelled Example, and the real questions under a heading saying Answer these, stops students from answering the examples too or mistaking them for instructions. Removing the examples and describing each label instead is tempting, but that throws away the benefit of few-shot examples; the real problem is the missing boundary, which tags fix.

distractor_explanations.B: Role placement does not mark where one example ends and the next begins. The course uses consistent XML structure for that.
distractor_explanations.C: There are no required official tag names. Descriptive names that match the content work best.
distractor_explanations.D: That throws away the benefit of few-shot examples. The real problem is the missing boundary, which tags fix.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Hard Tier)
prompt: A team implements manual compaction for a long-running API coding agent with the summarizer prompt `Summarize the conversation so far.` After each compaction, the agent re-edits files it had already fixed and retries an approach that had already failed. What does the course recommend?

options.text: Replace compaction with `/clear` at each milestone; starting from an empty context avoids carrying a lossy summary forward into later work.
Keep the summarizer prompt but raise `max_tokens` on the summarization call, so the summary has room to include everything that happened.
Compact less often, since each pass loses detail, and wait until the API returns a context-window error before running the summarizer at all.
Rewrite the summarizer prompt to require every file path modified, every decision made, and every error encountered with its resolution.

explanation: With manual compaction in an API session, the summarizer prompt decides what the agent knows afterward. The course calls state lost through an underspecified summarizer one of the most common sources of multi-session agent failures, and the fix is to require file paths modified, decisions made, and errors with their resolutions; server-side compaction (beta) is the documented primary API strategy when the platform should summarize for you. Analogy: a mechanic handing a car to the next shift writes a handover note; a note saying only worked on the car leads the next mechanic to re-replace parts and retry a fix that already failed, while a note listing parts replaced, decisions taken, and what did not work prevents both. Compacting less often is tempting, but waiting for the context ceiling risks failing mid-task, and the defect is the summary itself.

distractor_explanations.A: Clearing discards all state. It suits an unrelated next task, not continuing the same work.
distractor_explanations.B: A longer generic summary still leaves the summarizer to decide what to keep. The prompt has to name the task-critical state.
distractor_explanations.C: Waiting for the ceiling risks failing in the middle of the task. The defect is an underspecified summary, not how often it runs.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Hard Tier)
prompt: A RAG assistant over an engineering wiki fails in two ways: questions about a specific error code (`E-4417`) retrieve semantically similar but wrong pages, and facts that span two adjacent paragraphs are rarely retrieved together. Which TWO changes address these failures? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Retrieve more chunks per query and paste them unstructured into the prompt, so the model can sort out which ones are relevant.
Run a keyword match alongside embedding search, so exact identifiers such as `E-4417` are found even when other pages score as more similar.
Use section- or sentence-based chunks with a little overlap, so facts that cross a chunk boundary are not split apart.
Increase chunk size to whole wiki pages, so each fact that spans paragraphs sits inside a single retrievable chunk.
Switch to a larger, higher-dimensional embedding model; a stronger embedding guarantees that exact identifiers like `E-4417` rank first in similarity search.

explanation: The course names three places a RAG path breaks: chunking, the embedding match, and assembly. Overlapping sentence- or section-based chunks keep facts that cross a boundary together, and because embedding search returns semantically close results that may not contain the exact identifier, a lexical match is often run alongside it; assembly then presents the chunks in the structure the prompt expects. Analogy: a post office sorting mail for box E-4417 matches the exact box number rather than any box that merely looks similar, and when a long letter spills across two envelopes, repeating the last line of the first page at the top of the second keeps the sentence intact. Switching to a larger embedding model is tempting, but embedding search retrieves semantically close content and is not guaranteed to surface an exact term.

distractor_explanations.A: Retrieved chunks have to reach the model in the structure the prompt expects. Dumping more unstructured text risks the model answering from memory.
distractor_explanations.D: Very large chunks dilute the match with unrelated text, which makes similarity retrieval worse.
distractor_explanations.E: Embedding search retrieves semantically close content; it is not guaranteed to surface an exact term.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Hard Tier)
prompt: A ticket router now returns a single uppercase label reliably after the team added an output constraint and two examples. It still fails on tickets that genuinely touch two categories (for example, a double charge that also broke a feature), where it returns an explanation instead of a label. What does the course suggest?

options.text: Add a paragraph describing each category's boundaries in more detail, so the model can tell which category dominates on mixed tickets.
Allow a combined label such as `BILLING/TECHNICAL`, so ambiguous tickets always have a valid output that the router can still accept.
Name the variant in the constraint (how to pick one label when two apply) or add an example covering an ambiguous two-category ticket.
Turn on extended thinking so the model can reason through the ambiguity and weigh both categories before it commits to a single label.

explanation: The diagnosis table's fourth row covers this case: output is clean on tested inputs but breaks on a variant because the prompt has no rule for it. The fix is to name the variant in the constraint, such as how to pick one label when two apply, or to add an example that covers it; more description, more reasoning, or a new output shape all leave the missing rule unwritten. Analogy: a referee who knows fouls and offsides well freezes and starts explaining when a player commits both at once; the fix is a written precedence rule saying which call wins, or a worked example in the training video, not a longer description of each offence. Allowing a combined label such as `BILLING/TECHNICAL` is tempting, but it breaks the router's fixed label set, the exact parser failure in the course's example.

distractor_explanations.A: Adding description is the six-pass anti-pattern. The gap is a constraint or example for the variant.
distractor_explanations.B: That breaks the router's fixed label set, the exact parser failure in the course's example. The fix is a decision rule, not a new label shape.
distractor_explanations.D: Reasoning depth does not supply a missing rule for the variant, and it adds cost to a classification task.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Hard Tier)
prompt: An API response must be machine-readable JSON. The team currently prefills the assistant turn with `{` and adds `Return only valid JSON` to the prompt, which still breaks on rare edge cases. They decide to adopt structured outputs through `output_config.format`. What else must change?

options.text: Remove the `stop_reason` checks, because a schema-constrained response is guaranteed to parse into the expected structure in every case.
Enable strict mode with a top-level `strict` flag on the request; JSON outputs only take effect once strict mode has been turned on.
Remove the assistant prefill, because JSON outputs and prefilling cannot be used on the same request; the schema replaces it.
Keep the prefill, because it guarantees the response opens as a JSON object while the schema constrains the remaining fields that follow it.

explanation: Structured outputs move output control from the prompt into the API through constrained decoding. The course lists the costs and limits: first-call compilation latency, injected input tokens, refusals and `max_tokens` truncations that still need `stop_reason` checks, and incompatibility with assistant prefilling; strict tool use (`strict: true` on a tool) is a separate setting that constrains tool inputs. Analogy: a courier's printed waybill already has fixed boxes for every field, so stapling your own handwritten first line on top gets the form rejected and you drop the staple; and because even a perfect waybill can come back undeliverable, you keep checking the delivery status. Keeping the prefill is tempting because it seems to guarantee the opening brace, but the two patterns are incompatible on one request, so choose structured outputs and drop the prefill.

distractor_explanations.A: A refusal or a `max_tokens` truncation can still return output that doesn't match the schema, so the `stop_reason` checks stay.
distractor_explanations.B: `strict: true` is set on individual tool definitions for strict tool use. JSON outputs are configured with `output_config.format`.
distractor_explanations.D: The two patterns are incompatible on one request. Choose structured outputs and drop the prefill.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Hard Tier)
prompt: An agent has `get_invoice_history(customer_id)` and `get_payment_methods(customer_id)`. Both descriptions read `Retrieves customer billing data.`, and the input schemas are identical. Claude often calls the wrong one. What does the course identify as the cause and the first fix?

options.text: With identical signatures, routing rests on the descriptions alone, so each needs disambiguating language: when to use it and when not to.
Rename the parameter in one tool (for example to `cust_id`) to differentiate the schemas, since parameter types are Claude's primary routing signal.
Tool names are the primary routing signal, so giving the tools more distinctive names fixes selection without needing to touch the descriptions.
Merge both tools right away into `get_billing_data` with a `type` parameter, since overlapping tools should always be consolidated as the first fix.

explanation: Claude routes on name plus description, with parameter types as a secondary signal.
