Compact after each ticket, so a summary of the closed tickets carries forward while the raw lookup results from each one are condensed.
Add a cache breakpoint at the end of the history each turn, because cached reads make the growing context cheap to carry.

explanation: Pruning, compaction, clearing, and subagent handoffs each buy back headroom, and the one to apply depends on whether you still need the earlier state. Compaction fits a session that continues the same work and needs what it has learned; clearing, a new session in the API, fits when the next task is unrelated and earlier context would only add cost or confusion, with anything that must persist kept somewhere external. Analogy: a hotel turns over a room between guests by stripping it completely, not by folding the last guest's belongings into a neat pile in the corner, and the front-desk register records what must be remembered. Each ticket is a new guest, the new session is the fresh room, and external storage is the register. Compaction is tempting because it sounds careful, but it keeps a summary that no later ticket needs.

distractor_explanations.B: A larger window delays the ceiling without stopping the growth, and every request still pays for tokens no ticket uses.
distractor_explanations.C: Compaction suits continuing the same work with knowledge built up. Here the earlier state is not needed, so a summary only spends tokens.
distractor_explanations.D: Caching lowers what repeated tokens cost but does not shrink the window, so the session still reaches the limit.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: A RAG system splits a policy manual into fixed 200-token chunks with no overlap. Questions whose answers span the end of one section and the start of the next often come back incomplete. Which change addresses this?

options.text: Shrink chunks to 50 tokens so each one matches more precisely and boundary-spanning facts land in a single chunk.
Switch from semantic search to lexical matching alone; an exact term stays within one chunk however the manual happens to be split.
Load the whole manual into every request, since retrieval cannot answer a question that spans two sections of a document.
Chunk by sentence or section with a little overlap, so that facts crossing a chunk boundary are not split apart and lost.

explanation: Chunking decides what a unit of retrievable context is. Too small and a chunk lacks surrounding context; too large and the match is diluted. The course's reasonable default is sentence- or section-based chunking with a little overlap, because facts that cross a boundary would otherwise be split apart and become hard to retrieve.

distractor_explanations.A: Chunks that small lack the surrounding context to be useful, and smaller chunks create more boundaries.
distractor_explanations.B: Lexical matching helps with identifiers, but it does not reunite facts split across chunks.
distractor_explanations.C: Overlapping chunks fix this; loading everything gives up the scaling that makes retrieval worthwhile.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: A team is choosing between a fetch-once retrieval index and agentic search across rounds for two internal knowledge tools. Which TWO statements match the course's trade-offs? (Select TWO.)

options.text: A fetch-once index removes staleness, with the model reading current files at query time rather than a stored snapshot.
For a changing corpus or multi-step questions, iterative search is usually the simpler system, despite costing more per query.
Mixed traffic should send everything to agentic search; a routing call in front of retrieval costs more than it saves.
Agentic search is cheaper per query than fetch-once, because it skips the index and reads only the passages each step needs.
For a stable corpus queried with simple lookups, the index is worth owning, since its retrieval can be inspected and tested.

explanation: A fetch-once index gives you a system you can reason about: you can see which chunks were retrieved and test retrieval directly, at the cost of building, syncing, and securing the index. Agentic search removes that infrastructure and its staleness by reading current material at query time, but it spends more tokens and time and is less inspectable. Analogy: a library card catalogue is fast and auditable, since you can see which card was pulled, but someone must update it whenever books change; a student who browses the stacks every time always sees the newest books but takes longer. The cheaper-per-query claim is tempting because there is no index, yet the per-query bill is exactly what agentic search pays more of.

distractor_explanations.A: This is reversed: reading current files at query time is agentic search, while an index must be kept in sync.
distractor_explanations.C: The course's router earns its cost precisely when traffic is mixed.
distractor_explanations.D: It removes index infrastructure but spends more tokens and time per query.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: A ticket-summary task returns a short Markdown block with four fixed headings. Opus gets the headings right zero-shot; on Haiku the content is right, but heading order and casing vary. An eval shows Haiku would hold the bar if the format were stable. What is the most cost-effective next step?

options.text: Add three paragraphs describing the heading rules, since a precise written description pins down structure better than examples.
Stay on Opus: a cheaper tier that needs examples will cost more per call than a larger tier that works without them.
Add one or two worked input-output examples for Haiku, since examples let a cheaper model match a format a larger one infers.
Enable adaptive thinking at high effort on Haiku, treating format drift as a reasoning failure that extra thinking reliably corrects.

explanation: Few-shot examples show the shape of an answer rather than describe it, and the course notes that prompting mode and model choice interact: a capable model may succeed zero-shot where a smaller one needs a couple of examples, so adding examples can let the cheaper model do the job. Try the simplest model and fewest examples that meet the eval. Analogy: an experienced barista can make a drink from a one-line description, while a trainee gets it right as soon as you show a photo of the finished cup; showing the photo is cheaper than hiring a second senior barista. Staying on Opus is tempting because it already works, but it pays premium rates for a gap two examples close.

distractor_explanations.A: Claude often cannot infer an exact structure from a description; one correct example shows it.
distractor_explanations.B: A few examples cost some tokens, but the course notes they can let a cheaper model do the job.
distractor_explanations.D: Format tasks do not benefit from thinking, which adds output-token cost.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: A team's MCP server exposes runbooks as a templated resource, and its logs show the right runbook returned whenever one is requested. Yet in the team's own MCP client, that content never reaches Claude's context at the start of a turn. What should they check first?

options.text: Whether their client has a mechanism to inject fetched resources into context, because resource support varies across MCP clients.
Whether the server runs over stdio, which cannot carry resources, and should move to Streamable HTTP to deliver them.
Whether the runbooks should be a direct resource instead; templated resources return data to the client but do not pass it on to the model.
Whether Claude is calling the resource during the turn, as a resource enters context once the model invokes it like a tool.

explanation: A resource is read-only data the client fetches by address and places into context directly, without a model tool call; a templated resource adds a parameter such as a runbook ID. Here the server side works, so the gap is on the client: resource support varies across MCP clients, and the course says to verify that your client has a mechanism to inject resources into context before relying on the pattern.

distractor_explanations.B: Transport does not limit which primitives a server exposes, and this server is already returning the data.
distractor_explanations.C: Both forms return read-only data for the client to place in context. The template only adds a parameter to the address.
distractor_explanations.D: Resources are fetched by the client, not called by the model; that is what separates them from tools.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: A project's settings allow the whole GitHub MCP server with a rule on `mcp__github`. A security lead then adds a deny rule on `mcp__github__merge_pull_request` in the same file. How do the merge tool and the server's other tools now behave?

options.text: The merge tool is blocked, and every other GitHub tool now prompts again, as a deny on a server cancels that server's allow rule.
The merge tool prompts the developer to choose, because conflicting allow and deny rules on one tool resolve to an ask.
All of them run without a prompt: the server-level allow is the broader rule and takes precedence over a narrower deny on one tool.
The merge tool is blocked, since a deny on one tool overrides the allow on the server, while the other tools still run without a prompt.

explanation: Permission rules can name a whole server or a single tool as `mcp__server__tool`, and a deny on one tool overrides an allow on the server. The merge tool is therefore blocked while the server-level allow keeps covering every other GitHub tool. The general precedence is deny over ask over allow, so a deny never turns into a prompt.

distractor_explanations.A: The deny targets one tool. The server-level allow still covers the rest, so they keep running without a prompt.
distractor_explanations.B: The order is deny over ask over allow, so a deny that conflicts with an allow blocks the call rather than prompting.
distractor_explanations.C: Breadth does not decide precedence. A deny on one tool overrides an allow on the server.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: A backend service calls the Messages API and wants Claude to use an internal MCP server that the team currently runs locally over stdio. They plan to attach it through the API's MCP Connector. What has to change?

options.text: Expose the server over Streamable HTTP, since the connector supports only remote HTTP servers; stdio needs an SDK-managed client.
Switch the server to the SSE transport, since SSE is how the connector reaches servers that were originally written for stdio.
Add the server to a committed `.mcp.json`, which the connector reads as project-scoped MCP configuration at request time.
Nothing; the connector spawns stdio servers as subprocesses inside the code execution container whenever a request names them.

explanation: The API's MCP Connector supports only HTTP-exposed remote servers. Local stdio servers need Claude Desktop or Claude Code as the client, or an MCP client connection you manage yourself through the SDK. Moving the server to Streamable HTTP, the current remote transport, makes it reachable from the connector.

distractor_explanations.B: The SSE-only transport is deprecated; new remote integrations use Streamable HTTP.
distractor_explanations.C: `.mcp.json` configures Claude Code. The connector is configured in the API request itself.
distractor_explanations.D: The connector does not launch local servers; stdio servers need Claude Desktop, Claude Code, or a client you manage.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: A team commits a `.mcp.json` that launches a stdio MCP server through `npx`. It works for most developers, but on one teammate's laptop, which has no Node runtime installed, the server never starts. What explains this?

options.text: The server runs once on the author's machine and is shared over the network, so the teammate's client is waiting on the author.
A project-scoped stdio server runs on each teammate's machine from the committed launch command, so every clone needs Node.
The teammate also needs a user-scope entry for the server, since a project-scoped server only launches with a matching user entry.
Project scope applies only to HTTP servers, so the stdio entry is ignored for anyone who did not create it on their own machine.

explanation: Project scope shares configuration, not execution. For a stdio server, the committed `.mcp.json` stores the launch command, and every clone spawns its own local subprocess, so each teammate needs the runtime, such as Node for an `npx`-launched server, installed locally. Analogy: a board-game rulebook tells every household to roll a twenty-sided die; each family plays with its own copy at its own table, and the rulebook does not ship the die, so the family without one cannot start. The tempting idea that project scope ignores stdio entries fails because the entry did load; the subprocess simply had nothing to run on.

distractor_explanations.A: stdio servers run as local subprocesses; nothing is shared over the network.
distractor_explanations.C: No matching user entry is required; scopes are independent configuration locations.
distractor_explanations.D: The entry is loaded. It fails because the local runtime it launches with is missing.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: Through the API's MCP Connector, a team attaches a server with 80 tools. They want every definition deferred until needed except two core tools loaded upfront, and one admin tool hidden from the model. Which TWO configurations achieve this? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Set `defer_loading: true` on each of the 78 other tools in `configs`; `default_config` accepts only the `enabled` flag.
Add a `configs` entry for the admin tool with `enabled: false`, so the model never sees it while the remaining tools stay available.
Leave off the `mcp-client-2025-11-20` header, since that header forces every tool to load upfront and blocks per-tool configs.
Add a Claude Code deny rule on the admin tool, relying on permission rules in settings files to hide it from API requests too.
Set `defer_loading: true` in the toolset's `default_config`, then override the two core tools in `configs` with `defer_loading: false`.

explanation: An `mcp_toolset` carries a `default_config` that applies to every tool on the server, and `configs` keyed by tool name override it per tool. `defer_loading` delays loading a definition until the model needs it, `enabled` decides whether the model sees a tool at all, and the connector needs the `mcp-client-2025-11-20` beta header. Analogy: a restaurant's house rule moves every dish's full description into a back booklet, but the two specials are printed on the front page and one dish under testing is left off the menu entirely; the house rule sets the default, and each special note overrides it for one dish. Listing all 78 tools individually is tempting but unnecessary, because the default block already applies to every tool.

distractor_explanations.A: `default_config` can carry `defer_loading`, applying it to every tool, with per-tool overrides in `configs`.
distractor_explanations.C: The header is required; without it the `mcp_toolset` configuration does not apply as described.
distractor_explanations.D: Claude Code settings do not govern API requests, and a permission rule controls whether a tool may run, not whether it is seen.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: An agent's assistant turn contains a `tool_use` block with id `toolu_7A`. The application runs the tool and replies with a `tool_result` whose `tool_use_id` is `toolu_7B`, copied from an earlier turn. The next request fails validation. What fixes it?

options.text: Send the `tool_result` in the next assistant turn instead, since tool results are returned in the assistant role rather than the user's.
Set the `tool_result`'s `tool_use_id` to `toolu_7A`, matching the `tool_use` block it answers in the preceding assistant turn.
Mark every input field as required in the tool's schema, so the call carries enough information for the API to accept it.
Add an exclusion sentence to the tool's description, so Claude stops issuing calls whose IDs collide with IDs from earlier turns.

explanation: Every `tool_use` block must be answered by a `tool_result` carrying the same ID in the user turn that immediately follows. A mismatched, missing, or out-of-order result fails validation, and no prompt change fixes it: the pairing is structural, so the code must copy the ID from the block it is answering.

distractor_explanations.A: tool_result blocks are sent in the user role, in the turn immediately following the tool_use.
distractor_explanations.C: Required fields shape Claude's call; the rejection comes from the mismatched result ID.
distractor_explanations.D: Descriptions affect which tool Claude selects. This is a structural pairing error in the application's code.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: A procurement agent reads only the company's own supplier database and can call a `send_payment_instruction` tool. Reviewers say injection isn't a risk because nothing is fetched from the web, but suppliers can edit the notes on their own profiles. What is the right assessment?

options.text: It isn't a risk, since injection requires a fetched web page, and records stored in an internal database are trusted by definition.
It isn't a risk once the system prompt tells the agent to ignore instructions in notes, which fully closes the injection path.
It is a risk: content that others can write is a vector, so treat the notes as data and constrain the payment action.
It is a risk only for notes edited today; an indirect injection has to arrive in the same interaction in which it is acted on.

explanation: Prompt injection is not limited to web pages. Any content the agent reads that someone else can write, such as a shared document, an email body, a tool's output, or a database record, can carry instructions, and an injection can be planted long before the agent reads it. The durable posture is to treat anything the agent did not author as data and constrain consequential actions regardless of what that data says. Analogy: an office mailroom that trusts anything in an internal envelope will happily wire money because a typed memo asks it to, even though anyone in the building can slip a memo into an envelope. The internal-database argument is tempting, but where content is stored says nothing about who wrote it.

distractor_explanations.A: The threat model covers any content others can write, including database records.
distractor_explanations.B: Prompt-level instructions are a soft boundary; the action boundary is what holds.
distractor_explanations.D: Indirect injection can be planted earlier, in content the agent reads later.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: A bank's security team will review a new Claude integration next month. According to the course, which three questions should the team be ready to answer during scoping?

options.text: Where data is processed, how access is logged, and whether an administrator can control the configuration centrally.
Which model versions are pinned, how incidents are escalated, and whether the integration has passed a penetration test.
How quickly the first token arrives, whether caching is enabled, and which developer wrote the system prompt.
Whether users sign in through SSO, how API keys are rotated, and whether prompt changes are reviewed before each release.

explanation: A financial or healthcare reviewer asks early where data is processed, how access is logged, and whether an administrator can control the configuration centrally. Each maps to something concrete: the deployment path for residency, hook-based audit logs for access, and managed settings for central control. Naming them during scoping turns the review from a blocker into a checklist.

distractor_explanations.B: Version pinning and incident process are operational details; none answers residency, audit logging, or central control.
distractor_explanations.C: Latency and authorship do not tell a reviewer where data goes or how access is controlled and recorded.
distractor_explanations.D: Identity and change control matter, but the three early questions are where data is processed, how access is logged, and who controls configuration.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: A team argues that because current Claude models are trained to resist injected instructions and Anthropic runs classifiers on untrusted content, their file-writing agent can skip least-privilege scoping and PreToolUse hooks. What is the best response?

options.text: Those defenses are probabilistic and no agent reading untrusted content is fully immune, so least privilege and hooks still apply.
The argument holds for internal users: injection risk depends on who submits the prompt rather than on the content the agent reads.
The argument holds if fetched content is wrapped in delimiters, because delimiters give the model a hard boundary injected text can't cross.
The argument holds once OS-level sandboxing is enabled, with the sandbox replacing the need for least-privilege identities and hooks.

explanation: Security is layered: training and classifiers reduce how often an injection lands, treating content as data reduces how often a landed injection is acted on, least privilege bounds what a successful action can reach, and hooks enforce those bounds before the action and log it. Anthropic is explicit that no agent reading untrusted content is fully immune, so model-side defenses never replace application-side ones. Analogy: a car with lane-keeping assist and automatic braking still needs seatbelts and airbags, because the clever systems make crashes rarer, not impossible, and the belts decide how bad a crash is. Sandboxing is the tempting substitute, but it is the residual layer that catches gaps, not a reason to remove the others.

distractor_explanations.B: Injected instructions arrive through content the agent reads, so trusting the user does nothing.
distractor_explanations.C: Delimiters are a soft boundary; content can mimic them or argue for an exception.
distractor_explanations.D: Sandboxing is the residual control in a layered defense, not a substitute for the other layers.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: An agent's system prompt says `Only modify files under reports/.` In testing, a fetched page persuades it to edit `deploy/settings.yaml`. The team wants the restriction to hold no matter what the model decides. What should they add?

options.text: A stronger rule restated at the end of the system prompt, since a rule near the user turn is more binding than one placed at the very top.
A PreToolUse hook that denies edits outside `reports/` and logs every blocked attempt, enforcing the rule before the tool runs.
A PostToolUse hook that detects edits outside `reports/`, running after the tool and reliably rolling back any bad change.
A Stop hook that reviews every file edited during the turn, running once the model finishes so it can undo unwanted edits.

explanation: A rule that lives only in a prompt is not enforced; a hook that runs before a tool executes is. A PreToolUse hook can inspect the call and deny it, by exiting with code 2 or returning a `permissionDecision` of deny, and logging the block gives reviewers evidence. PostToolUse and Stop hooks fire after the action, so they can record or react but not prevent.

distractor_explanations.A: No prompt instruction is a security control; a steered model can still ignore it.
distractor_explanations.C: PostToolUse runs after the call and cannot block it; it suits audit logging and formatting.
distractor_explanations.D: Stop runs at the end of the turn, after the edit has already happened.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: A team moves its SQL style guidance into `.claude/rules/database/sql-style.md`, expecting it to load only when Claude works on SQL files. The file has no frontmatter. Context audits show it loading in every session. Why, and what is the fix?

options.text: Scoping comes only from a `paths` glob in YAML frontmatter, not the folder, so add `paths` such as `src/db/**/*.sql` to the file.
The folder name must mirror a source directory, so renaming `database/` to `src/db/` would scope the rule to those files.
Rules in subdirectories load globally by design, so the file must move to the top level of `.claude/rules/` to become path-scoped.
Rules files load like CLAUDE.md by design, so path-specific guidance belongs in a skill whose description names the SQL files.

explanation: Rules files in `.claude/rules/` add a narrower layer on top of CLAUDE.md, but the scoping comes from a `paths` glob in the file's YAML frontmatter. Subdirectories are organizational only, and a rules file without `paths` loads unconditionally at launch, with the same priority as CLAUDE.md. Analogy: putting a note in the filing-cabinet drawer labelled Kitchen does not make it appear only in the kitchen; the note itself has to say post this by the stove. The folder is the drawer label, and `paths` is the instruction written on the note. Moving the file around is the tempting fix, but no location inside the rules directory scopes it.

distractor_explanations.B: Folder names never scope a rule; only the frontmatter `paths` field does.
distractor_explanations.C: Placement inside `.claude/rules/` is organizational only; an unscoped file loads at launch wherever it sits.
distractor_explanations.D: Rules files can be scoped with `paths`; only unscoped ones load like CLAUDE.md.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: A RAG feature's retriever unit tests and its model-call functional test all pass, but the end-to-end test fails: the retriever returns a list of chunk dictionaries while the prompt builder expects a plain string. Which test level would have caught this earliest?

options.text: An integration test that drives the retriever and the prompt builder together on real retrieved data, exercising the handoff itself.
A second functional test on the model call, since malformed context means the call's output shape is what needs checking.
An LLM-as-judge pass over final answers, scoring whether each one actually came from the retrieved context rather than from the model's memory.
A stricter unit test on the retriever; the defect lives inside the retrieval function and appears when it returns chunks.

explanation: Unit tests isolate one function, functional tests check one Claude call's output shape, integration tests exercise the handoff between two components, and end-to-end tests run the whole flow. Most silent failures hide at the integration level, because each side passes its own tests while the handoff between them is broken. A test that drives retrieval into prompt building with real data surfaces the mismatch before a user does.

distractor_explanations.B: A functional test on well-formed input passes; it never sees what the builder hands over.
distractor_explanations.C: A judge might notice a bad answer but cannot localize it, and it is an eval method rather than the test level for a seam.
distractor_explanations.D: The retriever works on its own; the break is in the contract between two components.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: A team budgets a summarization feature with a rule of thumb of about four characters per token, measured on the model they ran last year. After moving to a newer model generation, the bill rises roughly 15% on identical documents. What is the most likely explanation?

options.text: Newer models bill input by character length rather than by token, since longer documents cost proportionally more regardless of how they are tokenized.
The old rule is stale; characters per token depends on the tokenizer, which differs by generation, so count tokens on every new model.
The old rule only affects estimates of response length; input is tokenized identically across generations, so the extra cost came from longer outputs.
Tokens map to a fixed number of characters on every Claude model, so the increase must come from a higher per-token price on the newer tier.

explanation: Claude counts tokens, not characters or words, and the average number of characters per token depends on the tokenizer of the model in use, which differs between model generations. A rule of thumb measured on one model should not be carried to another. Re-measure token counts on the model you actually deploy, and confirm tokenizer behavior again whenever the model changes.

distractor_explanations.A: Tokens are the unit of both pricing and budget on every model. Billing is not done in characters or words.
distractor_explanations.C: Tokenization of the input changes between generations as well. The rule of thumb is model-dependent for input and output alike.
distractor_explanations.D: Characters per token is not constant. It varies with the tokenizer of each model generation, so identical text can produce a different token count.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: A summarizer's test suite checks that each response is valid JSON with a non-empty `actions` array, and it passes on every run. The team now also wants to know whether each summary is faithful to the source thread. Which approach fits?

options.text: Add an eval with a model-graded judge and a faithfulness rubric, and keep all the structural checks as property assertions.
Set temperature to 0 and compare the response text with a stored copy, which makes an exact comparison dependable for faithfulness.
Extend the structural checks with more required fields, because a response that parses and carries every field must also be faithful.
Assert that each response exactly matches a stored reference summary, so any difference in wording is flagged as a regression.

explanation: Because sampling makes output non-deterministic, tests should assert on properties that must hold, such as a field being present or the structure parsing. Judging meaning, for example whether a summary is faithful, is a different job that structure checks cannot do, so an eval with a model-graded judge and a clear rubric is the right tool for that part.

distractor_explanations.B: Temperature 0 makes output more repeatable but never guarantees identical text. Also, the newest models reject non-default sampling values.
distractor_explanations.C: Structure checks show that a response is well formed. They say nothing about whether its content is faithful to the source.
distractor_explanations.D: Identical inputs do not guarantee identical outputs, and the same correct answer can be worded many ways, so exact-text assertions fail inconsistently.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: A developer includes three worked examples in the first request so Claude will learn the required output format, then drops them from later requests to save tokens. Later responses drift back to the old format. Why?

options.text: Three samples were too few for the format to stick; roughly ten examples are needed before the model keeps the pattern in later requests.
Sampling randomness overrode the earlier examples, so lowering the temperature would have kept the format stable in the later requests.
The API caches the examples per conversation, and the format fades once the default cache lifetime ends, so they have to be added again.
Examples work only while they are in the prompt, because they are not training data, so they must accompany every call that needs them.

explanation: Zero-shot, one-shot, and multi-shot describe how many worked examples sit in the prompt. The examples are not training data: they show the model the shape of the answer only for the request that contains them. If a later call needs the format, the examples have to be in that call, which is also why each example costs tokens on every request.

distractor_explanations.A: Examples are not training data at any count. They influence a response only while they are present in the prompt.
distractor_explanations.B: The examples were no longer in the prompt, so there was nothing for the model to follow. Temperature does not restore removed context.
distractor_explanations.C: Caching is a cost and latency mechanism for repeated prefixes. It does not act as memory of examples from earlier requests.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: A support engineer pastes one screenshot of a UI bug into an internal tool, which sends it with a question and waits for the answer. The image is never reused. A teammate proposes adding a Files API upload step first. What is the better call?

options.text: Submit it through the Message Batches API, which lowers the per-token cost of each request that carries an image, interactive or not.
Host the image at a short-lived signed URL and pass that, so Claude fetches it when the request runs and no bytes travel inline.
Upload through the Files API anyway, because a `file_id` always reduces the number of visual tokens charged for the image.
Send it inline as base64 in the message; a one-off image gains nothing from an extra upload step to the Files API.

explanation: Inline base64 is best for a one-off image where an upload step would add complexity without a payoff. The Files API pays off when the same asset appears in many requests, and a URL source needs a stable public address. Batch is for offline workloads, not for a person who is waiting.

distractor_explanations.A: Batch suits offline work. Here a person is waiting on an immediate answer, so the added latency is unacceptable.
distractor_explanations.B: URL references need a stable, public, reachable address. A short-lived signed link is the case to avoid.
distractor_explanations.C: A `file_id` removes payload weight from later requests. It does not change the visual token cost, and a single use gets no benefit.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: A service sends 1,120 × 840 pixel page images to Claude, one visual token per 28 × 28 pixel patch, with no downscaling. A request may spend at most 20,000 visual tokens on images. How many such images can one request carry?

options.text: 285 images, found by adding the two patch counts (40 + 30) to get 70 visual tokens per image and dividing 20,000 by that.
500 images, found by counting only the 40 patches across the width of each image and ignoring the 30 rows down its height.
17 images, since 20,000 / 1,200 is about 16.7, and a fraction of an image still rounds up to a full one.
16 images, because each costs 40 × 30 = 1,200 visual tokens and 20,000 / 1,200 is about 16.7.

explanation: An image costs ⌈width / 28⌉ × ⌈height / 28⌉ visual tokens. Here 1,120 / 28 = 40 and 840 / 28 = 30, so each page image costs 40 × 30 = 1,200 tokens. Twenty thousand divided by 1,200 is about 16.7, and since a partial image cannot be sent, 16 images fit; a seventeenth would reach 20,400 tokens. Adding the patch counts or counting only one dimension gives far larger, wrong capacities.

distractor_explanations.A: The patches form a grid, so the counts are multiplied, giving 1,200 tokens per image rather than 70.
distractor_explanations.B: Both dimensions count. Each image spans 40 patches across and 30 down, which is 1,200 tokens, not 40.
distractor_explanations.C: A seventeenth image would push the request to 20,400 tokens, over the limit, so only whole images that fit can be counted.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: A team estimates the cost of a 6,000 × 4,000 pixel photo by applying ⌈w / 28⌉ × ⌈h / 28⌉ to the original size and gets a very large number. The model's documented image limits are far smaller than that photo. How should they estimate the cost?

options.text: Keep the original-size figure, since the API charges visual tokens on the uploaded pixels and shrinks the image only for display.
Apply the formula to the scaled size, because oversized images are downscaled first; confirm limits at build time.
Treat the model's visual-token limit as the cost of each image, with larger images simply rejected by the API instead of being resized.
Send it through the Files API, which resizes each uploaded image to one standard size, so each image costs the same number of tokens.

explanation: Each model has a maximum native image resolution, given as a long-edge limit and a visual-token limit, and an image above either limit is downscaled before processing. The patch formula therefore runs on the scaled dimensions. Analogy: a mail slot only takes envelopes up to a set size, so a poster mailed through it is folded down first, and the postage is charged on the folded package rather than on the flat poster. The photo is the poster, the model's limits are the slot, and visual tokens are the postage. Using the original size overstates the cost, and the limits differ by model tier and change over time, so confirm them at build time.

distractor_explanations.A: Images above the limits are downscaled before processing, so the formula runs on the scaled dimensions, not the uploaded ones.
distractor_explanations.C: Oversized images are downscaled rather than rejected, and smaller images cost less than the limit.
distractor_explanations.D: The Files API changes how an image is sent. It does not set a standard size or a fixed token cost.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: A pipeline attaches several high-resolution photos to each request and runs past its token budget once real volume arrives. What is the most direct first fix?

options.text: Move the photos into the system prompt, where input tokens are counted at a lower rate than they are in the user turn of a request.
Send the job through the Message Batches API, which keeps the images out of the context window during processing.
Add a resize step that shrinks images before sending, after measuring a typical production image against the context limit.
Recompress each photo as a smaller JPEG file, which lowers the visual-token count along with the number of encoded bytes.

explanation: Images are charged in visual tokens, ⌈width / 28⌉ × ⌈height / 28⌉ per image, so cost follows pixel dimensions rather than file size. The fix for an over-budget image pipeline is often a short resize step. It is far cheaper to find the problem before deployment, by measuring a typical production image against the context limit before writing the ingestion code.

distractor_explanations.A: Every block in the request counts toward the budget in the same way, wherever it sits in the request.
distractor_explanations.B: Batches change the price and when results arrive, not how many visual tokens each image uses.
distractor_explanations.D: Visual tokens come from pixel dimensions in 28 by 28 patches, so a smaller file with the same dimensions costs the same.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: A team maps the work on a Claude application onto the systems lifecycle. Which TWO activities belong in the test phase? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Writing an integration check that passes real retrieval output into the prompt builder and the model call.
Running the eval suite against the graded cases and reading the per-case results to see what failed.
Instrumenting token cost, latency, and error rate for each call once the system is live in production.
Pinning the full model ID and keeping the prior version available as a rollback target ahead of the release.
Choosing the platform that satisfies the customer's residency requirement before the building work starts.

explanation: The lifecycle runs requirements, design, build, test, deploy, operate, and iterate. The test phase is where the built system is checked: evals against graded cases, plus unit, integration, and end-to-end checks that each catch a different kind of break. Pinning a version is deploy work, choosing the platform is design work, and instrumenting live traffic is operate work. Analogy: before a new bridge opens, inspectors load-test each span and check that the spans meet cleanly at the joints. That inspection day is the test phase, while picking the river crossing was design, hanging the opening-day signs is deploy, and counting traffic afterward is operate.

distractor_explanations.C: Instrumenting live traffic belongs to the operate phase, after release.
distractor_explanations.D: Pinning a version and keeping a rollback target is deploy-phase work, not a test activity.
distractor_explanations.E: Choosing the platform and its constraints is design-phase work. Test checks a built system.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: A partner wants to embed an agent in its own product, with iteration, tool execution, observation, and termination handled for it, much as Claude Code does in a terminal. Which package provides that loop?

options.text: The Claude Agent SDK, which exposes the same agent loop that powers Claude Code and can be embedded inside a product.
The async client in the Anthropic SDK, where non-blocking calls let the model plan and run its own follow-up steps.
A raw REST client, where the endpoint itself runs the tool-execution loop and returns just the final answer to the caller.
Claude Managed Agents, installed as a library so that the hosted loop and its sandbox run inside the partner's own process.

explanation: The Claude Agent SDK gives programmatic access to the same agent loop that powers Claude Code: iteration, tool execution, observation, and termination. That lets a partner embed an agent in its own product instead of running Claude Code in a terminal. It is distinct from the Anthropic SDK, which is a thin convenience wrapper over the API and does not run an agent loop. Neither an async client nor a raw REST call adds a loop.

distractor_explanations.B: Async calls avoid blocking the application's thread. They add no agent behavior.
distractor_explanations.C: The REST endpoint returns one response per request. Looping over tool calls is left to the caller's code or to an SDK that provides it.
distractor_explanations.D: Managed Agents is the path where Anthropic runs the loop and the sandbox; the application streams events to it rather than running it in-process.

topic: Claude Agent SDK vs Anthropic SDK

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: A team's design document has a failure-handling section for a Claude-powered feature. Which entry is written concretely enough that a reviewer can check the built system against it?

options.text: The feature should handle errors gracefully and keep the user informed whenever something goes wrong with the call to the model, as far as is practical.
429 and 529 are retriable, up to three backoff attempts honoring `retry-after`; 400 and 401 are terminal, with a clear user message.
The team will retry on failures where it makes sense and escalate to an engineer when the same problem keeps appearing over a longer period.
The system must stay available and responsive under typical production traffic, without noticeable problems for the people who use the feature daily.

explanation: The failure-handling decision in a design document lists the errors production will throw, marks each one retriable or terminal, and says what the user gets when a failure cannot be recovered. Writing it concretely is what lets a reviewer check the build, and it stops the first real rate-limit response from being the moment a team discovers it has no error path.

distractor_explanations.A: This states an intention but does not classify any failure as retriable or terminal, and it names no behavior that can be verified.
distractor_explanations.C: No failure type, retry limit, or user-facing outcome is named, so the built system cannot be checked against it.
distractor_explanations.D: This is a general quality wish, not a list of the failures the system must survive and what it does for each.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: A team will use Claude Code to modernize a large, unfamiliar legacy codebase that many other systems depend on. Which TWO decisions should the team settle before the session starts? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Rely on plan mode to define who approves each phase, because the mode itself decides who signs off at each boundary of the work.
Decide on audit logging after the migration, once the final diff shows which files the agent ended up touching during the work.
Define and document who approves each phase before the next one begins, instead of leaving that decision implied by default.
Let the agent start editing right away and add review points after the first incident shows where they are actually needed.
Work out the blast radius of a wrong edit by listing the systems that depend on the changed code and what breaks downstream.

explanation: Large changes to unfamiliar legacy code carry high blast radius, unpredictable dependencies, and limited reversibility, so three questions come before the session: what breaks if an edit is wrong, how changes are audited, and who approves each phase. Analogy: before renovating an old house you find out which walls carry load and which pipes feed other flats, and you agree with the owner who signs off after each stage; the builder's cautious pace alone does not say who approves. Plan mode is that cautious pace, not the sign-off itself, and leaving the audit trail until after the migration fails the same test.

distractor_explanations.A: Plan mode enforces the boundary between exploring and executing, but the approval decision is the team's to define and document.
distractor_explanations.B: Auditing is scoped before work begins, for example with a hook that logs every tool call. A final diff does not record what the agent touched along the way.
distractor_explanations.D: Unfamiliar code with high blast radius and limited reversibility needs its review points defined up front, not discovered after damage.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: A customer's internal policy allows workloads only on the cloud vendor its CIO has cleared. Midway through the project, an engineer finds that a different route would be quicker to build on. What should the team do?

options.text: Switch to the quicker route and request an exception at the end, with a working integration as the best argument for approval.
Run both routes in parallel until launch and let measured production latency decide which one the customer keeps in service.
Keep building on the SDK client and endpoint setup of the cleared vendor, because procurement rules out other code paths first.
Compare per-token prices across the platforms and pick the cheapest, treating total cost as the deciding factor over any vendor policy.

explanation: For a customer with an internal data-residency policy, procurement has already ruled out routes before engineering preferences enter the discussion. In code terms, that means the SDK client and endpoint configuration its CIO has cleared, and the team builds against that route instead of switching mid-project because another looks easier. Analogy: a school trip may use buses from the district's approved company. Even if another company's bus is faster, the teacher boards the approved one, because the rule was settled before anyone compared buses. The tempting wrong options treat the policy as one trade-off among many, which it is not.

distractor_explanations.A: The policy rules a path out before engineering preference enters. Building first and asking later risks a full rebuild.
distractor_explanations.B: The decision is a procurement constraint, not a latency contest. Production data cannot override a policy on where workloads may run.
distractor_explanations.D: For a pass-or-fail constraint, cost does not decide. The cleared vendor is the placement.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: A team picks a three-subagent design for a new feature and plans to estimate cost and latency after the first prototype runs. Which change to the process follows the design-document guidance?

options.text: Set cost, latency, and reliability-floor budgets before choosing architecture, so the design is checked against all three.
Estimate cost after the prototype runs, when real token counts for the architecture running from start to finish are available.
Leave every budget to the operate phase, when instrumentation can report the actual cost and latency of each call in production.
Set only a monthly cost ceiling now, since latency and reliability targets depend on the model chosen and should follow that choice.

explanation: A design document names the cost and latency ceiling and the reliability floor the system must stay within, and the guidance is to set these hard budgets before the architecture is determined. The numbers then become the budget you instrument against and the floor you refuse to optimize below. Checking a three-subagent design against them on paper is far cheaper than finding out after building it.

distractor_explanations.B: Budgets are set before architecture is chosen, so the design can be checked against them before a line of code is written.
distractor_explanations.C: Instrumentation measures against a budget that already exists. Without numbers set in advance there is nothing to compare it with.
distractor_explanations.D: The document states cost, latency, and the minimum reliability the design must hold, all before the architecture is settled.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: A team will use an agentic coding tool to build a large feature. Following the design-document approach, what should they give the tool before it writes any code?

options.text: The eval score from a previous feature, which shows the tool how much quality the new feature has to reach before it ships to users.
A short statement of the overall goal alone, with detailed constraints left out so the tool has more options for a good solution.
Nothing beyond the repository, since the tool will infer success criteria from the existing tests and apply them as it builds.
A written design document with success criteria and constraints, so the tool assumes less and output can be checked.

explanation: The design document is a short written record of what the feature must do, the failures it must survive, its cost and latency limits, and its trust boundary, and it comes before implementation. Handing it to an agentic coding tool lets the tool plan against explicit criteria and constraints instead of assumptions, and it gives the team something concrete to check the result against.

distractor_explanations.A: Another feature's score says nothing about this feature's own success criteria or constraints.
distractor_explanations.B: Clear success criteria and explicit constraints reduce assumptions. A bare goal leaves the tool guessing what correct means.
distractor_explanations.C: Inferred criteria are exactly the assumptions the document is meant to remove. Defining correct up front prevents rationalizing whatever gets produced.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: Three months after launch, logs show many users asking about a product line the assistant was never scoped to cover. The team decides to add that to the assistant's requirements and plan a new release. Which lifecycle phase does this activity belong to?

options.text: Iterate, the phase where findings from production are fed back into the requirements for the next release.
Design, where the platform, the model, and the trust boundaries are chosen for the application.
Deploy, where the version is pinned and promotion is gated on the eval against the pinned baseline.
Operate, where the running system is instrumented for cost, latency, and errors and guardrails are enforced.

explanation: A Claude application moves through requirements, design, build, test, deploy, operate, and iterate. Operate is where the team watches the running system and collects findings, while iterate is where those findings flow back into the requirements for the next cycle. The scope gap seen in the logs becomes a new requirement, so the work lands in iterate.

distractor_explanations.B: Design follows requirements. The team is revising the requirements themselves, which comes before any redesign.
distractor_explanations.C: Deploy ships a version that already exists. Here the team is changing what the system must do.
distractor_explanations.D: Operate produces the findings, such as the logs. Turning them into new requirements is the iterate phase.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: A team on a one-off internal experiment wants to skip the lifecycle phases and gates, and a team on a regulated deployment asks to do the same. What does the lifecycle guidance say?

options.text: Both teams may collapse phases, since phases are a suggestion and the gates add paperwork without adding control.
Neither team may collapse phases, so every Claude application is expected to run all seven phases and gates in full.
The regulated team alone may collapse phases, since its compliance review replaces the gates.
A one-off experiment may collapse phases, but a regulated deployment cannot skip its phases or their gates.

explanation: The lifecycle gates exist so that a regulated engagement stays reviewable: no move from design to build until the platform satisfies the residency requirement, and no move toward full production until the new version clears the eval against the pinned baseline. A one-off experiment has no review to satisfy and may collapse phases, but a regulated deployment cannot.

distractor_explanations.A: A regulated deployment keeps control through its gates, so it cannot treat them as optional.
distractor_explanations.B: A one-off experiment may collapse phases. The full set matters for work that must stay reviewable.
distractor_explanations.C: A compliance review does not replace the gates. The gates are how a regulated engagement keeps control.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: A federal contractor plans to buy Claude Enterprise through AWS Marketplace to satisfy a FedRAMP requirement. What is wrong with that plan?

options.text: Marketplace purchases are authorized at FedRAMP Moderate, so the plan works for a workload that stays below the High level.
Claude Enterprise on AWS Marketplace is not FedRAMP authorized, so the team needs one of the three authorized routes instead.
Claude Enterprise is authorized through a single vendor, so the contractor has to buy from that vendor and not from a cloud.
Nothing is wrong, since a Claude product billed through an AWS account inherits AWS's own FedRAMP authorization automatically.

explanation: As of publish time, three routes are FedRAMP authorized: Claude for Government (C4G), Claude via Amazon Bedrock GovCloud, and Claude via Vertex AI Assured Workloads. Claude Enterprise on AWS Marketplace is not FedRAMP authorized, so a team that needs FedRAMP compliance must use one of the three routes. Verify current authorization status at the Anthropic Trust Center before configuring anything.

distractor_explanations.A: Claude Enterprise on AWS Marketplace is listed as not FedRAMP authorized at any level, so it is not a valid route.
distractor_explanations.C: Three routes are authorized: Claude for Government, Claude via Amazon Bedrock GovCloud, and Claude via Vertex AI Assured Workloads.
distractor_explanations.D: Billing through AWS does not transfer authorization. Claude Platform on AWS, for example, runs inference outside the AWS boundary.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: A team lead summarizes how the four decisions in a design document are used by the rest of the system. Which TWO statements are accurate? (Select TWO.)

options.text: The document is a one-time sign-off, so once it is approved the later layers can each define their own targets independently of it.
The cost and latency numbers become test cases for the eval, since the grader scores each response against its dollar budget.
The list of failures becomes the system prompt, where the instructions that define retry and terminal behavior are written.
The success criteria become the cases the eval is graded against, which is why writing them first is what makes the eval possible.
The trust boundary becomes the input treated as data and the action gated with a hook, rather than a setting someone adds later.

explanation: The design document records four decisions before any production code: success criteria, failure handling, cost and latency budget, and trust boundary. Each feeds a layer: criteria feed the eval, failures feed error handling, budgets feed instrumentation, and the trust boundary feeds the hook and least-privilege setup. Analogy: for a house, the room list becomes the inspection checklist, the weather the roof must survive becomes the structural tests, the budget becomes the cost tracker, and the lock plan becomes the fitted locks; if each trade invented its own plan, nothing would fit together. The tempting wrong answers swap which layer consumes which decision.

distractor_explanations.A: The document exists to keep the layers consistent. Without it, each layer ends up solving a different problem.
distractor_explanations.B: They become the budget the system is instrumented against and the floor it refuses to optimize below. Eval cases come from the success criteria.
distractor_explanations.C: The failure list becomes the retriable and terminal cases the error-handling code must cover, not the system prompt.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: A ticket classifier returns `This looks like a billing issue.` on some runs and `BILLING` on others. A teammate suggests lowering the temperature so the output takes the right shape. Will that fix the problem?

options.text: Yes, but only when the value is set to exactly 0; any other low setting leaves the form of the answer random from run to run.
No, as temperature has no effect on a classification task, which returns a fixed label whatever sampling configuration is used.
Yes, because a lower temperature forces the model to choose the single likeliest token each time, which always produces the required label.
Not reliably; temperature affects only wording variation, not answer form, which an output constraint and examples define.

explanation: Sampling draws each next token from a probability distribution, and temperature shapes that distribution: lower values make output more repeatable and higher values make it more varied. Neither changes which form the answer should take. A response that comes back in the wrong shape is missing an output constraint, usually backed by a couple of examples of the exact label and format.

distractor_explanations.A: Even at 0, outputs are not guaranteed identical, and the setting still does not tell the model which form to use.
distractor_explanations.B: Sampling does affect classification: a lower temperature makes the chosen label more repeatable. It is just not what fixes the output shape.
distractor_explanations.C: Lower temperature makes output more repeatable, but the likeliest wording is not necessarily the required label. The prompt never defined the shape.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: A team writes down what it knows about context windows before choosing a model. Which TWO statements are accurate? (Select TWO.)

options.text: The window holds the user's messages and the tool results, while the system prompt and the reply are metered separately.
With a 1M-token window the input needs no trimming, because the API silently drops the oldest turns as the limit nears.
A 40k-token cap set as a cost control is a budget the team chose, not a limit that the model itself imposes on it.
Current Claude models carry a window of at least 200k tokens, and the newest flagship models serve 1M tokens by default.
Models in the family share one window size, so window size does not vary between tiers or generations of Claude.

explanation: Current Claude API models carry at least a 200k-token window, and the newest flagship models serve 1M tokens by default. A cap such as 40k tokens is a budget a team chooses for cost control, not a limit the model imposes. The window itself holds the system prompt, the conversation, tool definitions and results, and the model's own output, and the application must trim history because the API never does it silently. Analogy: a car's tank holds 60 liters, but a road-trip budget lets you buy only 20 liters of fuel. The 20 is your own decision, not the car's limit, and the tank size is what the model choice sets.

distractor_explanations.A: The window holds everything at once: system prompt, history, documents, tool definitions, tool results, and the model's own output.
distractor_explanations.B: The API does not silently drop or truncate old turns. An oversized input is rejected, so managing history is the application's job.
distractor_explanations.E: Window size does vary: at least 200k on current models, with 1M on the newest flagships.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: A team moves a contract-clause extractor from Sonnet to Haiku to save about $40 a day. The eval shows a small accuracy drop, and each missed clause later costs a reviewer hours of rework. How should the team decide?

options.text: Weigh the downstream cost of the extra errors against the savings, since a move down is sound only if measured quality holds.
Move down, as a lower per-token price makes the smaller model the right choice whenever the accuracy drop is only a few points.
Decide on latency alone; the tier with the fastest responses is the right choice regardless of cost or accuracy differences.
Stay on Sonnet permanently, because a larger tier is always more accurate and so can never cost more once errors are counted.

explanation: Moving down a tier trades quality risk for lower cost and latency, so the decision rests on measurement rather than price alone. The cost of a mistake belongs in that calculation: saving a few dollars a day is not a sound trade if the quality drop introduces errors with significant downstream cost. Move to the smaller model only when the eval shows the quality bar still holds for this task.

distractor_explanations.B: The cost of a mistake belongs in the calculation. A small daily saving is not sound if the added errors carry significant downstream cost.
distractor_explanations.C: Latency is one of three factors. Cost, latency, and quality are weighed together and measured on an eval.
distractor_explanations.D: There is no globally correct tier. Moving down is right whenever an eval shows the cheaper model holds the quality bar for the task.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: A team hesitates to try Haiku on a classification workload because it assumes the application and prompts would need rewriting for each tier. What does the guidance say?

options.text: Each tier needs its own prompt format, so a move means a rewrite that should be budgeted as a small migration project.
The same prompt runs on any tier, so tier is a per-workload lever that changes without a rewrite; a move still needs eval evidence.
The prompt carries over within a single model generation, which allows an upgrade in tier but does not allow a step down to a cheaper one.
The prompt carries over unchanged, so the switch can ship at once with the lower price list as sufficient proof of quality.

explanation: The same prompt runs on any Claude tier, so model choice is a lever you set per workload and can change without rewriting the application. The lever still has a gate: a model change is promoted on a measured score against your own cases, in both directions. Analogy: a restaurant can serve the same menu card from a small kitchen or a large one, so swapping kitchens needs no new menu, but the owner still tastes the dishes before sending the change to every table. The tempting wrong answers either inflate the cost of switching or skip the tasting.

distractor_explanations.A: The same prompt runs on any tier. Choosing a model does not require rewriting the application.
distractor_explanations.C: Tier is set per workload and can move in either direction, as long as the eval supports it.
distractor_explanations.D: A move down is promoted on a measured eval score showing the quality drop is acceptable, not on price.

topic: Model Choice as a Per-Workload Lever

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: A team splits a short set of independent lookups across a lead agent and four parallel subagents to cut response time. Elapsed time improves only slightly. What best explains it?

options.text: Each subagent re-reads the lead's full conversation before starting, so the plan step ends up as long as the original task.
The parallel work shortens only the independent part, while the lead still plans the split and compiles the returns.
Subagents queue behind one another by default, so adding more of them does not shorten elapsed time on any task.
Parallel subagents use about as many tokens as a single agent, so the slowdown must come from rate limits on the extra requests.

explanation: Parallel subagents can cut wall-clock time on independent work, but the lead agent still has to plan the split and compile the returns, and that coordination adds latency of its own. On a short task the fixed overhead can eat most of the gain, while the token cost still multiplies. Analogy: a head chef can hand four cooks one dish each, but writing the order cards and plating the finished dishes still happens one step at a time, so a two-minute meal does not become half as long. The tempting wrong options blame queueing or shared history rather than that fixed hand-off cost.

distractor_explanations.A: Subagents start from a clean context holding only the task and what it needs. They do not inherit the lead's full history.
distractor_explanations.C: Subagents run in parallel, and for independent work that can cut wall-clock time. The gain is limited by planning and compiling overhead.
distractor_explanations.D: Orchestrator-worker setups use roughly fifteen times the tokens, since every subagent spends its own. Token use is not the explanation here.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: A document pipeline has three steps: look up a customer's plan name, decide whether a refund meets a policy that combines four conditions, and convert the decision into a fixed JSON layout. On which step does extended thinking most clearly earn its cost?

options.text: The plan-name lookup, as a wrong name would send each later step down the wrong path and reasoning prevents that outcome entirely.
The refund decision, because it holds several constraints at once and the reasoning pass works through their dependencies.
The JSON conversion, as schema mistakes are expensive and reasoning makes a format conversion more accurate in practice.
All three equally, with thinking content omitted from the response and therefore adding nothing at all to the bill.

explanation: Extended thinking pays off on multi-step problems where the model must hold several constraints at once. Mechanical work such as lookups, extracting a field, or converting a format gains nothing from it, and a clear output constraint is the right tool there. Because thinking is billed like output, applying it only to the refund decision keeps the cost where the benefit is.

distractor_explanations.A: A lookup is a mechanical task. Thinking adds token cost without improving the answer.
distractor_explanations.C: Format conversion is a task where thinking is left off; a prompt with an output constraint does the job.
distractor_explanations.D: Thinking is billed as output whether or not the content is displayed, so using it on mechanical steps is wasted spend.

topic: When Extended Thinking Earns Its Cost

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: A team plans the budget for a nightly Message Batches job. Which TWO statements are accurate? (Select TWO.)

options.text: A batch finishes in a predictable few minutes, with the discount paid for by a shorter queue than synchronous traffic gets.
Adding prompt caching to a batch cancels the batch discount, so the two are not combined on one scheduled job.
Streaming and batching never compete for the same request, because each request is either user-facing or it is not.
Batch results come back in the order the requests were submitted, so a result can be matched to its input by position.
The batch discount is a version-pinned figure, so the budget should confirm the current rate rather than hardcode it.

explanation: The Batches API lowers the cost of non-urgent, high-volume work, and the current discount is version-pinned, so a budget should confirm the rate against the reference at build time instead of baking in a number. Streaming improves how fast one response feels to a user in the loop, while batching lowers the bill where nobody waits, so the two never compete for the same request.

distractor_explanations.A: Batch latency is non-deterministic and can reach 24 hours. The lower price is paid for with that latency.
distractor_explanations.B: The two compound. The discount lowers each request, and caching lowers the repeated prefix inside each one.
distractor_explanations.D: Results arrive in arbitrary order. A `custom_id` on each request is what joins results to inputs.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: A Sonnet-based planning agent misses its eval bar. In one release the team moves to Opus, raises the effort setting, and rewrites the system prompt. The score improves and the team credits the model upgrade. What is the flaw in that conclusion?

options.text: Moving up a tier is not justified until a prompt rewrite has been tried on every failing case, whatever the eval shows.
Raising effort should never be combined with a model change; the two settings conflict and cancel each other out in practice.
Three changes shipped together, so no single one earns credit; change only one lever at a time and re-run the eval.
The eval should have been skipped, since a model upgrade is validated by reading a few outputs rather than by scores across cases.

explanation: The eval workflow is to change one component at a time: if you rewrite the prompt, adjust the reasoning effort, and switch the model in one pass and the score moves, you have learned nothing about which change caused it. Analogy: if you change the recipe, the oven temperature, and the brand of flour in one bake and the cake improves, you cannot say which change mattered or which was wasted money. The Opus upgrade is the priciest of the three, so crediting it without isolating it could lock in avoidable cost.

distractor_explanations.A: Step up a tier when an eval shows the current model missing the bar on the hardest cases and a wrong answer is costly. No rewrite-first rule exists.
distractor_explanations.B: Model choice and reasoning effort are independent levers that compose. The flaw is changing them together, not combining them.
distractor_explanations.D: A model change is promoted on a measured score against your cases, so the eval is the right instrument.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: A team runs two features. Feature A answers high-volume lookup questions where the output shape is obvious. Feature B plans dependent multi-step changes where a wrong plan is costly. Which pairing of model and reasoning settings fits?

options.text: Both features on the smallest tier with the highest effort; extra reasoning lets the cheapest model cover every level of difficulty seen.
Feature A on a smaller or balanced tier with reasoning off; feature B on a capable tier with a higher effort setting for its planning.
Feature A on the most capable tier with high effort for safety; feature B on the smallest tier with reasoning off to hold cost down further.
Both features on the most capable tier with reasoning off, because choosing the model already decides how much the model thinks.

explanation: Model choice and reasoning mode are separate and composable levers. A capable model with reasoning off is fast and direct, while the most demanding tasks pair a capable model with a higher effort setting. Simple, high-volume lookups need neither extra capability nor extra thinking, so spending on them is wasted.

distractor_explanations.A: Reasoning does not turn a small model into a larger one, and high effort is wasted on lookups.
distractor_explanations.C: This reverses the fit: the simple feature gets expensive capacity and the hard one gets none.
distractor_explanations.D: Model choice and reasoning mode are separate decisions; thinking is set per request.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: A team is deciding between a workflow and an agent. Which condition counts in favor of building an agent?

options.text: The cost of an error is real, and step-level guardrails have to sit in front of each stage of the process.
Every execution follows the same sequence of steps, so the whole path can be written down ahead of time by the team.
Observability with standard tooling is required, with each step showing up in ordinary operational dashboards.
Non-determinism is acceptable, and what the agent can do is constrained by the toolset registered for that agent.

explanation: The decision table pairs each agent condition with a workflow condition. A workflow fits when you can enumerate the steps, when errors are costly enough for step-level guardrails, when standard observability is required, and when inputs are constrained. An agent fits when you can specify the goal and the tools but not the path, and when non-determinism is acceptable because the agent's possible actions are constrained by its registered toolset.

distractor_explanations.A: Step-level guardrails attach to the steps of a workflow. They are a reason to prefer one.
distractor_explanations.B: A fixed, enumerable path points to a workflow. An agent adds behavior the task does not need.
distractor_explanations.C: Standard-tool observability is a reason to choose a workflow, where each step is enumerated in code.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: A team deploys an agent for open-ended vendor research. Operations asks why the usual per-step success dashboards no longer explain what happened in a failed run. What is the underlying reason?

options.text: Agent runs are unobservable by design, so teams should rely on final-output checks and skip inspection of intermediate steps.
The dashboards were built for workflows, which fail more often than agents, since their thresholds are tuned to the wrong error rates here.
Agents run outside the application's process, so their steps are unable to reach a logging system the team already runs.
Because the path emerges from the model's reasoning over context, observability needs transcript-level tooling, not standard logging.

explanation: An agent chooses its own path at run time, shaped by the model's reasoning over accumulated context, instead of following branches written in your code. That is why observability moves from standard operational logging to transcript-level tooling. Analogy: a city bus follows a fixed route, so a timetable dashboard shows exactly where it was late, while a taxi picks its own streets, and to understand a bad trip you need the driver's trip log rather than a bus timetable. The bus is a workflow, the taxi is the agent, and the trip log is the transcript. Agent runs are not unobservable; they just need a different kind of record than per-step dashboards.

distractor_explanations.A: Agent runs can be inspected through transcripts. Skipping intermediate steps leaves failures impossible to localize.
distractor_explanations.B: Failure rates are not the point. An agent's route through a task is chosen at run time, so a per-step view does not describe it.
distractor_explanations.C: Agent loops run in your process or a hosted one, and nothing prevents logging. The issue is that the path is not a fixed sequence of steps.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: A team is choosing how an agent carries state between sessions. Which statement describes the two opposite ways a wrong memory-scope choice fails?

options.text: Too much in-context state inflates every call and its bill, while too little persisted state means unwritten facts vanish at session end.
Too much in-context state corrupts the stored summaries, while too little persisted state forces the loop to restart on every turn of a session.
Both failures appear in stateless agents, since in-context and persisted memory carry no cost that grows with session length.
Too much in-context state makes calls cheaper because the model re-reads less, while too little persisted state raises retrieval latency on each call.

explanation: Memory scope sets what an agent knows when a new session starts, and a wrong choice fails in opposite directions. Holding too much state in the active conversation inflates every API call, because the model re-reads the whole conversation each turn and the bill grows with session length. Holding too little in persistent storage strips the agent of memory across sessions, because anything not written down disappears when the conversation ends.

distractor_explanations.B: In-context state does not corrupt stored summaries. The real risk is a growing token bill and a filling window.
distractor_explanations.C: In-context memory scales cost with session length. Stateless agents avoid that by keeping nothing between sessions.
distractor_explanations.D: The model re-reads the full conversation on every turn, so more in-context state raises the bill rather than lowering it.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: A bot reviews pull requests and the team lets its approval merge changes automatically, including changes to the payment-authorization module the team has marked sensitive. The bot's findings are usually right. What should change?
