options.text: Run the bot's review after the merge instead, with findings arriving when a wrong change can still be corrected at no cost to the team.
Add a second automated reviewer on a different model, since two agreeing approvals can stand in for the human sign-off step.
Treat the bot's work as input and require a person to review sensitive-code changes before merge, however confident the bot or its review sounds.
Nothing, since a bot with a strong accuracy record has earned the right to be the only reviewer of low-volume sensitive code.

explanation: Gates go where an action is hard to undo or touches code the team has marked sensitive. There the agent's work is an input to a human decision, not a replacement for one, so a person must review before merge no matter how confident the bot or its review sounds. Analogy: a spell-checker can flag typos in a legal contract, but a lawyer still signs it, because the signature is the step that is hard to reverse. The bot is the spell-checker, and the merge is the signature. A second bot is just another spell-checker.

distractor_explanations.A: A review after merge lets the risky change land first. The gate has to sit before the point where a finding turns into a hard-to-reverse action.
distractor_explanations.B: Two automated approvals are still no human decision, and both can share the same blind spots.
distractor_explanations.D: The agent should never be the only gate on code marked sensitive; its accuracy record does not remove that rule.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: An escalation-support agent kept its full history in context during development, in continuous sessions of 10 to 15 turns. In production, state accumulates across several shorter sessions, and by session four over 45,000 tokens are used before the first tool call, so results come back incomplete. What should the team have done before choosing in-context memory?

options.text: Raise `max_tokens` on each request, so that the accumulated history has more room inside the model's context window.
Test with even longer single sessions in development, which would have shown the window filling at the same point as it did in production.
Measure expected state per session, including history and tool schemas, against the context limit, and use external storage if needed.
Make the agent stateless, since an agent working escalation cases never needs anything from an earlier session or earlier cases.

explanation: Memory scope is chosen at design time from the shape of the session. In-context memory is re-sent on every call, so token cost grows with each turn and across sessions that carry state forward, and the team should measure expected state size against the limit before relying on it. Analogy: packing for a trip by trying the suitcase with one weekend's clothes, then discovering it will not close once a month of laundry is added. The weekend is the single development session, the month is production's accumulated state, and the storage locker is external storage. Packing a longer weekend bag in development would only have repeated the same shape and missed the problem.

distractor_explanations.A: `max_tokens` limits output length. It does not enlarge the context window or reduce what the history already occupies.
distractor_explanations.B: Development used one long session while production accumulates state across sessions. Those shapes differ, so the test would still have missed it.
distractor_explanations.D: Escalation cases continue across sessions, so the agent needs state carried forward. Stateless fits self-contained jobs.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: A teammate argues that an agent is an upgrade over a simpler pattern in every case. What does choosing an agent add compared with a workflow?

options.text: Lower token use on each task, with the model skipping the steps that a workflow would run on every input it receives.
A fixed run path that follows the same enumerated steps, which makes the behavior easy to predict and to test.
Coordination overhead, expanded context costs, and more surface area for failure than a simpler pattern carries.
Standard operational logging that fully explains each run, which removes the need for transcript-level tooling when debugging.

explanation: Agents carry coordination overhead, expanded context costs, and more surface area for failure than simpler patterns. That is why the first design decision is whether the problem needs an agent at all, and why the progression runs from a single call to a workflow to an agent.

distractor_explanations.A: Agents usually add context cost, since tool results and reasoning accumulate in the window.
distractor_explanations.B: A fixed path is the property of a workflow. An agent's path emerges from the model's reasoning.
distractor_explanations.D: Agents need transcript-level tooling to explain a run, because the path is not enumerated in code.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: A team reviews a product that handles free-form requests. Which TWO statements about choosing between a workflow and an agent are accurate? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Inputs drawn from a small, well-constrained set are a sign that an agent fits better, since the model can sequence tools for them.
An agent is the safer default for a new feature, since it can do what a workflow does with no added cost.
A workflow suits requests whose path cannot be listed ahead of time, as its steps are easy to observe in logs.
Variable inputs that would need dozens of conditional branches in a workflow are a sign that an agent may fit better.
A workflow chosen where an agent is needed breaks the first time an input falls outside the path it was built for.

explanation: Choosing the pattern is the first decision, and it fails in two directions. An agent where a workflow would do adds behavioral complexity without adding capability. A workflow where an agent is needed produces a system that breaks whenever input deviates from the predetermined path, and inputs that would need dozens of conditional branches are the usual signal that the path cannot be enumerated.

distractor_explanations.A: Well-constrained inputs and a fixed sequence point to a workflow. An agent fits when the path cannot be enumerated in advance.
distractor_explanations.B: An agent adds behavioral complexity and cost. The guidance starts from the simplest pattern that works.
distractor_explanations.C: A workflow needs enumerable steps. An unlistable path is a reason to consider an agent.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: A team compares memory approaches for several agents. Which TWO statements about what each approach costs or loses are accurate? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Stateless agents carry the heaviest read and write logic, with every independent session rebuilt from stored history.
Summarized memory costs fewer tokens than replaying history, since the agent sees only what the summarizer chose to keep.
In-context memory adds retrieval latency to every call, because the state has to be fetched from a store before each turn.
External storage adds retrieval latency to calls and requires read and write logic that the team must build and maintain.
Summarized memory preserves every detail of earlier sessions, so it needs no carefully written summarizer prompt at all.

explanation: Each memory scope has its own cost. In-context memory has zero retrieval overhead but inflates tokens as the conversation grows and vanishes when the session ends. External storage persists state but adds latency and read and write code. Summarized memory is cheaper than full replay but depends on what the summarizer keeps. Stateless agents carry no overhead and lose all prior context. Analogy: a notebook you keep on your desk is quick to read but fills up, a filing cabinet down the hall keeps everything but takes a walk each time, and a one-page recap is quick to read but only has what the writer chose to include. The tempting mistakes hand one approach's cost to another, such as retrieval latency to in-context memory.

distractor_explanations.A: Stateless agents store and retrieve nothing, so they have no such overhead. They lose all prior context.
distractor_explanations.C: In-context memory has no retrieval overhead. Its cost is that tokens grow with the conversation and everything is lost when the session ends.
distractor_explanations.E: Summarization drops detail by nature. Anything the summarizer does not preserve is unavailable to the agent.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: A new extraction feature has a strict JSON contract, several known edge cases that examples can cover, and inputs that mix instructions with pasted documents. Which prompt approach fits?

options.text: Few-shot examples alone, as a well-chosen set of examples replaces the need for tags or an explicit output constraint.
A longer system prompt with detailed descriptions only, since descriptive text is what pins down edge cases and formats well.
Stack all four, using a system prompt for the contract, XML tags for inputs, examples of edge cases, and an output constraint.
A single zero-shot instruction, since added techniques only lengthen the prompt and cannot improve a well-defined task like this one.

explanation: Stacking all four techniques fits a clearly defined output contract with edge cases that examples can cover: the system prompt carries the contract, XML tags separate inputs from instructions, few-shot examples show the exact shape, and an output constraint fixes the form. A simple task such as summarizing a paragraph would only need one of them.

distractor_explanations.A: Examples show the pattern, but the constraint states the form, and tags keep inputs and examples separate from the instructions.
distractor_explanations.B: Description alone does not pin down structure. Examples and an output constraint show and fix the shape.
distractor_explanations.D: A strict contract with known edge cases is where the added techniques pay off. Zero-shot suits simple tasks with an obvious shape.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: A team needs few-shot examples for a ticket-labeling prompt and already has an eval set with scored outputs. Where should the examples come from, and how should they be laid out?

options.text: Paste the pairs as plain paragraphs after the instructions; tags are needed only when code is mixed with documentation.
Draw examples from the top-scoring eval outputs and wrap each pair in tags like `<sample_input>` and `<ideal_output>`.
Pick the lowest-scoring outputs, so the examples show Claude exactly which mistakes to avoid in later responses.
Write each example by hand; model outputs from an eval would teach the prompt to repeat its own earlier mistakes.

explanation: Few-shot examples show a pattern instead of describing it, and one correct input and output pair gives Claude the exact shape to match. You can reuse some of your highest-scoring eval outputs rather than writing examples from scratch, and wrapping them in consistent tags keeps Claude from reading an example as part of the instructions.

distractor_explanations.A: Consistent XML structure keeps the boundary between examples and the actual prompt clear, so Claude does not read them as part of the task.
distractor_explanations.C: Examples show the pattern to match, so they should be correct input and output pairs, not failures.
distractor_explanations.D: Examples can be drawn from the highest-scoring eval outputs rather than written from scratch.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: A team plans to use structured outputs in a production pipeline. Which TWO statements about the two mechanisms are accurate? (Select TWO.)

options.text: JSON outputs constrain the final response to a schema, which removes parse-and-retry code that would otherwise wrap each call.
Strict tool use and JSON outputs constrain different parts of a request, so they can be used alone or together in one request.
A response that matches the schema is certain to arrive, so the application no longer needs to check `stop_reason`.
Both mechanisms can be combined with prefilling the assistant message to anchor the opening of the structure in the reply.
Strict tool use constrains the model's final prose answer, while JSON outputs validate the arguments that Claude passes to tools.

explanation: Structured outputs move output control from the prompt into the API. JSON outputs, set through `output_config.format` with a schema, constrain the final response, and they remove the parse-and-retry code you would otherwise write around each call. Strict tool use validates the arguments Claude passes to a tool before your code runs. The two constrain different parts of a request, so you can use either alone or both together.

distractor_explanations.C: A refusal or a `max_tokens` truncation can still return output that does not match, so the code still checks `stop_reason`.
distractor_explanations.D: JSON outputs and prefilling are incompatible, so the two patterns cannot run on one request.
distractor_explanations.E: It is the other way round: JSON outputs constrain the final response, and strict tool use validates tool arguments.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: In a six-pass classifier trace, the last pass replaces all the descriptive instructions with a JSON schema and two few-shot examples. What does the trace report for that final pass?

options.text: Parsing becomes reliable and latency drops, while accuracy on ambiguous tickets stays where pass 4 had already left it.
It leaves latency unchanged, as the model still reads about as much instruction text as it did before the rewrite.
It shortens the output but fixes nothing about parsing, with pass 4 having already made the output reliable for the parser.
It lifts accuracy on ambiguous tickets well above pass 4, with the examples teaching the boundary between the categories.

explanation: In the six-pass trace, pass 6 swaps the pile of descriptive text for an output constraint and two examples. The parser now works on every ticket and latency drops, but accuracy on ambiguous tickets matches pass 4: the rewrite fixed the form and the length of the output, not the model's judgment. Analogy: replacing a rambling instruction manual with a short form that has tick-boxes means the clerk fills it in quickly and consistently, but the form does not make the clerk better at deciding the hard cases. The tempting wrong answers credit the rewrite with accuracy it never produced.

distractor_explanations.B: The rewrite removes the long instructions and the verbose output they induced, and latency drops.
distractor_explanations.C: Pass 4 still returned full explanations on ambiguous tickets, which broke the parser. The rewrite is what fixed parsing.
distractor_explanations.D: The trace reports accuracy on ambiguous tickets matching pass 4. The gain is in parsing and latency, not accuracy.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: In a classifier prompt's revision log, a pass that adds `Never return two categories.` still breaks on ambiguous tickets. A later pass adds two paragraphs of edge cases, and responses grow past 2,000 characters with higher latency and no accuracy gain. Which statement separates the two failures?

options.text: Both are diagnostic failures, since adding any text to a prompt is wrong, and the fix for each is to remove the prompt and start over again.
The second is the diagnostic failure, as the longer prompt hid the real defect, while the first merely shows that edge cases exist.
The first is a diagnostic failure (description instead of a constraint); the second is an engineering failure from prompt length.
Both are engineering failures caused by latency, as neither pass changed the model that handles the tickets or its settings.

explanation: Two different failures hide in a growing prompt. Describing a problem where a constraint is missing is a diagnostic failure, and a prompt so long that it induces long, unfocused output and slower responses is an engineering failure, which can appear even after the first is fixed. Analogy: a driver who is lost keeps adding stops to the route instead of checking the map, which is the wrong diagnosis, and the heavily loaded car then runs slower, which is a separate cost of all that extra baggage. Both fixes are the same structural move: an output constraint and two examples.

distractor_explanations.A: The two failures are distinct. A prompt still needs its constraint and examples, and the second failure is about length and latency.
distractor_explanations.B: This reverses them. The first pass misidentified the problem by describing it, while the second is the length and latency regression.
distractor_explanations.D: Only the second shows a latency effect. The first is a misdiagnosis: a constraint was needed, not description.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: A ticket assistant returns a full sentence where the router expects a label, and over a long chat its tone drifts into casual advice. A teammate proposes one long prompt rewrite. What does the diagnosis table suggest?

options.text: Do the single long rewrite, letting one longer prompt hold both the label contract and the tone rules without a new technique.
Treat them as two failures: an output constraint for the label shape, and a more specific system prompt for the drift.
Add few-shot examples only, expecting a handful of examples to fix both the answer shape and the tone drift at once.
Add an output constraint alone, expecting that forcing the label shape will also stop the tone from drifting in later turns.

explanation: The diagnosis table maps each failure to the technique that is missing: a wrong shape points to an output constraint, and drift across turns points to a more specific system prompt. Two different symptoms mean two different missing pieces, and each gets its own fix rather than one longer rewrite. Analogy: a car that pulls to the left and has a squeaking brake needs the alignment checked and the brake pad replaced; tightening every bolt in the garage fixes neither. The tempting wrong options give one technique credit for both jobs.

distractor_explanations.A: A longer prompt is the instinct the course warns against. Each failure type names the one technique that is missing.
distractor_explanations.C: Examples address an invented structure. Drift across turns points to an underspecified system prompt, a separate technique.
distractor_explanations.D: An output constraint fixes the form of the response. It does not hold role, scope, and tone steady across turns.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: A team registers two tools named `tool1` and `tool2`, and Claude often picks the wrong one. Which change to the name field helps most?

options.text: Keep the generic names but add an alphabetical prefix, as Claude checks tool names in sorted order.
Lengthen each name into a full sentence, since Claude routes on the number of words in a tool's name.
Use specific names that say what each tool does, such as `get_account_balance` in place of a generic label.
Leave the names alone, with the `input_schema` used as the main signal when Claude decides which tool to select.

explanation: A tool schema has a name, a description, and an input schema. The name is a short identifier that should be specific, so `get_account_balance` tells Claude far more than `get_data` or `tool1` does. The description does the heavier lifting, but a generic name throws away a free signal.

distractor_explanations.A: Claude does not pick tools by alphabetical order. It reads the name and the description.
distractor_explanations.B: The name should be a short identifier that is specific. A sentence in the name field is not the fix.
distractor_explanations.D: Claude reads the name and description to decide whether to call a tool. The input schema is a secondary signal.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: A team grows from one MCP server to six, all configured in a `.mcp.json` file that is committed to the repository. Where does the risk concentrate?

options.text: In the context window, where each server's tool definitions carry its secrets into the prompt that Claude reads.
In each server's stdio subprocess, where every extra process echoes its environment variables back to the other servers.
In the tool-result blocks, where each server logs the credentials it receives into the results it returns to Claude.
In the committed `.mcp.json`, because each added server is another place a credential could be written inline by mistake.

explanation: Adding MCP servers increases the number of places a secret could be mishandled, and the risk concentrates on the `.mcp.json` file because it is committed to the repository. A value written inline rides along with every clone and enters repository history, where overwriting it later does not remove it. The configuration file should hold only the server address and a variable reference, with the value kept in an environment variable.

distractor_explanations.A: Tool definitions add context cost, but they do not carry credentials into the prompt.
distractor_explanations.B: Servers do not share environment values with each other. The exposure comes from what is written in the committed file.
distractor_explanations.C: Credentials in a configuration file are not copied into tool results. The risk is the file entering version control.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: A team can connect a maintained MCP server for a service. Which situation still justifies writing tool schemas by hand instead?

options.text: The team wants to narrow the exposed tools, and a connected server's list cannot be restricted.
No server covers the use case, or the team needs description quality that a general server's tools lack.
The team wants Claude to route among the tools by description, and tools from an MCP server are chosen differently.
The service's API changes over time, and hand-written schemas are the way to stay in step with an evolving service.

explanation: Hand-written schemas make sense when no MCP server covers the use case, or when the team needs a precision of description quality that a general-purpose server does not offer. Scope control alone is not a reason, because the MCP Connector can allowlist and denylist tools per server. Analogy: buying a ready-made suit covers most people, and you only visit a tailor when no suit exists in your size or when the sleeve length has to be exact. Needing fewer pockets is a job the shop can do without custom cutting. The tempting wrong options treat scope or routing as things only a tailor can fix.

distractor_explanations.A: The API MCP Connector can allowlist or denylist tools per server through `mcp_toolset`, so scope alone does not justify manual work.
distractor_explanations.C: From Claude's side, MCP tools are selected through the same description-based routing as hand-written ones.
distractor_explanations.D: A maintained server tracks the service's current API. Keeping up with changes is a reason to prefer one.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: A team reviews why Claude confuses two of its tools. Which TWO statements about tool selection are accurate? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Claude chooses a tool by comparing the input schemas first, so identical parameter shapes do not cause confusion.
Claude routes on name plus description, with parameter types serving as a secondary signal for that choice.
Tools that do similar things are best kept apart by extending each description to several paragraphs of product detail.
Overlapping parameter types between tools are the most common source of wrong-tool calls made by an agent.
Adding more required fields to each schema is the usual way to keep two similar tools apart in practice.

explanation: Claude reads the tool name and the description to decide which tool fits, and treats parameter types as a secondary signal. When two tools accept the same parameter shape, routing collapses to the description alone, which is why overlapping parameter types are the most common source of wrong-tool calls. Analogy: two mailboxes with identical slot sizes cannot be told apart by the slot, so the labels on the front decide where the letter goes. If the labels also read alike, letters land in the wrong box. The tempting options add fields or words rather than clearer labels.

distractor_explanations.A: Claude relies on name and description first. Identical signatures push routing onto descriptions alone.
distractor_explanations.C: Overlong descriptions bury the trigger conditions. Exclusion conditions or a merge into one tool work better.
distractor_explanations.E: Marking fields required does not separate similar tools. Required fields are for inputs the call cannot do without.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: A team wants Claude to use a project-tracking service. A well-known MCP server for it already exists. Before choosing it over hand-written tool schemas, what should the team verify?

options.text: That the server covers the specific operations they need and is actively maintained against the service's current API as that API changes over time.
That the server uses the older SSE transport, which is the transport clients expect from third-party servers and hosted integrations.
That each tool description has been cut to a single sentence, so the server's definitions cost less context than hand-written ones.
That the server was written by the same team that owns the application, since only in-house servers can be connected by an MCP client.

explanation: When a well-maintained MCP server already exists, connecting to it saves writing and owning schemas for no extra capability, and from Claude's point of view the tools look the same as ones you wrote. The checks are whether it covers the specific operations you need and whether it is actively maintained against the service's current API. If not, writing your own schemas is the better path.

distractor_explanations.B: SSE-only is deprecated, and new integrations use Streamable HTTP for remote servers. Transport is not what decides adoption.
distractor_explanations.C: Tool definitions from a server still occupy context, and one-sentence descriptions route poorly. Coverage and maintenance are the checks.
distractor_explanations.D: Any MCP server can be connected by a client. Ownership is not a requirement.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: A developer inspecting a response sees a block of internal reasoning positioned just ahead of the block that holds the answer. Which setting must have been enabled?

options.text: Prompt caching, where a cache write stores a copy of the model's reasoning ahead of each cached answer in the reply.
Parallel tool use, where each tool call in a turn is preceded by a block that holds the model's planning notes.
Extended thinking, because a thinking block appears in a response only when extended thinking is enabled for it.
Structured outputs, which put the reasoning behind a schema-constrained response ahead of the JSON it returns.

explanation: A tool-use conversation is built from blocks: text, tool_use, tool_result, and thinking. The thinking block carries Claude's internal reasoning, sits just ahead of the block that holds the answer, and appears only when extended thinking is enabled. On the newest models its content is omitted by default unless a summarized display is requested.

distractor_explanations.A: Caching stores the processing work for a prefix. It does not produce reasoning blocks.
distractor_explanations.B: Parallel tool use adds more tool_use blocks. Reasoning appears as a thinking block only with extended thinking.
distractor_explanations.D: Structured outputs constrain the response against a schema. They do not add a reasoning block.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: A security lead reviews an agent that reads untrusted pages. Which statement describes the design the course recommends?

options.text: Layer several controls, so a bypass of one degrades the defense instead of collapsing it, because no layer is enough alone.
Rely on one strong hook, as an enforced control that runs deterministically makes the other layers redundant for the team.
Rely on a detailed system prompt, as clear wording of the rules is the control that holds when the other layers fail.
Rely on the model's training against injected instructions, as current models resist them well enough to need no other layer.

explanation: Security is layered, and each layer does a different job. The model's training and the classifiers lower how often an injection lands, treating fetched content as data lowers how often a landed one is acted on, and least privilege and hooks bound what an acted-on one can reach. No single layer is sufficient, and a defense that depends on one control holding is one bug away from an incident.

distractor_explanations.B: Hooks must name what they protect. A defense that depends on one control is one bug away from an incident.
distractor_explanations.C: A prompt instruction is not a security control. Enforcement belongs in hooks, identity, and isolation.
distractor_explanations.D: Training and classifiers are probabilistic. No agent that reads untrusted content is fully immune.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: A developer asks why Claude acted on a sentence hidden in a retrieved web page even though the system prompt said which instructions to follow. What is the underlying mechanism?

options.text: Claude follows instructions that sit inside XML tags, and the page used tags resembling the application's own formatting and structure.
Claude loses access to the system prompt once tool results are present, since it follows whichever text it can read at the time.
Retrieved pages receive higher priority than the system prompt, because text arriving later in the context overrides earlier instructions in it.
The model reads the system prompt, the user's message, and the page as one text stream, with no built-in marker of which tokens are trusted.

explanation: A model reads its entire context as one stream of tokens, so it has no built-in way to tell your instructions from instructions embedded in a page, document, or tool result that someone else wrote. That is the mechanism of prompt injection. Because the boundary is not in the text, the reliable defense is to treat fetched content as data and to constrain what the agent can do, rather than to word the prompt more carefully.

distractor_explanations.A: Models do not require tags to follow instructions. Delimiters help, but they are a soft boundary rather than a rule the model enforces.
distractor_explanations.B: The system prompt remains in context. The problem is that nothing separates it from injected text in the stream.
distractor_explanations.C: No such priority rule exists. The model treats everything in context together, with no structural marker of trust.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: A reviewer asks what each defense layer contributes against a hostile instruction hidden in fetched content. Which statement assigns the jobs correctly?

options.text: Least privilege lowers how often an injection lands, while training and classifiers bound what a successful action can go on to reach.
Hooks lower how often an injection lands by rewriting the page, while classifiers enforce the boundary before each tool call runs.
Training and classifiers cut how often injections land, data handling cuts how often they are acted on, and least privilege bounds reach.
Treating fetched content as data stops injections from landing at all, so least privilege matters for jailbreak attempts alone.

explanation: Each layer does a different job. The model's training and the classifiers over untrusted content reduce how often an injection lands. Treating fetched content as data reduces how often a landed injection is acted on. Least privilege and locked configuration bound what an acted-on instruction can reach, and hooks enforce those bounds before the action and record them. Analogy: a building has a guard who turns most strangers away, a sign saying visitors are not staff, locked doors, and a camera. Each handles a different failure, so removing the locks because the guard is good leaves the building exposed. The wrong options swap the jobs.

distractor_explanations.A: The jobs are reversed. Training and classifiers act on the model; identity scope bounds the damage.
distractor_explanations.B: Hooks enforce the boundary before a tool runs and log the attempt. They do not rewrite pages or stop injections from landing.
distractor_explanations.D: Data handling reduces how often an injection is acted on. It does not stop injections from landing, and least privilege applies to both threats.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: A reviewer asks what to log when a steered agent tries to reach a file path or network endpoint that no hook or permission rule names. Which entry fits?

options.text: Each attempted access outside the sandbox boundary, with the triggering tool call and the denied path or endpoint.
The fetched source, the action the agent attempted, and the block that stopped it, as for a prompt injection through content.
Each privileged action together with the identity that performed it, as for an identity scoped wider than its task.
The flagged prompt and the model's refusal of it, as for a jailbreak attempt aimed at the model's safety rules.

explanation: The defense checklist pairs each threat with what gets logged. A sandbox escape attempt, where a steered agent reaches for a path or endpoint that no hook or rule names, is logged as every attempted access outside the boundary together with the tool call that triggered it and the path or endpoint denied. Analogy: a building's door log for the fire exit records who pushed on a door they should not have, and which door, whereas the visitor book and the key-card list answer different questions. The wrong options are real entries for other rows of the table.

distractor_explanations.B: That is the entry for a prompt injection. A sandbox escape is logged by the access attempted and what was denied.
distractor_explanations.C: That entry fits over-broad access. For an escape attempt the record names the denied path or endpoint and the triggering call.
distractor_explanations.D: That is the entry for a jailbreak. A steered agent's out-of-bounds access is recorded as the attempt and its denial.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: A developer wants fewer prompts than default mode, but refuses to run in a full bypass on a machine that holds live credentials. Which mode fits, and what is its limit?

options.text: `acceptEdits`, which approves each shell command and file write on the machine, including paths outside the working directory.
`dontAsk`, which approves tool calls after a classifier review and is the usual way to cut friction on interactive local work.
`plan`, which approves edits once the plan is accepted and keeps a classifier on each later command.
Auto mode, where a classifier vets each action first; it is a research preview, not a replacement for review.

explanation: Auto mode approves actions after a separate classifier reviews each one first, blocking anything that escalates beyond the request, targets unrecognized infrastructure, or looks driven by hostile content. By default it blocks production deploys, mass deletes, credential exfiltration, and force-push to main. It reduces prompts without a full bypass, but it is a research preview that does not guarantee safety and does not replace reviewing sensitive operations.

distractor_explanations.A: `acceptEdits` approves edits and common filesystem commands inside the working directory. Other shell commands and protected paths still prompt.
distractor_explanations.B: `dontAsk` auto-denies everything not on an allow list. It is built for locked-down CI, not for reducing local friction.
distractor_explanations.C: Plan mode makes no edits and runs no commands until a plan is approved. It has no classifier.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: A feature returns the three capital cities of a region as a JSON array, and a correct run sometimes lists them in a different order than the reference. Which grading method fits best?

options.text: A code-graded check that parses the JSON and tests that all three cities are present, whatever order they appear in.
No automated grader at all, as outputs that vary from run to run cannot be scored by a program with any reliability.
Exact string match against the reference text, since the output has a single correct form that can be compared character by character.
An LLM judge with a rubric, as only a second model can tell whether a differently ordered list is still correct.

explanation: The grading method follows the shape of the output: one correct form takes an exact match, a structural rule takes a code check, and open-ended quality takes a judge. A JSON array of known cities has a rule that a function can validate, so a parse-and-membership check scores a reordered answer correctly at near-zero cost.

distractor_explanations.B: Code checks suit outputs that must satisfy a rule, such as valid JSON with the right members, even when the exact text varies.
distractor_explanations.C: A reordered but correct array would score zero, since exact match fails every valid reordering or paraphrase.
distractor_explanations.D: A rule that a function can validate does not need a judge. It would add cost and variance for no gain.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: A team building a claims assistant has already captured its requirements, including that data stay in one region. Now it picks the platform, chooses the model tier, and lists which inputs it will treat as untrusted. Which lifecycle phase is this work?

options.text: Build, which is where the team turns the settled choices into working code.
Deploy, which is where the version is pinned and promotion is gated on the eval against the pinned baseline.
Requirements, which is where the functional and infrastructure needs of the application are first captured.
Design, which is where the platform, the model, and the trust boundaries are chosen for the application.

explanation: The course lays the lifecycle out as requirements, design, build, test, deploy, operate, and iterate. Design is the phase in which the team chooses the platform, the model, and the trust boundaries, working from requirements that have already been captured. Build then writes the agent, tools, and prompts, and a regulated engagement does not move from design to build until the platform satisfies the residency requirement.

distractor_explanations.A: Build turns choices into working code. The platform, model, and boundaries are chosen before that work begins.
distractor_explanations.B: Deploy releases a specific version safely. It does not choose the platform or define trust boundaries.
distractor_explanations.C: Requirements were already captured in this scenario. Choosing the platform, model, and boundaries comes after them.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: A team is sorting its engineering tasks into lifecycle phases. Which TWO of these tasks belong in the build phase? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Writing the system prompt and the other prompts that the agent will run on once it is in production.
Feeding what the production logs show back into the requirements for the next release.
Running the eval suite and the integration checks against the system once it has been built.
Writing the agent loop and registering the tools that the agent is allowed to call during a run.
Instrumenting cost, latency, and error rate and enforcing guardrails once the system is live.

explanation: The lifecycle runs requirements, design, build, test, deploy, operate, and iterate. The build phase is where the agent, its tools, and its prompts are written. Running checks on the built system belongs to test, feeding production findings back belongs to iterate, and instrumenting a live system belongs to operate.

distractor_explanations.B: Feeding production findings back into the requirements is iterate-phase work, after release.
distractor_explanations.C: Running evals and integration checks against a built system is test-phase work.
distractor_explanations.E: Instrumenting and guarding a live system is operate-phase work.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: A developer assumes that a streamed response is one live message object that the API holds open and keeps updating. What actually arrives?

options.text: A series of small events, each describing one change, which the handler applies to the partial message it builds.
A sequence of full messages, each replacing the one before it, so the handler keeps the latest and discards the rest.
A complete message sent in one piece after generation ends, with the events used as progress indicators.
A single message object that the API updates in place, which the handler reads whenever it needs the current content.

explanation: In a streamed request the API sends a series of events that describe the message as it is being built: a block started, a fragment added, a block finished, the message finished. Each event is its own small message describing a single change, and the model is not holding a live object open. The handler applies each event to the partial state it has built so far, and the message it ends up with is identical to a non-streamed one.

distractor_explanations.B: Events describe single changes such as a block starting or a fragment being added. They are not repeated full messages.
distractor_explanations.C: The events are the response. The handler reassembles the message from them as they arrive.
distractor_explanations.D: The API does not hold a live object open. Each event is its own small message.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: A team spends a sprint tuning the step of a flow that it assumes is the slowest, and end-to-end latency barely moves. What does the observability guidance say to do?

options.text: Record latency per call with traces, because the slow step is rarely the one expected and timing shows which it is.
Add streaming to each step, which lowers the total generation time of every call in the flow.
Move the whole flow to a smaller model, since the model tier is the main source of delay in a flow.
Trust the team's own sense of which step is slowest and keep tuning that one, since the developers know the flow best.

explanation: Latency is invisible in development and decisive in production, and the slow step is rarely the one a team expected. Per-call timing, together with a trace of the run, shows which step is responsible, so optimization goes where it matters instead of where intuition points. Analogy: a restaurant owner who assumes the grill is slow may find with a stopwatch that plates wait at the pass for a runner. The stopwatch is per-call timing, the pass is the slow step, and the wrong options trust the owner's hunch or change the kitchen without measuring.

distractor_explanations.B: Streaming changes how latency is perceived by a user. It does not shorten the total time a step takes.
distractor_explanations.C: A model change may help, but without per-call timing the team cannot tell it is the right lever.
distractor_explanations.D: The slow step is rarely the one a team expects, which is why the sprint of tuning failed. Per-call timing identifies it.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: A backend service calls Claude for a short summary inside a larger pipeline, and no person watches the output arrive. Which call style fits best?

options.text: A non-streamed call, which is simpler and removes the partial-state risk that comes with assembling a stream.
A streamed call kept open for the whole run, as an open stream is what keeps a job inside its rate limits.
A streamed call, as partial output should be committed to history the moment each event arrives in the loop and kept.
A streamed call, as streaming lowers the token price of long outputs for each kind of workload that runs.

explanation: Streaming pays off for long responses and user-facing interfaces, where showing output as it generates removes the blank-screen wait. For short responses or backend jobs where no one is waiting, a non-streamed call is simpler and removes the partial-state risk entirely, since the full message arrives as one object.

distractor_explanations.B: Rate limits do not depend on whether a call streams.
distractor_explanations.C: A turn is committed only after `message_stop`. Committing partial output corrupts history.
distractor_explanations.D: Streaming changes how latency is perceived. It does not change the token price.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: An agent's `lookup_price` tool wraps a vendor API. It sometimes fails with a read timeout and sometimes with `unknown SKU format`. The wrapper retries every failure three times, then returns an empty string. What is the right handling?

options.text: Retry neither failure, and raise each tool error to the end user outside the loop, treating tool errors as terminal.
Skip the retries and pass the vendor's raw error text back as ordinary result content, with no error flag on the block.
Retry the timeout, whose cause is transient, but not the bad SKU; return a final failure with `is_error: true` for Claude.
Keep retrying both failures and return the empty string if the attempts run out, so Claude can fall back on its own knowledge.

explanation: For a tool-result error the course's decision table says retriability depends on the tool: retry only when the underlying cause is transient, and hand the failure back to Claude with the error flag instead of silencing it. A timeout may clear on retry, while a malformed SKU will fail the same way every time. Analogy: a courier who finds a locked gate tries again in a few minutes, but when the address does not exist, he leaves a note saying so instead of returning an empty box. The note is `is_error: true`, and the empty box is the blank string that Claude would treat as a real delivery.

distractor_explanations.A: Whether a tool error is retriable depends on the tool and its cause. Raising it outside the loop also denies Claude the chance to adapt.
distractor_explanations.B: Without the error flag the model cannot tell a failure from data. The block has to carry `is_error: true`.
distractor_explanations.D: An empty result looks like valid data, so Claude continues on a false premise. A malformed SKU also fails identically on every retry.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: A team wants to know how close it is to its limit while calling the API. What do the rate-limit headers on each response tell it?

options.text: Whether the request should be retried, with 429 and 529 marked retriable and 400 and 401 marked terminal.
How many tokens the request used and what it cost, so no separate instrumentation is needed for spend.
Which model tier handled the request, and whether the response was read back from a prompt cache.
How much of the limit remains and when it resets, with `retry-after` giving the wait after a 429 or 529.

explanation: The API returns rate-limit headers on every response that say how much of the limit remains and when it resets. The most useful is `retry-after`, which a 429 or 529 includes to say how long to wait before trying again. It is the authoritative wait when present, and the team's own backoff is the fallback when it is absent.

distractor_explanations.A: The retriable-versus-terminal decision comes from the status code, not from the rate-limit headers.
distractor_explanations.B: Token usage comes from the usage fields the API returns. Per-call instrumentation is still the team's job.
distractor_explanations.C: Rate-limit headers describe limit usage and reset timing, not the tier or the cache.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: A team ships a working agent under deadline and plans to parameterize it and write its documentation once the next engagement starts. What does the packaging guidance say about that plan?

options.text: It is fine, as a bundled eval can be written at a later date without the context of the original engagement.
It costs more later, because why a value was hardcoded is hardest to rebuild once its authors have left.
It is fine, since the source code already communicates the assumptions that a later team will need to know.
It saves effort, since parameters chosen before a second customer exists tend to fit that customer poorly.

explanation: Packaging for reuse is cheaper while the build is fresh. The knowledge of what is customer-specific, and why a value was hardcoded, is most expensive to reconstruct once the people who held it have moved on. Analogy: a cook who writes the recipe the same evening records every pinch and timing, while a cook asked months later has only a taste memory and a stained card. The build is the dish, the parameters and documentation are the recipe, and the tempting wrong options assume the dish itself explains how it was made.

distractor_explanations.A: The eval that defines whether the asset still works is best written while the build and its intent are fresh.
distractor_explanations.C: Code describes behavior. Environment assumptions and the reasons behind values are what a future builder cannot infer from it.
distractor_explanations.D: Packaging while the build is fresh is cheaper than reconstructing the intent months later.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: A service's SDK client is set to make up to 3 attempts per call, counting the first try. The team's own wrapper also makes up to 4 attempts at each logical call. During a sustained rate-limit episode, what is the worst-case number of requests one logical call can send?

options.text: 4, on the basis that the wrapper's cap overrides the SDK and stops its retrying once the wrapper takes over.
12, since each of the wrapper's 4 attempts can trigger up to 3 SDK attempts, so the two layers multiply rather than add.
3, on the basis that the SDK's limit applies to the whole logical call, whatever happens to wrap it.
7, because the two limits add together: 4 wrapper attempts plus the 3 attempts the SDK makes in total.

explanation: Two retry loops around one call multiply attempts rather than cap them. Each of the wrapper's four attempts is a new SDK call that can itself try three times, so one logical call can send 4 x 3 = 12 requests. That is the reason the course says to decide where the retry lives and not to stack both.

distractor_explanations.A: Neither layer knows about the other. The SDK keeps retrying inside each wrapper attempt.
distractor_explanations.C: The SDK limit counts attempts per call it receives, and the wrapper makes a fresh call on each of its attempts.
distractor_explanations.D: The SDK's attempts happen inside every wrapper attempt, so the counts multiply rather than add.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: A five-step document flow logs input tokens, output tokens, and latency for every call. The dashboard shows step 3 accounts for about 90% of the spend, though all five steps look alike in code. Where should optimization start?

options.text: On adding streaming to each step, because streaming lowers the token cost of long outputs in a flow like this.
On step 3, with the lever that fits it, such as trimming its context, cutting its tool calls, or using a smaller model.
On the monthly invoice total, because billing figures are more dependable than per-step measurements taken in code for budgeting.
On all five steps equally, so each shrinks by the same percentage and no single step becomes a bottleneck.

explanation: Per-call logging turns a mysterious bill into rows you can sort, and a flow that looks evenly expensive often has one step doing most of the spending. Optimization effort belongs there, using whichever lever matches the cause: model choice, prompt and context size, number of tool calls, or caching. Streaming and batching address latency perception and scheduling, not the token count of a given step.

distractor_explanations.A: Streaming changes how fast output appears to a user. It does not reduce the tokens a step consumes.
distractor_explanations.C: The total cannot say which step is expensive. Per-call metrics exist to answer that question.
distractor_explanations.D: Spreading effort evenly spends most of it on steps that hold little of the bill. The data shows where the money goes.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: A user-facing flow's design sets a four-second latency ceiling and allows three retries per dependency. To save money on a slow dependency, a developer proposes cutting the retries from three to two. What should decide whether to accept it?

options.text: Nothing, given that retries consume tokens and the floor merely caps how high spending is allowed to go.
Whether the failure rate with two retries still meets the reliability floor, since otherwise the saving is paid for in failed requests.
Nothing needs deciding, given that a retry count belongs to the floor and can never change once it has been chosen.
Whether the monthly bill drops enough to matter, since cost is the louder signal and the retry count should closely follow it.

explanation: The reliability floor, built from a retry budget and a latency ceiling, is the line below which cost savings do not go. Cutting retries from three to two is acceptable only if the failure rate it produces still satisfies the floor; otherwise the team has swapped a lower bill for more failed requests. Analogy: a bridge builder may swap a heavier steel beam for a lighter one to save money only if the bridge still carries the rated load. The load rating is the floor, the beam swap is the retry cut, and the loudness of the budget does not change the rating.

distractor_explanations.A: The floor is a reliability baseline, and a retry budget is part of it. It does not limit spending.
distractor_explanations.C: The floor is a boundary to stay above, not a frozen setting. A change is acceptable if it still meets the floor.
distractor_explanations.D: Cost is tuned above the floor and does not set it. A saving that crosses the floor replaces a visible cost with silent failures.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: A team builds a packaging checklist for reusable assets. Which TWO assignments of what to document to asset type are correct? (Select TWO.)

options.text: An agent template: the rubric logic and what the scores mean, as each template ships with its own judge.

An eval suite: the rubric logic, what the scores mean, and the baseline that the asset is pinned to.

An eval suite: the expected inputs for each tool and its scope boundaries, as the suite acts on the customer's system.

explanation: Each asset type documents what a future builder cannot infer from its source. An eval suite documents the rubric logic, what scores mean, and the baseline it is pinned to, while an MCP server documents each tool's expected inputs, its scope boundaries, and the failure modes it handles. Analogy: a sports league handbook explains the scoring rules and the current record to beat, while a stadium manual lists which gates open to whom and what happens in a power cut. Swapping the manuals leaves both readers stuck. The wrong options swap which asset needs which notes.

distractor_explanations.A: An agent template documents its environment assumptions, expected inputs, handled failure modes, and the eval that defines working.
distractor_explanations.B: The rubric and baseline describe an eval suite. A server documents tool inputs, scope boundaries, and failure modes.
distractor_explanations.E: Tool inputs and scope boundaries are documented for an MCP server. An eval suite documents its rubric and pinned baseline.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: Per-call logs for a travel assistant show ordinary prompt sizes and a modest model tier, but one flow makes nine sequential tool calls where four would give the same answer. Users complain about latency and cost. Which lever do the numbers point to?

options.text: Model selection, by moving to a larger tier so that each call completes faster and the flow needs fewer round trips.
Streaming, which cuts the cost of every tool call by delivering each tool result to the model in smaller pieces.
The number of tool calls, since each call adds cost and latency and extra calls are a measurable source of waste.
Prompt caching, because a cache read makes the repeated calls nearly free and so addresses both complaints at once.

explanation: The course lists four measurable levers: model selection, prompt and context size, the number of tool calls, and streamed versus batched output with caching. When the logs show normal prompts but a flow that makes more calls than it needs, the call count is the lever, because every call adds both cost and latency. Per-call instrumentation is what makes this visible.

distractor_explanations.A: The logs show redundant calls, not a weak model. A bigger tier raises per-call cost without removing the extra calls.
distractor_explanations.B: Streaming affects how a response arrives to a user, and it does not change how many calls the flow makes.
distractor_explanations.D: Caching reduces the cost of a repeated stable prefix. It does not remove the round trips or their latency.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)

The plugin replaces a page of manual setup steps with a versioned, auditable install.

distractor_explanations.B: `.mcp.json` holds MCP server configuration. Marketplaces are added through the plugin command.

Analogy: a hotel concierge gives directions to the hotel's own gym from the lobby, and to a guest's own car from the parking garage entrance; each starting point has to match what you are looking for. The plugin root is the lobby, the project directory is the garage, and a bare relative path assumes everyone is standing in the same spot.

distractor_explanations.B: The project's `schema-check.sh` is not inside the plugin, so a plugin-root path would not find it.
distractor_explanations.C: A relative path depends on the directory the session started in, which varies, and it would freeze a copy of the project's script.
distractor_explanations.D: Bundled plugin files live under the plugin root. The project directory is where the teammate's own scripts live.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: A team is asked to package a bespoke script for a customer who has said that no other engagement will reuse it. What does the packaging guidance say?

options.text: Contribute it to the Cookbook instead, as a bespoke customer script is the best fit for a focused reference example.

Ship the build and move on, because the packaging overhead is not worth it for a one-off that will never be reused.

distractor_explanations.A: The Cookbook is for focused, self-contained patterns. A bespoke customer script does not match that channel.
distractor_explanations.B: That knowledge is expensive to reconstruct later. The better reason to skip packaging is that this asset will not be reused.
distractor_explanations.D: Packaging adds real time to the first build. For a one-off no one will reuse, that overhead is not worth paying.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)

distractor_explanations.C: Engagement code may carry licensing constraints and is not rebuilt for installers. The packaged asset travels as a unit.

prompt: A team is packaging two assets from an engagement for reuse. Which TWO statements match the asset type to the right packaging? (Select TWO.)

An agent template bundles the prompt, tool schemas, and loop, with per-customer values moved into configuration with documented defaults.

Analogy: a board game box includes the board, pieces, and rulebook together so any family can play, while the kind of game decides what goes inside. The template is the playbook with adjustable house rules, and the eval suite is the scoring sheet plus the practice rounds. Hardcoding values or sending loose scripts is like handing over a hand-drawn board.

distractor_explanations.C: Hardcoded values force the next team to rewrite the template, which is the failure packaging is meant to prevent.
distractor_explanations.D: Copied scripts diverge. A parameterized template lets teams configure one asset instead.
distractor_explanations.E: The installing team should set the scopes, so the server installs into a new environment without code edits.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: A 20,000-token system prompt is marked for caching with the default five-minute lifetime. Three requests send it two minutes apart, and then no more arrive. Counting only that prefix, how does the total input cost compare with sending it uncached three times?

options.text: Lower: about 1.45 prefix-units, one 1.25x write plus two 0.1x reads, against 3.0 units for three uncached sends.
About 0.3 units: cached reads bill at 0.1x, and all three requests count as reads once caching is switched on.
Higher: each request inside the window pays the 1.25x write again, so about 3.75 units against 3.0 uncached.
Equal: the one-time write premium and the two read discounts roughly cancel out across three sends of the prefix.

explanation: Cache writes cost more than base input (1.25x for the five-minute lifetime) and reads cost 0.1x, so caching pays when reads outnumber writes. Here one write is followed by two reads inside the window: 1.25 + 0.1 + 0.1 = 1.45 units, against 3.0 for three uncached sends. Analogy: laminating a menu costs a little more than printing one paper copy, but after that every diner reads the same laminated card for almost nothing. The lamination fee is the 1.25x write, each diner reading it is a 0.1x read, and the more diners per card the better the deal. Charging the write premium on every request misreads the mechanism: only the first request writes, and the later ones read while the cache is still warm.

distractor_explanations.B: The first request has to write the cache, at a premium. Only the later request that hits the cache reads at 0.1x.
distractor_explanations.C: Only the first request writes the cache. The two later requests inside the five-minute window read it at 0.1x.
distractor_explanations.D: They do not cancel. A 25% premium paid once against two 90% discounts leaves a large net saving.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: A developer expects a cache hit to return the stored answer to an identical request and skip generation. What does a hit actually save?

options.text: The output tokens only, as a hit reuses the earlier answer while the input is still reprocessed from scratch.
The whole request, since a hit replays the earlier output and the model generates nothing for the repeated request.
The tokenization of the latest user message, as a hit stores the tokens of the newest turn for the next request.
The processing work for the cached input prefix; the model still generates a fresh response to the new request.

explanation: Before the model generates anything, it processes the input, and on an ordinary request that work is thrown away once the response returns. Prompt caching stores the processing work for a stable prefix so a later request can read it back instead of recomputing it. The response itself is still generated fresh each time. Analogy: a library that keeps a pre-built index card for a heavy reference book saves you from re-reading the book's contents page every visit, but you still ask a new question and get a new answer. The wrong options imagine the answer being replayed.

distractor_explanations.A: Caching works on the input side: the processing of the stable prefix is what is reused.
distractor_explanations.B: A hit reads back processed input. The response is still generated each time.
distractor_explanations.C: A hit reuses the processing of a stable prefix. The newest message is not what gets cached.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: A team wants to cache a large prefix that includes a product-availability table the warehouse updates every few minutes. Besides the minimum length, what is the key trade-off to weigh before doing so?

options.text: Every cache read is re-validated against the source, which adds latency that cancels most of the saving.
A cached copy may be stale for as long as it lives, so the use case has to tolerate that consistency window.
Each time the table changes, the extra processing is billed at the one-hour write rate of 2x.
Changing data is not allowed in a prefix, because the API rejects a request whose cached content differs from before.

explanation: Caching stores processing work for a stretch of content and assumes that content is still correct on the later request. If the prefix reflects data that can change, the cache may hold an out-of-date version for as long as it lives, a consistency window your use case must be able to tolerate. A fixed system prompt or stable tool schema has nothing to go stale, which is why they are the safe, high-value things to cache. Analogy: a printed daily specials board is cheap to reuse all lunch, but it will show a sold-out dish until someone reprints it. The board is the cached prefix, the kitchen's live stock is the changing table, and the staleness is the price of not reprinting. Treating cache reads as re-validated is the tempting mistake.

distractor_explanations.A: Reads reuse stored processing work and are not re-validated against any source, so the data can lag behind reality.
distractor_explanations.C: The write rate depends on the lifetime you chose, and a data change does not switch it to the one-hour rate.
distractor_explanations.D: Nothing is rejected. A changed prefix simply fails to match, and the cost of that miss is a fresh write.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: A request marks a cache breakpoint at the end of a long system prompt, and the user message changes on every turn. How is the user message handled?

options.text: It is skipped by the API until the cache lifetime expires, with the message billed on the first turn of a session.
It is added to the cache on first use, so a repeated question is read back from the cache on later requests.
It is processed normally each time, because content after the last breakpoint is not part of the cached prefix.
It invalidates the cached system prompt, so each new message forces a fresh write of the whole request.

explanation: A cache breakpoint marks the last block to cache, and the cache covers everything up to and including that block. Content after the last breakpoint is processed normally on each request. That is why a long, stable system prompt is a good candidate while a user message that changes every turn simply follows it.

distractor_explanations.A: Every request carries and bills its own new message. Nothing is skipped.
distractor_explanations.B: Only content up to and including the marked block is cached. Later content is processed normally.
distractor_explanations.D: The cached prefix is matched on its own content. A different message after the breakpoint does not invalidate it.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: A team budgets an orchestrator-worker feature at about fifteen times a single agent's tokens. In production, a subagent loops and a tool returns an oversized result. What happens to the budget?

options.text: The cost can climb well past the fifteen-times baseline, so that figure is an estimate and not a ceiling.

It doubles to thirty times exactly, with a runaway doubling the baseline multiplier for these designs by rule.
It stays at fifteen times, as the multiplier is set by the number of subagents and is fixed during a run.

explanation: In an orchestrator-worker design every subagent spends its own tokens against its own context, and Anthropic reports roughly fifteen times a normal chat as the baseline. That multiplier compounds when something misbehaves: a runaway subagent or an oversized tool result can push well past it before the request completes. A team that budgets at fifteen times is treating the baseline as a ceiling when it is closer to a floor.

distractor_explanations.B: Each loop adds more tokens against that subagent's context, which raises the cost.
distractor_explanations.C: There is no fixed doubling. The overrun depends on how far the loop and the result size go.
distractor_explanations.D: The multiplier is a reported baseline. A runaway subagent or an oversized result can push well past it.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)

distractor_explanations.B: The family evolves, and identifiers and the lineup change over time, so they must be confirmed.
distractor_explanations.D: An alias resolves to a recommended version that updates over time. A pinned full model ID is the fixed snapshot.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: A nightly batch of 40,000 records was submitted five hours ago and still shows as in progress. An engineer wants to cancel it and rerun the records through synchronous calls. What is the better judgment?

options.text: Cancel and rerun, on the view that any batch not finished within a few hours has failed and will not recover.

distractor_explanations.A: Batches complete within an asynchronous window of up to 24 hours. A slow batch is not a failed one.
distractor_explanations.C: This pays twice for the same work and gains nothing, since results arrive within the same window.
distractor_explanations.D: The lower price belongs to the batch pattern. Synchronous calls cost more and loop into rate limits at this volume.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: A team is adding token counting to its pipeline. Which TWO statements about using `count_tokens` are accurate? (Select TWO.)

options.text: It counts the user's message alone, as tool definitions and tool results are metered outside the window.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: A team's agent must call a proprietary command-line binary that is installed only on its own build servers. They are weighing Claude Managed Agents. Which consideration does this raise?

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: A team is picking a wiring path for a production agent and is tempted to take whichever is fastest to prototype. What should decide the choice?

options.text: The size of the tool set, as a raw loop is the one path that can register many tools without extra configuration.
Deployment and compliance constraints, because the path decides how much of the runtime the team owns and maintains.
The model tier in use, since each wiring path supports a different set of tiers.
Prototype speed, as the quickest path to a first demo is also the cheapest one to change later.

explanation: A single-agent system is the same pattern on all three wiring paths: a loop that calls tools, manages context, and runs until a goal is met. What changes is how much of the loop the team writes versus hands to a library or a hosted service, so the path decides who maintains the surrounding parts. That makes deployment and compliance constraints the right basis for choosing. Analogy: whether you cook at home, order a meal kit, or eat at a restaurant, the meal is still dinner. You choose by your kitchen, allergies, and budget, not by which is quickest to try once.

distractor_explanations.A: Tool registration works the same on every path. Tool count does not select the path.
distractor_explanations.C: Wiring paths are not tied to model tiers. They differ in how much of the runtime the team owns.
distractor_explanations.D: Speed to prototype is the temptation to avoid. The choice rests on deployment and compliance constraints.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: A design splits a task across a planner, an executor, and an evaluator running as separate agents. How do these agents hand work to one another?

options.text: Through structured artifacts, which adds design decisions beyond the loop that a single agent needs.
Through the model's own memory, which each agent reads automatically at the start of each turn it runs.
Through a copy of the planner's full context window, handed to each agent as its starting state in turn.
Through one shared conversation history that the three agents append to and read in full on each turn.

explanation: Multi-agent architectures, where a planner, an executor, and an evaluator run as separate agents, hand off through structured artifacts, and that introduces design decisions beyond the loop itself. Each agent keeps its own context, and the artifact is what crosses between them. Analogy: in a relay race the baton, not the runner's whole memory of the lap, is what passes between teammates. The artifact is the baton, and the wrong options imagine runners sharing one head or copying the first runner's brain.

distractor_explanations.B: Memory has to be designed and scoped. It is not shared between agents automatically.
distractor_explanations.C: Copying a full context window defeats the purpose of separate contexts. Agents exchange structured artifacts instead.
distractor_explanations.D: Each agent works from its own context. Work passes between them as structured artifacts.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: A company on AWS wants Claude Managed Agents and plans to reach it through Claude Platform on AWS. What should it do before committing?

options.text: Plan on stateless sessions, since an AWS-hosted deployment avoids storing sessions on the server side.
Move to Amazon Bedrock instead, since Managed Agents is offered through Bedrock's InvokeModel API and nowhere else on AWS.
Nothing further, since the platform exposes the first-party API unchanged, with features identical to it in each respect.
Verify capability parity for that deployment surface, since Managed Agents there has some feature differences.

explanation: The course lists Claude Managed Agents as also available on Claude Platform on AWS with some feature differences, and tells you to verify capability parity against your deployment surface before committing. The feature is also a public beta, so building with a migration plan in place is sensible.

distractor_explanations.A: Sessions are stateful and stored server-side, which is also why they fall outside ZDR and HIPAA BAA coverage.
distractor_explanations.B: Managed Agents is not limited to Bedrock, and nothing in the course ties it to InvokeModel.
distractor_explanations.C: Managed Agents is available there with some feature differences, so parity has to be checked.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: A team compares wiring paths for a production agent. Which TWO statements are accurate? (Select TWO.)

options.text: With the Agent SDK the SDK also executes each tool the agent calls, so the team just writes the exit conditions.
With a raw Messages API loop the API itself runs the iteration, so the team only sends the request and reads the final message.
With Claude Managed Agents, the app sends user events and streams results back while Anthropic runs the loop and the sandbox.
The same four steps hold on each path: register tools, set a scoped system prompt, handle the tool-use loop, define exits.
With Managed Agents the team writes the iteration loop and hands the sandbox to Anthropic, which provisions it per session.

explanation: The four steps of the loop are constant across paths: register tools, set a system prompt scoped to the task, handle the tool-use loop, and define exit conditions. What differs is how much you write versus inherit. On Claude Managed Agents, Anthropic runs the loop and the sandbox while the application sends user events and streams results back over server-sent events. Analogy: a restaurant's recipe has the same steps whether you cook at home, use a meal kit, or are served at a table. What changes is who stands at the stove. The wrong options misplace the stove.

distractor_explanations.A: With the Agent SDK the team's code still executes the tools. The SDK supplies the loop structure and context management.
distractor_explanations.B: On a raw loop the team's own code runs every iteration, executing the tools and appending the results.
distractor_explanations.E: On Managed Agents, Anthropic runs both the loop and the sandbox.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: A team reviews how an agent's context grows over a long session. Which TWO statements about tool results are accurate? (Select TWO.)

options.text: The API trims the oldest tool results automatically, so a long session does not reach the window limit.
Every tool result is appended to the context window and stays there for the rest of the session.
Tool results count against the output budget, so they leave the input side of the window untouched.
Once the window fills, the agent either compacts and loses detail or stalls before the task is finished.
A tool result is dropped from the window after the next turn, so only the latest result counts against the budget.

explanation: In a single-turn prompt the cost of tool results is invisible, but in an agent session that runs ten or twenty tool calls the window fills fast. Every tool result Claude returns is appended to the context window and stays for the rest of the session. Once the window fills, the agent either compacts, losing detail, or stalls before the task is done.
