distractor_explanations.A: The API never trims history silently. The application has to prune or summarize.
distractor_explanations.C: Tool results are part of the input that fills the context window.
distractor_explanations.E: Tool results accumulate for the rest of the session unless the application prunes them.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: After a 15-turn debugging detour proved unproductive, a developer rewinds to the message before it and continues from there. During the detour Claude had learned how the project's test fixtures are laid out. What happens to that knowledge?

options.text: It is written to CLAUDE.md, which Claude updates itself whenever the conversation is rewound.
It is condensed into a summary that is carried forward automatically into the continued session.
It stays available, since rewinding only hides the later messages on screen while Claude keeps them in context.
It is gone along with the rewound turns, so Claude has to relearn it unless the developer states it again.

explanation: Pruning lets you jump back to an earlier message and continue from there, which removes everything that came after. That is ideal for an unproductive path, but whatever Claude learned during the removed stretch is lost, so it must be restated or relearned. Compaction, by contrast, keeps a condensed record of the history.

distractor_explanations.A: Rewinding does not edit CLAUDE.md. Anything worth keeping has to be put there deliberately.
distractor_explanations.B: Summarizing is what compaction does. Pruning simply discards the later turns.
distractor_explanations.C: Rewinding removes the conversation that came after the chosen message, so Claude no longer has it.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: A team building a long-horizon agent decides up front what enters the context window, what comes back out as a summary, and what never enters at all. A manager asks why not wait until the agent reaches its limit. What is the best answer?

options.text: Making these decisions later means refactoring under production pressure, while the same choices cost little during design.
Compaction and pruning cannot be added to an agent after it has shipped, so they must exist in the first release.
The window limit applies to the model's output alone, so input size can be reviewed once replies begin to truncate.
A full window is trimmed silently by the API, so waiting costs nothing until answer quality begins to drop.

explanation: Context engineering is the practice of deciding in advance what goes into the window, what comes back out as a summary, and what never enters. The course notes that the refactor to move state out of the live context is mechanical, but doing it under production pressure costs timing and attention, whereas making the call in the design phase is cheap. Deferring it also hides the problem, because development inputs are short and the window rarely fills until real traffic arrives.

distractor_explanations.B: They can be added later, but the work then lands during a deadline, which is what makes it expensive.
distractor_explanations.C: The window holds the input and the output together, so input size is part of the budget from the start.
distractor_explanations.D: The API does not silently drop turns. An oversized request fails validation, and generation can stop at the ceiling.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: A developer compacts a long coding session. How does the summary compare with the original turns?

options.text: It costs more tokens than the original, since the summary is stored alongside the turns that it replaces.
It costs fewer tokens and keeps the key information Claude has learned, though some detail can be lost.
It costs nothing, as a summary is not counted toward the context window once compaction has happened.
It costs the same number of tokens as the original turns, as compaction only reorders the history it received.

explanation: Compaction summarizes the conversation history into a condensed version that preserves the key information Claude has learned, and the summary costs fewer tokens than the original turns. The trade-off is that details can be lost in the summarization, and anything not captured in the summary will not be available to Claude going forward.

distractor_explanations.A: The summary replaces the turns and is shorter than them.
distractor_explanations.C: The summary sits in the context window and counts toward it, just at a smaller size.
distractor_explanations.D: Compaction condenses the history, and the summary costs fewer tokens than the original turns.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: An agent is capped at 40,000 tokens by its team as a cost control, though its model's window is at least 200,000. In production, tool results average four times the size seen in testing, and the cap is reached at turn eight. What should the team have done before shipping?

options.text: Lowered `max_tokens`, leaving each reply more room in the window for the tool output that accumulates.
Moved to a model with a 1M-token window, since a bigger window removes the need to manage context in long sessions.
Tested on a larger number of short fixtures, keeping the average result per call comfortably under the cap.
Measured tool-result sizes against the largest real inputs, then planned pruning and compaction ahead of the cap.

explanation: In development test inputs are short, and in production tool outputs are often three to five times longer, so a window that held twenty turns fills at turn eight. The course's remedy is to measure the token cost of a tool result against the largest input you can find in the target data before shipping, then prune after use and compact before the budget is reached. Here the 40,000 cap was a deliberate team budget, not a model limit.

distractor_explanations.A: `max_tokens` limits the length of Claude's reply and does not change how much tool output accumulates.
distractor_explanations.B: The 40,000 cap was a budget the team chose. A larger window does not stop outputs from crowding out instructions.
distractor_explanations.C: Short fixtures are the problem. Production inputs were several times larger than what testing used.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: A research agent running on a 1M-token window still fails on a long-horizon task whose work will not fit in one context. A teammate suggests simply asking for an even larger window. What approach does the course favor?

options.text: Pass the parent's complete history to each subagent, so that each of them starts with the full picture of the task.
Merge each subagent's full context back into the parent after each step, so that no detail is ever lost along the way.
Move the state into the system prompt, where it is cached and costs nothing to reread, however large it grows over the task.
Decompose the task, giving each subagent a scoped job, the minimal relevant context, its own tools, and clear exit conditions.

explanation: When a task is too large for one context window, a bigger window is not the answer. The solution is to decompose the work and pass each subagent a scoped task, the minimum relevant context, its tools, and clear exit conditions, with the parent collecting results. Analogy: a general contractor does not hand every subcontractor the entire filing cabinet of blueprints; the plumber gets the plumbing pages and a deadline, and reports back. The filing cabinet is the full history, each subcontractor is a subagent with its own scoped window, and the summary report is what returns. Copying everything to everyone is the tempting shortcut that brings the overflow back.

distractor_explanations.A: Handing over everything defeats the purpose. A subagent should start with only what its task needs.
distractor_explanations.B: Merging contexts recreates the overflow. The parent should collect results, not every intermediate step.
distractor_explanations.C: A growing system prompt still occupies the window, and cached reads are discounted, not free.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: A colleague asks how classical retrieval-augmented generation differs from agentic search. Which TWO statements are accurate? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Claude Code loading only the MCP tools a task needs is an example of agentic search rather than a pre-built index.
Agentic search needs a vector database to be built before the first question is asked, which classical RAG avoids.
Classical RAG fetches live files at the moment of each question, so it never needs a maintained index of any kind.
Both forms load the whole source library into the prompt, and differ only in how the library is split into pieces.
Classical RAG chunks the sources and builds embeddings in advance, while agentic search skips upfront indexing.

explanation: Both forms of retrieval find a relevant slice of material and generate from it, and the difference is timing. Classical RAG does the work upfront: it splits the sources into chunks, converts each to an embedding, and matches a question against that index. Agentic search skips the index and fetches what it needs at the moment of need, as Claude Code does when it loads only the MCP tools a task calls for.

distractor_explanations.B: It is the other way round: classical RAG builds an index in advance, and agentic search does not.
distractor_explanations.C: Fetching at the moment of need is agentic search. Classical RAG matches against an index built in advance.
distractor_explanations.D: Both find a relevant slice of material and generate from it. Neither loads the whole library.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: A developer wants a personal SQLite MCP tool available in every project on their laptop, without adding anything to any repository or exposing it to teammates. Which scope fits?

options.text: User scope, kept in personal settings and available across all of the developer's projects on the laptop.
Local scope, since it applies to every project on the machine without being shared with any teammate.
Enterprise scope, deployed to the developer's laptop through administrator-managed configuration.
Project scope, by adding the server to the `.mcp.json` file in the root of each repository it is used in.

explanation: MCP configuration scope decides who loads a server. User scope stores the server in personal Claude settings and makes it available across all of your projects, while staying personal: teammates do not see it and it is not written into the repository. Local scope is limited to one project, project scope travels with the repository, and enterprise scope is pushed by an administrator.

distractor_explanations.B: Local scope covers only the current project, stored under that project's path in `~/.claude.json`.
distractor_explanations.C: Enterprise scope is for servers an administrator pushes to the whole organization.
distractor_explanations.D: That would put the configuration in every repository and share it with everyone who clones it.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: A CI job runs Claude Code in `dontAsk` mode with a single allow rule, `mcp__github__list_pull_requests`. During a run, Claude tries `mcp__github__create_issue`, which has no rule. What happens?

options.text: The call runs, because an allow rule on one tool of a server extends to the server's other tools as well.
The call waits for confirmation in the CI log, since MCP tools without a rule fall back to prompting in this mode.
The call is denied automatically with no prompt, because `dontAsk` permits only the tools on its allow list.
The call runs as a dry run, since write-capable tools are downgraded to read-only in locked-down modes.

explanation: `dontAsk` mode auto-approves only tools covered by an allow rule, plus read-only commands, and automatically denies everything else, with no queue for confirmation. An MCP permission rule targets one tool by its `mcp__server__tool` name, so allowing the list tool says nothing about the create tool. Analogy: a members-only club with a guest list at the door turns away anyone not on it without calling the manager, and being on the list for the lounge does not admit you to the vault. The list is the allow rule, the unlisted visitor is create_issue, and the missing manager is the absent prompt. Expecting a prompt mixes up the strict door with an ordinary front desk.

distractor_explanations.A: A rule names a single tool in the `mcp__server__tool` form and does not cover the rest of the server.
distractor_explanations.B: Prompting is what default mode does. `dontAsk` has no confirmation queue.
distractor_explanations.D: No such downgrade exists. Tools not on the allow list are simply denied.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: One developer needs a tool for a single project that nobody else will reuse. Which approach is simpler?

options.text: Deploy a server at enterprise scope, so the tool is available to the whole organization from the first day.
Wire the tool directly in the API call, as a separate MCP server is not worth maintaining for one person.
Expose the logic as an MCP prompt, as prompts are the primitive for actions that a person wants to run.
Build an MCP server anyway, since MCP is required for a tool that reaches an external service of any kind.

explanation: An MCP server pays off when a capability is reused across sessions or applications and is stable enough to maintain as a separate process. For a one-off task where the tool logic can live in the codebase, or a single-project integration used by one person, wiring the tool directly in the API call may be simpler than maintaining a server. Analogy: you build a community kitchen for a street of families, but you do not build one to cook a single pot of soup for yourself. The wrong options build the kitchen anyway.

distractor_explanations.A: Enterprise scope is for servers that must be present across the organization. This tool is for one person.
distractor_explanations.C: A prompt is a pre-written instruction template. It does not run an action.
distractor_explanations.D: MCP is not required. Wiring a tool directly can be simpler for a one-person, single-project integration.

topic: When Not to Build an MCP Server

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: A team has an integration that several people use across many sessions, and its capability is stable. Which approach fits it best?

options.text: An MCP prompt, since a prompt is what exposes a stable integration to several users at once.
A reusable MCP server maintained as a separate process, with the GitHub server as a typical example.
A separate MCP server built and discarded for each session, so that each session starts from a clean integration.
A custom tool wired directly into each developer's own API call, with each person keeping a private copy.

explanation: An MCP server fits a reusable integration used across multiple sessions and shared with a team, where the capability is stable enough to maintain as a separate process. The GitHub server is a good example, because teammates connect to it instead of rebuilding the integration in each application.

distractor_explanations.A: A prompt is an instruction template. It does not expose a service's operations as tools.
distractor_explanations.C: A server earns its upkeep by persisting across sessions and applications. Rebuilding it each time removes that benefit.
distractor_explanations.D: Private copies duplicate the integration. A shared, stable capability is what an MCP server is for.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: A team moves an MCP server from a local stdio subprocess to a remote Streamable HTTP deployment. Once the client is connected and has received the tool definitions, what changes in how the application handles tool calls?

options.text: Claude needs a separate set of tool definitions for remote servers, written in a different schema format.
Tool results must be returned as plain text, because HTTP carries no structured content blocks.
Nothing in the loop changes, since both transports are treated identically once the connection is made.
Each tool call has to be streamed, since the HTTP transport supports streamed responses and little else.

explanation: Transport is how the client reaches the server: stdio launches a local subprocess, while Streamable HTTP connects over the network to a server hosted elsewhere. The choice affects setup, not the loop. After the connection is established and the tool definitions are received, the application code treats both transports identically, and the usual pairing of `tool_use` and `tool_result` blocks still applies.

distractor_explanations.A: The definitions arrive from the server in the same form, and from Claude's view the tools look the same.
distractor_explanations.B: The loop is unchanged. Claude still issues a `tool_use` block and the application still returns a `tool_result`.
distractor_explanations.D: Transport choice does not force streaming on the tool calls. It decides where the server runs and how the client reaches it.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: A team reviews the MCP setup reference. Which TWO rows are accurate? (Select TWO.)

options.text: A personal local tool uses HTTP at enterprise scope, with its secrets stored in the committed configuration file.
A personal experiment not ready to share can use stdio or HTTP at local scope, with secrets in environment variables.
An organization-wide deployment uses stdio at user scope, with each developer managing the secrets on a laptop.
A shared team server uses stdio at project scope in `.mcp.json`, with the API key written inline for easy cloning.
An organization-wide deployment uses HTTP at enterprise scope, with administrator-managed secrets and a locked config.

explanation: The setup reference matches each deployment context to a transport, a scope, and a secrets rule. A personal experiment that is not ready to share stays at local scope, over stdio or HTTP, with secrets in environment variables only. An organization-wide deployment uses HTTP at enterprise scope, where the administrator manages the secrets and the configuration is locked against override.

distractor_explanations.A: A personal local tool uses stdio at local scope, with secrets in environment variables only.
distractor_explanations.C: Organization-wide deployment uses HTTP at enterprise scope, with the administrator managing secrets and locking the configuration.
distractor_explanations.D: A shared team server uses HTTP at project scope, and an API key must never be committed to `.mcp.json`.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: A team keeps a CLAUDE.md line forbidding inline credentials in `.mcp.json` and has also added a PreToolUse hook that blocks edits writing credential-like strings there. A teammate calls the CLAUDE.md line redundant. How should the team respond?

options.text: Remove the instruction, since the hook on its own stops the model from ever proposing such an edit in the first place.
Remove the hook, since a clear CLAUDE.md instruction is followed at each tool call without exception in a long session.
Keep both, since the instruction conveys intent to the model and the hook enforces the rule even when it is ignored.
Keep the instruction alone and rotate the key each quarter, on the view that rotation makes a leaked value harmless.

explanation: The course gives the credential rule two layers: a CLAUDE.md convention that tells the model the intent, and a PreToolUse hook that inspects writes to `.mcp.json` and blocks any that contain a credential. The instruction can be followed inconsistently, whereas the hook runs at every relevant tool call regardless of what the model decides. Analogy: a sign saying 'staff only' tells people where not to go, while a keycard lock stops them whether or not they read it. The sign is the instruction, the lock is the hook, and removing either leaves a gap, either guessing about intent or discovering a blocked action only at the door.

distractor_explanations.A: The hook blocks the action at execution. It does not change what the model proposes, and the instruction signals intent.
distractor_explanations.B: An instruction can be followed inconsistently as a file grows or context shifts, which is why a hook fires deterministically.
distractor_explanations.D: Rotation is the response to exposure, and it does not prevent the credential from being written to a committed file.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: A PreToolUse hook blocks a tool call by exiting with code 2. What should it write to stderr?

options.text: Nothing at all, as the exit code alone is passed back to the model as a bare number.
The full tool-call payload, which the agent replays to retry the same call after the block.
The reason for the block, which the agent sees as feedback it can act on afterward.
The command that bypasses the block, which the agent runs if it disagrees with the decision.

explanation: A PreToolUse hook runs before a tool call executes, so it can examine the call and exit with code 2 to block it. It writes the reason to stderr, and that reason is feedback the agent sees. This is how an access control is enforced at the configuration layer instead of hoping the agent respects an instruction in CLAUDE.md.

distractor_explanations.A: The reason is written to stderr so the agent sees why the call was blocked.
distractor_explanations.B: The stderr text is the reason for the block, not a payload to replay.
distractor_explanations.D: A guardrail does not hand the agent a bypass. It supplies the reason for the block.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: A PreToolUse hook denies writes outside `/workspace/output` and logs each denial. A security reviewer asks for evidence of everything the agent actually did with its write access. What is missing?

options.text: A CLAUDE.md note describing which paths the agent is expected to write during a normal working session.
A second hook that sends the model's reasoning for each denial to the reviewer along with the blocked path and the time.
Nothing, since denials are the only events that matter in an audit of write access to the output folder.
Logging of permitted privileged actions too, with path and result, so evidence exists before a reviewer asks.

explanation: A hook is both a control and a source of evidence. The course's example blocks the disallowed write and logs it, and also logs every permitted privileged action, so the control and its evidence exist before a reviewer ever asks. Analogy: a building's door scanner that records only rejected badges cannot tell a manager who actually went into the server room. The rejected badges are the denials, the successful swipes are the permitted writes, and the manager's question is about the second group. Logging only denials answers a question nobody asked.

distractor_explanations.A: An instruction describes intent, and a reviewer wants a record of what happened.
distractor_explanations.B: The request is for a record of actions that were taken. Explaining denials does not show them.
distractor_explanations.C: Permitted privileged actions are the ones that changed something, so they belong in the record.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: A hook blocks a file write that a fetched web page tried to trigger through hidden text. For the audit trail, which record best serves a reviewer?

options.text: The page's full HTML alone, with no record of the action or the decision taken.
The fetched source, the action that was attempted, and the fact that it was blocked.
The model's private reasoning about why it chose to write, with the page left out.
Only the final summary the user received, since blocked actions never reach the user.

explanation: For prompt injection the course's defense checklist logs the fetched source, the action attempted, and the block. That record shows where the hostile instruction entered, what it tried to do, and that the control stopped it, which is the evidence a regulated review looks for.

distractor_explanations.A: Without the action and the block, the reviewer cannot see what was attempted or that it was stopped.
distractor_explanations.C: The record should identify where the instruction came from and what the control did.
distractor_explanations.D: The summary omits the attempted action and its source, which are what a reviewer needs to see.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: A team wants Claude Code to confirm, at the start of every session, that the `DEPLOY_TOKEN` environment variable is set and a required service is reachable before any work begins. Which mechanism fits?

options.text: A Stop hook, which runs each time the model finishes responding at the end of a turn in the session.
A path-scoped rules file that loads when Claude begins working on files that sit in the deployment folder.
A SessionStart hook, which runs when a session starts or resumes and can validate the environment first.
A CLAUDE.md line asking Claude to check them, since the file loads every session and is followed without exception.

explanation: Hooks are bound to lifecycle events, and SessionStart runs when a session starts or resumes, which makes it the place to initialize state, validate environment variables, or confirm required services are reachable before the agent begins. Instructions in CLAUDE.md or rules files are guidance the model reads, not checks that run.

distractor_explanations.A: Stop fires at the end of a turn, long after work has begun.
distractor_explanations.B: Rules files supply guidance when matching files are used. They do not run checks at session start.
distractor_explanations.D: A CLAUDE.md line is a convention that can be followed inconsistently. A hook is what runs deterministically.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: An end-to-end test of a support bot fails. Its trace shows: step 1 `retrieve` returned 0 chunks, step 2 `build_prompt` ok, step 3 `model.call` returned a generic answer, step 4 `assert` failed. The parser and call-shape tests pass. What does the trace add that the failing test alone could not?

options.text: It proves the model call is at fault, since the generic answer was produced at step 3 of the trace.
Nothing, since an end-to-end test already reports which step failed as part of its normal result output.
It shows the prompt wording is wrong, since the prompt-building step sits between retrieval and the model in the flow.
It localizes the break to step 1, the retrieval, since the end-to-end test shows only that the answer was wrong.

explanation: A test says that a failure exists, and a trace shows which step produced it. An end-to-end test sees only the final output, so it is hard to localize on its own, whereas the trace records each step's output and timing and reveals that retrieval returned nothing. Analogy: a late parcel tells you the delivery failed, but the tracking log shows it never left the first depot. The failed delivery is the end-to-end failure, the tracking log is the trace, and blaming the last driver is the tempting wrong target.

distractor_explanations.A: Step 3 answered from an empty context, so it behaved as it should. The missing input came from retrieval.
distractor_explanations.B: An end-to-end test sees only the final result, which is why a trace is needed to localize the failing step.
distractor_explanations.C: The prompt step ran without error, and its input was empty. Rewording it would not repair the missing chunks.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: A team compares OAuth with a service-account key held in an environment variable for its MCP integrations. What does OAuth add that the key does not?

options.text: A small overhead on each tool call from the audit hook that logs it to the record kept for compliance review.
A requirement to commit the issued token to `.mcp.json` so teammates can connect without their own sign-in.
A secret rotation schedule that the team has to run for each connected service on a fixed calendar.
A one-time browser sign-in setup step for each user and each service connected through OAuth to Claude.

explanation: The patterns carry different costs. OAuth adds a one-time setup step per user per service, because each person signs in through the browser and approves access. An API key held in an environment variable adds a rotation process instead, and audit logging through a PostToolUse hook adds a small overhead to every tool call whichever pattern is used.

distractor_explanations.A: Audit logging is a PostToolUse hook concern and applies to every pattern, not just OAuth.
distractor_explanations.B: Tokens are issued per user and stored by the client. They are not committed to the repository.
distractor_explanations.C: Rotation is the cost of a key. OAuth tokens are issued and stored by the client after the user approves access.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: A prototype connects Claude to an internal system and works well in a demo. Which gaps would make it fail a regulated customer's security review?

options.text: A user-identity service using OAuth, an audit hook on each call, and a configuration locked through managed settings.
No dashboard of model accuracy, no A/B test between two prompts, and no fallback to a smaller model for easy requests.
A pinned model ID, a regional endpoint, and a prior version kept for rollback as the previous release's fallback.
Hardcoded credentials, no audit log of tool calls, and no way for an administrator to lock the whole configuration.

explanation: A prototype answers one question: does the connection work? A regulated review asks more, and a system that uses hardcoded credentials, has no audit log, and cannot be centrally locked will not pass. Those fixes are not hard, but they take attention before the review rather than after a failed one.

distractor_explanations.A: Those are the controls a reviewer expects to see, so they are not gaps.
distractor_explanations.B: Those are quality and cost concerns. A security review asks about identity, data location, access logging, and configuration control.
distractor_explanations.C: Those are deployment and versioning practices. They are not the identity, logging, and lock gaps a prototype usually has.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: A leaked service key lived inline in a committed file. Which practice did that break, and when does rotation help with recovery?

options.text: Separation was broken; rotation does not help once a key is in history, so deleting the repository is the sole recovery.
Storage was broken; rotation is unnecessary once the key moves to a secret store, since the old value stops working there.
Rotation was broken; separation helps when keys are rotated on a schedule that matches the repository's release cadence.
Separation was broken; rotation helps recovery when the value also lives outside the file and is referenced by its name.

explanation: Three practices keep a credential safe: separation, a proper home for the value, and rotation. A key written inline into a committed file breaks separation, and the value rides along with every clone. Rotation helps with recovery only when the first two are held, because only then do consumers read the value by name and keep working when it changes. Analogy: changing the lock on a shared office door is easy if everyone gets keys from the front desk, but if staff copied keys onto personal key rings, every copy has to be hunted down. The wrong options blame the wrong practice or abandon rotation.

distractor_explanations.A: Rotation is the right response to a leak. It only works cleanly when consumers reference the value by name.
distractor_explanations.B: The old value stays in repository history and still works until it is rotated, wherever the new copy lives.
distractor_explanations.C: Separation is the first practice and the one the inline key broke. Rotation depends on it rather than the other way round.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: A team is building a demo that connects Claude to a sample dataset and will never see production data. The security lead asks whether the full enterprise checklist is needed: managed-settings lock, audit store, and separate registrations per environment. What does the guidance suggest?

options.text: Apply just the audit store and the managed-settings lock, since those two cover what a reviewer inspects first on an integration.
Apply the full checklist anyway, so the same configuration is used for the demo and for production and nothing drifts later.
Skip each item, including secret handling, so the demo stays easy to share and can be tidied up once it is approved for use.
The full checklist is not warranted for a demo with no production data, but secrets in environment variables cost nothing.

explanation: Enterprise integration controls exist for production data that a regulated customer cares about. A demo or proof of concept that will never see such data does not need the full checklist, so the administrator lock, the audit store, and the per-environment registrations can wait. Using an environment variable for secrets is the one habit worth keeping, since it costs nothing.

distractor_explanations.A: Those two items are exactly what a demo with no production data can leave out. The cheap habit worth keeping is environment-variable secrets.
distractor_explanations.B: The guidance says a prototype that never sees production data does not need the full enterprise checklist.
distractor_explanations.C: Even for a demo, putting secrets in environment variables is recommended, because it costs nothing and builds the right habit.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: A policy asks how often a service-account key should be rotated. What does the guidance say?

options.text: On a regular schedule, and also immediately after any suspected exposure of that key to other parties.
At most once a year, so that consumers are not disturbed more often than that by a new value.
Only when the key expires or a consumer reports a failure, to avoid breaking consumers that depend on it.
Never, once the key lives in an environment variable, as a value held there cannot leak from the host.

explanation: Rotation is replacing a credential with a new one, on a schedule and immediately after any suspected exposure. It is the only appropriate response to a leaked key, because an exposed key cannot be made secret again. Reading the key by name from an environment variable or a secret store keeps rotation cheap, since the code that uses it does not change.

distractor_explanations.B: The guidance is a regular schedule plus an immediate rotation after suspected exposure, not a yearly ceiling.
distractor_explanations.C: Waiting for a failure leaves an exposed key in use. Rotation is scheduled and also follows any suspected exposure.
distractor_explanations.D: A value in an environment variable can still leak. Keeping it out of files makes rotation cheap but does not remove the need.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: A security policy requires a service key to be rotated every 90 days, with no edits to the code that uses it. Which design makes this possible?

options.text: Each consumer keeps its own copy of the key in its own file, so a rotation can be rolled out one service at a time as owners get to it.
Consumers hold the key as a constant in source, and a quarterly job regenerates that constant and commits the new value to the repository.
Consumers read the key from the configuration file, and each rotation overwrites that file in place in the repository.
Consumers read the credential by name from a secret store or environment variable, so only the value changes.

explanation: A credential read from a secret store or an environment variable rotates without touching the code that uses it, because the code refers to the value by name and the name does not change when the value behind it does. A value baked into code cannot be rotated cleanly: the old value stays in history and every consumer hardcoded to it breaks.

distractor_explanations.A: Separate copies multiply the places a value must be replaced, and any consumer missed breaks when the old key stops working.
distractor_explanations.B: A constant in source means every rotation is a code change, and the old value stays in history after the commit.
distractor_explanations.C: The configuration file would hold the value itself. Overwriting leaves the old key in repository history, where it can still be read.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: A team on Claude Platform on AWS pins `claude-opus-4-8` and asks which retirement schedule applies to it. What is the answer?

options.text: AWS's, as the model is billed through the AWS account and retires on the partner's own published dates.
Bedrock's, as the Claude routes on AWS share one retirement calendar and one model ID format between them.
Neither, as a pinned ID on a route through AWS stays available until the customer chooses to change it.
Anthropic's, because that route pins with the first-party API's ID format and follows Anthropic's schedule.

explanation: Claude Platform on AWS is reached through the customer's AWS account, but it uses Anthropic's own model IDs and lifecycle, with inference operated by Anthropic outside the AWS boundary. A team pins it with the same model ID format as the first-party API, and its lifecycle follows Anthropic's deprecation schedule. Analogy: a franchise shop that bills you through your local bank still stocks the head office's products and follows the head office's recall dates, while a store brand follows its own calendar. The wrong options attach the partner's calendar to this route.

distractor_explanations.A: On this route the model lifecycle follows Anthropic's deprecation schedule. Partner dates apply on Bedrock and Vertex AI.
distractor_explanations.B: The routes differ. Bedrock uses an `anthropic.`-prefixed ID and partner retirement dates.
distractor_explanations.C: A pinned ID is a fixed snapshot, but snapshots still retire on a schedule, here Anthropic's.

topic: Pinning on Claude Platform on AWS

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: A throwaway prototype never touches production. What does the deployment guidance say about using a moving model alias there?

options.text: It is acceptable on the condition that the prior version is kept as a rollback target for the prototype itself.
It is unacceptable, since a prototype has to pin a full model ID before its first call is made.
It breaks the eval, as a graded test set cannot be run against a model referred to by an alias.
A moving alias is fine there, because pinning is for work that ships, not for a throwaway one.

explanation: Pinning exists so that an upstream model update is a deliberate choice instead of a silent production change. A throwaway prototype that never touches production has no production behavior to protect, so a moving alias is fine there. The discipline applies to what ships.

distractor_explanations.A: A rollback target matters for a shipped system. A throwaway prototype has no release to roll back.
distractor_explanations.B: Pinning protects what ships. A prototype that never touches production does not need it.
distractor_explanations.C: An alias can be used with any request. It simply moves over time, which only matters for shipped work.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: A team reviews how its services refer to models. Which TWO statements are accurate? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Pinning gives identical output on each call, so no eval is needed before a version is promoted.
An unpinned deployment makes each upstream model update an untracked change to the application's output.
An alias such as `opus` or `sonnet` resolves to a recommended version that updates and can differ by platform.
A pinned full model ID can still move on its own, so keeping the prior version adds no rollback value to a release.
Aliases are fixed snapshots on partner platforms, so just the first-party API has an alias that moves over time.

explanation: An alias is convenient but it is a moving target: it resolves to a recommended version that updates over time and can differ across platforms. A deployment that follows an alias is unpinned, so each upstream model update becomes an untracked change to the application's output, which is how a parser can break overnight. Analogy: asking a shop for the current edition of a book means the text can change under you, while citing a fixed edition keeps your references stable. The alias is the current edition, the pinned ID is the fixed one, and the wrong options deny the moving target.

distractor_explanations.A: Pinning fixes which snapshot runs. A new version is still gated through the eval against the pinned baseline.
distractor_explanations.D: A pinned full ID resolves to a fixed snapshot, and keeping the prior version is what makes a regression a rollback.
distractor_explanations.E: Aliases can resolve to different versions across deployment platforms, and they evolve over time.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: A team picks Claude in Amazon Bedrock for its broad feature parity with the first-party API. What should it still do before relying on a specific feature?

options.text: Check feature-specific requirements in the Bedrock documentation, as a features-not-supported list exists.
Nothing further, as Claude in Amazon Bedrock supports each first-party feature with identical behavior.
Move to the legacy `InvokeModel` route, as that route carries the complete feature set of the first-party API.
Upload the files through the Files API, as it is available on Bedrock and closes a gap in feature support.

explanation: Claude in Amazon Bedrock serves the Messages API at `/anthropic/v1/messages` with broad feature parity with the first-party API, and it keeps data inside the customer's configured AWS boundary. Parity is broad but not total: a features-not-supported list exists, so the team should confirm any feature-specific requirement against the Bedrock documentation before it relies on it.

distractor_explanations.B: Parity is broad, not complete. A features-not-supported list exists, so specific features need checking.
distractor_explanations.C: The legacy route is the one tied to ARN identifiers and the older APIs. It is not a fuller feature route.
distractor_explanations.D: The Files API is a beta feature that is not available on Bedrock or Vertex AI.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: A platform decision for a regulated client will be reviewed next month by security and procurement staff who were not in the scoping meetings. What should the team's requirements record contain so the choice can be defended?

options.text: A price comparison of each platform's per-token rate, since cost is the criterion reviewers weigh most heavily.
The functional behaviors, the infrastructure constraints, and the regulation that each constraint comes from.
The prompt text and sampling settings used in testing, so reviewers can reproduce the behavior on the chosen platform.
A list of platforms the team has shipped on before, with notes on how quickly each one can be set up.

explanation: Requirements are written down because the deployment decision will be reviewed by people who did not gather them. A short record of the functional behaviors, the infrastructure constraints, and the regulation behind each constraint lets the team defend a platform choice as following from the requirements rather than from familiarity.

distractor_explanations.A: Per-token rates are broadly aligned, and the record is meant to show the choice follows from requirements, not from price.
distractor_explanations.C: A review of the platform decision reads constraints and their sources, not the prompt used during testing.
distractor_explanations.D: Familiarity is the reasoning a defensible record is meant to replace. It does not show that the platform satisfies the constraints.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: When are the infrastructure requirements for a Claude application easiest to capture?

options.text: During the operate phase, when users arrive and the infrastructure constraints first show up.
At the security review, when reviewers state the residency and identity rules for the first time.
At the start of the project, before a platform is chosen for other reasons such as familiarity.
After the build is finished, once real traffic reveals the latency, scale, and identity needs.

explanation: Infrastructure requirements are mostly not stated in the business problem. They are derived by asking the questions it implies about latency, scale, residency, and identity, and they are easiest to capture at the start, before a platform is chosen for other reasons.

distractor_explanations.A: By then the platform is deployed. These constraints decide the platform, so they come first.
distractor_explanations.B: A review that discovers them late rejects the build. They should be captured during scoping.
distractor_explanations.D: Learning them after the build means a platform may already be chosen for other reasons.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: In what order do the phases of the systems lifecycle for a Claude application run?

options.text: Requirements, design, test, build, deploy, iterate, operate.
Requirements, design, build, test, deploy, operate, iterate.
Design, requirements, build, deploy, test, operate, iterate.
Requirements, build, design, test, operate, deploy, iterate.

explanation: The lifecycle for a Claude application runs requirements, design, build, test, deploy, operate, and iterate. Each phase has its own work and its own gate, and iterate feeds production findings back into the requirements for the next release.

distractor_explanations.A: A system is built before it is tested, and it is operated before production findings are iterated on.
distractor_explanations.C: Requirements come first, because the platform and model are chosen from them in design.
distractor_explanations.D: Design precedes build, and deploy precedes operate.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: A regulated team discusses the lifecycle gates between phases. Which TWO statements are accurate? (Select TWO.)

options.text: A gate is a document written at the end of the lifecycle that summarizes what each earlier phase produced.
A gate is a decision to move from one phase to the next, and a regulated engagement keeps control there.
Placing work in the right phase and refusing to skip a gate is what keeps a Claude application reviewable.
Gates apply between test and deploy, as the earlier phases produce no decisions that a reviewer needs to see.
A team under deadline can skip a gate when the eval score looks strong, as a score replaces the decision.

explanation: A gate is a decision to move from one phase to the next, and it is where a regulated engagement keeps control. You do not move from design to build until the platform satisfies the residency requirement, and you do not move from deploy toward full production until the new version clears the eval against the pinned baseline. Placing work in the right phase and refusing to skip a gate keeps the application reviewable.

distractor_explanations.A: A gate is a decision to move between phases, not a summary document written afterward.
distractor_explanations.D: Gates also sit between design and build, where the platform must satisfy the residency requirement.
distractor_explanations.E: Refusing to skip a gate is what keeps the application reviewable, however strong a score looks.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: A team building for a hospital plans to write prompts, tools, and memory first, and to pick the endpoint and credentials in the final sprint. A reviewer objects. What is the reviewer's point?

options.text: A regulated customer's procurement team has to pick the endpoint before code is written, so developers should wait for its decision.
The governing constraint decides the endpoint, credentials, and log destination, so a wrong setup is costly to undo.
Prompts and tool schemas are tied to one endpoint, so they would have to be rewritten in full if the route changes late.
The endpoint affects just latency, so the team may defer it provided it measures from the customer's region at the end.

explanation: For regulated data, the governing constraint decides the delivery route before any choice about prompts, tools, or memory. It determines which endpoint your code calls, which credentials it carries, and where its logs land. Analogy: before packing for a trip you check which country you are flying to, because that decides your passport, your plug adapter, and where the receipts go. The constraint is the destination, and the endpoint, credentials, and logs are what it decides. Fixing the wrong client configuration after the agent is built is far more expensive than setting it correctly at the start.

distractor_explanations.A: Developers usually write the code that targets the endpoint. The point is to name the governing constraint at the start, not to wait.
distractor_explanations.C: The concern is the client configuration, endpoint, credentials, and log destination, not prompt or schema compatibility.
distractor_explanations.D: A regulated constraint rules routes out entirely. Endpoint choice is not a pure latency decision that can wait.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: A team's checklist for choosing a delivery route lists HIPAA, GDPR residency, FedRAMP, an internal data-residency policy, and SOC 2. Which one governs how the team's systems are built and operated, rather than which endpoint the code calls?

options.text: SOC 2, because it concerns security posture and audit, not the selection of an endpoint or its credentials.
HIPAA, because a BAA covers specific configurations, so it sets the way the team's own systems are built and run internally.
GDPR residency, because it governs how the team's own build process is operated rather than where inference happens on the platform.
FedRAMP, because it is a process standard for the team's engineering, with no bearing on which endpoint the code calls.

explanation: The constraints that directly determine endpoint selection and credential configuration are the data-handling ones: HIPAA, GDPR and residency, FedRAMP, and an internal data-residency policy. SOC 2 is different. It governs how systems are built and operated, which belongs to security posture and audit work, not to the choice of which endpoint your code calls.

distractor_explanations.B: HIPAA does determine routes: PHI may only go to an endpoint covered by a BAA for the configuration in use.
distractor_explanations.C: GDPR residency is about where the model executes, so it decides endpoint and region choices.
distractor_explanations.D: FedRAMP determines endpoint choice directly: code must call an endpoint on an authorized environment at the required level.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: A team moves a long-running research agent to Claude Managed Agents. Which TWO things does it take on in exchange for no longer running the loop and the sandbox? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Provisioning and tearing down the container in which each tool call executes, along with the tools installed in it.
Writing the iteration loop itself, including the retries that run inside it each time a model call or a tool call fails.
Keeping its own process alive for the hours a session runs, so the loop is not interrupted partway through the work.
Server-side session state that Anthropic stores for each session, subject to its data-handling policies and constraints.
A versioned agent definition held as an API resource, covering model, system prompt, tools, MCP servers, skills.

explanation: With Managed Agents, Anthropic runs the loop, the retries inside it, and the sandbox, so the team takes on a different set of work: defining the agent once as a versioned API resource and living with server-side session state governed by Anthropic's data handling. Analogy: hiring a catering company instead of cooking in your own kitchen means you stop buying stoves and washing pans, but you still write the menu and accept that the food is prepared in their premises. The menu is the agent definition and their premises are the server-side state. The loop, retries, sandbox, and long-lived process are the kitchen work you no longer do.

distractor_explanations.A: Sandbox provisioning and teardown are handled by the managed service, so the team no longer owns them.
distractor_explanations.B: Anthropic runs the loop and its in-loop retries server-side; this is one of the things the team stops owning.
distractor_explanations.C: Managed sessions run for minutes or hours without the team's process holding the loop open.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: A team needs a custom approval gate inside every iteration of its agent, run inside its own VPC with its own tool runtime. Tasks last under a minute. Which wiring path fits?

options.text: Claude Managed Agents, because a managed sandbox lowers cost and risk for short tasks that run inside a minute.
Claude Platform on AWS, which gives the team direct control over the agent loop through a different deployment platform.
Claude Managed Agents, because it runs the loop in the team's process while Anthropic hosts just the sandbox.
A raw Messages API loop or the Agent SDK, because both keep the loop and tool execution in the team's own environment.

explanation: The wiring path is chosen by how much of the runtime you want to own. Managed Agents suits long-running work and teams that would rather not build a loop and sandbox, but when you need full in-process control or your own tool runtime, you stay on the Agent SDK or a raw loop. Short tasks that need a per-iteration approval gate inside the team's own environment point the same way.

distractor_explanations.A: It suits long-running work or teams that want to avoid building a sandbox. It is not meant for in-process control.
distractor_explanations.B: A deployment platform decides where the model is reached from. The wiring path, who runs the loop, is a separate choice.
distractor_explanations.C: With Managed Agents Anthropic runs both the loop and the sandbox, so neither stays inside the team's environment.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: A team studies the default-plus-override routing pattern for model choice. Which TWO statements are accurate? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Routing needs a separate fine-tuned model for each tier before traffic can be split between the tiers of the family.
It applies the same routing idea used for retrieval to model choice, so the capable model is paid for where needed.
The pattern pays off most when each request has the same shape and one quality bar across the traffic it serves.
A cheap signal read from the request, such as task type, input length, or a difficulty classification, can choose the model.
The override tier is chosen by sending each request to the largest model first and passing the easy ones down to a cheaper one.

explanation: Routing is a default model plus an override. Most traffic goes to a balanced default, and specific request types go to a larger or smaller model, chosen by a cheap signal read from the request such as task type, input length, or a difficulty classification. It is the same routing idea used for retrieval, applied to model choice, so you pay for the capable model only on the requests that need it. Analogy: a hospital triage desk sends most visitors to the general clinic and only some to the specialist, using a quick check at the door. Sending everyone to the specialist first defeats the point.

distractor_explanations.A: The same prompt runs on any tier, so routing only chooses which tier receives each request.
distractor_explanations.C: For uniform traffic at one quality bar, the guidance is to pin a single model and skip the router.
distractor_explanations.E: That adds the most expensive call to every request. The signal should be cheap and read from the request.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: A latency-sensitive feature moves from Sonnet to Opus because an eval shows Sonnet missing the quality bar. What trade does the upgrade make?

options.text: No change in cost or latency, as the tiers differ just in the quality of the answers they produce for a request.
More quality, paid for with a higher per-token cost and usually higher latency than the Sonnet tier had.
Lower latency at a higher cost, as a larger tier is built for speed on short and simple requests.
More quality at the same cost, as the tiers differ in how many requests each one can serve per minute.

explanation: Upgrading a model tier trades quality against a higher per-token cost and usually higher latency, while downgrading buys speed and lower cost at the risk of a quality drop. A higher tier can occasionally be cheaper if it reaches a conclusion in fewer tokens, so the decision is made on measurement rather than assumption.

distractor_explanations.A: The tiers trade cost, latency, and capability against each other. A higher tier costs more per token and is usually slower.
distractor_explanations.C: Speed and cost efficiency are what Haiku is built for. Opus is built for demanding work.
distractor_explanations.D: The tiers differ in cost, latency, and capability. A higher tier costs more per token.

topic: Cost of Stepping Up a Tier

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: A team has trimmed prompts and added caching to a feature that runs on the top model tier, yet the bill is still large. An eval shows Sonnet meets the quality bar on it. Why could the earlier work not close the gap?

options.text: Cost levers optimize spend within a model, while the model choice sets the baseline they start from, so the tier needed review.
A cheaper tier would raise latency and total cost, so the earlier levers had already reached their best possible result.
The top tiers ignore trimming and bill for the full context window instead of for the tokens that were actually sent.
Caching and trimming reduce only output tokens, which are a small share of the bill on a top-tier model for this feature.

explanation: Cost management optimizes spend within a model, whereas model selection determines the baseline that optimization works from. Caching and trimming shrink what each call costs on the chosen tier, but if an eval shows a cheaper tier meets the bar, the biggest saving is moving the baseline itself. Analogy: haggling over the price of a tank of fuel for a gas-guzzling truck saves less than swapping to a car that makes the same trip on half the fuel. The truck is the top tier, the haggling is caching and trimming, and the quality bar is the trip you actually need to make.

distractor_explanations.B: Moving down a tier buys speed and lower cost at the risk of a quality drop, and here the eval shows the bar still holds.
distractor_explanations.C: Every tier bills for the tokens in the request, so trimming does lower the bill within a tier.
distractor_explanations.D: Caching and trimming act on input tokens. The gap comes from the per-token baseline of the chosen tier.

topic: Model Selection Sets the Cost Baseline

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: A team documents the three prompting modes. Which TWO statements are accurate? (Select TWO.)

options.text: One-shot retrains the model on its single example, so the change carries over into later requests.
Multi-shot suits output with no fixed structure, as a fixed structure is easiest to describe in words.
Zero-shot is the right mode when an edge case keeps being missed, as examples just lengthen the prompt.
Zero-shot gives the instruction with no examples, which suits a simple task whose output shape is obvious.
One-shot adds a single example of an input paired with the desired output, and multi-shot includes several.

explanation: The modes differ in how many worked examples sit in the prompt. Zero-shot gives the instruction and no examples, which suits a simple task whose output shape is obvious. One-shot adds a single input and desired-output pair, and multi-shot includes several. The examples are not training data, and each costs tokens on every call. Analogy: a recipe card with no photo suits a simple dish you know, a card with one photo shows the plating, and a card with several shows variations, but each photo makes the card heavier to carry. Add only as many as the dish needs.

distractor_explanations.A: Examples are not training data. They sit in the prompt and shape only the requests that carry them.
distractor_explanations.B: Examples are for output with a specific structure, casing, or edge case that a description keeps missing.
distractor_explanations.C: A description that keeps missing an edge case is the signal to add an example, at a token cost.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: On a 200,000-token context window, a multi-shot prompt has grown to 90 worked examples of about 2,000 tokens each. Requests that attach long documents now fail with a validation error before generation starts. What explains it, and what is the fix?

options.text: Examples count toward the window only on the first request, so the failures come from the documents alone and trimming examples cannot help.
The API drops the oldest examples silently when the window fills, so the error means one of the documents was malformed.
Examples are billed but not counted toward the window, so the fix is to raise `max_tokens` to leave more room for the reply.
The examples count against the window on every request alongside the document, so trim to the fewest examples that still pass the eval.

explanation: Few-shot examples are not training data; they sit in the prompt, so each one costs tokens on every call and consumes context budget. Ninety examples at about 2,000 tokens each take most of a 200,000-token window before a document is attached, and an input larger than the window is rejected with a validation error before generation begins. The discipline is to add the smallest amount of prompt that produces a reliable result, so trim the examples while watching the eval.

distractor_explanations.A: Examples sit in the prompt, so every call that carries them pays for them in tokens and in context budget.
distractor_explanations.B: The API never silently drops content. Input that is larger than the window is rejected with a validation error before generation.
distractor_explanations.C: Examples occupy the context window, and `max_tokens` limits only the output, not what fits on the input side.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: Haiku zero-shot misses the required structure, but Haiku with six worked examples passes, adding about 1,500 input tokens to each call. Sonnet passes zero-shot. Traffic is about two million calls a day. What should decide the choice?

options.text: Choose Haiku with examples, since a smaller tier is cheaper once it clears the bar, whatever the prompt around it looks like in tokens per call.
Choose Sonnet zero-shot, as worked examples are never worth the per-call tokens they add at high volume.
Compare the total cost per call at the real volume, because examples add input tokens to every call, and pick the cheaper passing option.
Keep Haiku zero-shot and accept the structural failures, since the content is right and the cost is lowest.

explanation: Prompting mode and model choice are related levers, and the discipline is to try the simplest model and the fewest examples that meet the eval. Examples can let a cheaper model succeed, but each one adds input tokens to every call, so the winner depends on the numbers at your volume. Analogy: comparing a cheaper printer with costly ink cartridges against a pricier printer with cheap ink means looking at cost per page, not the sticker price. The printer is the model tier, the ink is the examples carried on every call, and a page is one request. Both options pass the eval, so cost per call decides.

distractor_explanations.A: The examples add input tokens to every call, so at high volume the smaller tier's saving may shrink or vanish. It has to be measured.
distractor_explanations.B: Sometimes examples let a cheaper model do the job at lower total cost. The answer depends on measured cost, not on a blanket rule.
distractor_explanations.D: The task fails the eval on structure, so Haiku zero-shot does not meet the quality bar the decision is anchored to.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: A team ports an unchanged request from an older Claude model to one of the newest model generations. Output tokens per call rise sharply on short FAQ lookups, and responses contain no thinking content. What should the team check first?

options.text: Whether `temperature` was changed during the port, as sampling settings control how many tokens a response contains in total.
Whether `budget_tokens` is still being sent, since a leftover thinking budget doubles output billing on the newest model generations.
Whether the new model thinks adaptively by default, since defaults differ per model, and then set lower effort for simple calls.
Whether thinking blocks are being returned unchanged, as dropping them multiplies the output tokens on later calls in the same loop.

explanation: Whether the model reasons before answering is a per-call decision, but defaults differ by model: some of the newest models think adaptively by default or always. Thinking tokens cost the same as output tokens, and on the newest models their content is omitted by default, so a silent default shows up as higher output usage with nothing visible in the response. Analogy: a new rental car may have the headlights turned on automatically, and you only notice when the battery drains and nothing looks different from outside. The automatic headlights are the default thinking and the drained battery is the output bill. The old model's settings do not explain it.

distractor_explanations.A: On the newest models a non-default temperature returns a 400 error. Sampling settings do not set response length.
distractor_explanations.B: On the newest model generations a `budget_tokens` setting returns a 400 error, so it would fail the request instead of inflating the bill.
distractor_explanations.D: Dropping or editing a thinking block makes the next request fail in a tool loop. It does not raise output token counts.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: A document-review agent runs one hard step, resolving conflicting clauses across contracts, and a dozen routine steps that extract dates and copy fields. Evals show Haiku clears the bar on the routine steps and only Opus clears it on the conflict step. How should the team assign models?

options.text: Give each step the cheapest tier that clears its own bar: Opus for the conflict step and Haiku for the routine ones.
Run the whole chain on Sonnet, the balanced default, since splitting tiers within one run adds more risk than it removes.
Run the whole chain on Haiku, and ask the model to reason longer on the conflict step so it matches what Opus delivers.
Run the whole chain on Opus, so the steps behave consistently and the routine ones add little to the bill.

explanation: A model choice is a per-workload lever, and the same logic applies to the steps inside one agent run. Reserve the most capable model for the steps that need it and route simpler work to a cheaper one, using the eval as the evidence for each assignment. Here the evals already say Haiku holds on the routine steps and only Opus holds on the conflict step, so assigning models by step cuts the bill without risking the hard step.

distractor_explanations.B: The evals already assign a tier to each step, so one default would overpay on routine steps and may miss the bar on the hard one.
distractor_explanations.C: Only Opus cleared the conflict step on the eval. A tier change is promoted on a measured score, not on a guess that more reasoning closes the gap.
distractor_explanations.D: Reaching for the most capable model by default is the most common and most expensive selection mistake. The top tier belongs only on the steps that need it.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: A brainstorming feature drafts ten campaign slogans for a person to skim and discard. An eval shows Sonnet's output is weak on the hardest 6% of briefs, and a manager wants to step up to Opus. What does the guidance support?

options.text: Adding the highest effort setting to each brief, since a miss on hard cases means reasoning is missing from the requests.
Staying on Sonnet is reasonable, because stepping up needs a measured miss and a costly error, and slogans are cheap.
Stepping down to Haiku instead, as low-stakes output means quality no longer needs to be measured on an eval at all.
Stepping up now, as a measured miss on the hardest cases is enough to justify moving up to the next tier at once.

explanation: Step up a tier when an eval shows the current model failing on the hardest cases and the cost of a wrong answer is high. Both halves matter: here the weak slogans are skimmed and discarded, so the cost of a miss is low and the extra per-token price may not be worth it. Analogy: you pay for a professional mover for a piano, where a drop is a disaster, but not for a box of old magazines. The piano is the high-stakes answer, and the magazines are the discarded slogans. An eval miss alone is not the reason to climb a tier.

distractor_explanations.A: Reasoning on every call is wasted on simple requests, and it does not address the question of whether the miss is worth paying more for.
distractor_explanations.C: In both directions a model change is promoted on a measured score. Low stakes do not remove the need for the eval.
distractor_explanations.D: The guidance pairs the eval miss with a high cost of a wrong answer. Cheap, discarded output does not meet that second condition.

topic: When to Step Up a Tier

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: A team compares how CLAUDE.md loads in the Claude Code CLI and in the Agent SDK. Which statement is accurate?

options.text: It loads in each CLI session, but in the SDK `settingSources` decides if it loads, so set it explicitly.
It does not load in the SDK, as the CLI alone reads filesystem instruction files and the SDK ignores them.
It loads in the SDK by default exactly as it does in the CLI, so the SDK needs no setting to pick it up.
It loads in the SDK when the system prompt passed to the agent mentions the file by name.

explanation: In the Claude Code CLI, a CLAUDE.md file loads into every session regardless of the task. In the Agent SDK, whether filesystem settings including CLAUDE.md load is controlled by `settingSources`, and it should be set explicitly rather than left to a default. A team that assumes the CLI behavior can find its project rules silently missing from an SDK agent.

distractor_explanations.B: The SDK can load CLAUDE.md once `settingSources` names the filesystem sources it should use.
distractor_explanations.C: Whether filesystem settings such as CLAUDE.md load in the SDK depends on `settingSources`. A default should not be relied on.
distractor_explanations.D: Loading in the SDK is controlled by `settingSources`, not by what the system prompt mentions.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: What does a human-in-the-loop step do in an automated agent process?

options.text: It inserts a human review or approval step before a consequential action is taken by the agent.
It lets the model rewrite its own system prompt whenever a tool call fails during a run of the loop.
It replaces the agent's loop with a person who performs each tool call by hand for the whole task.
It records each action in an audit log after the action has already been carried out by the agent.

explanation: Human-in-the-loop means inserting a human review or approval step into an automated process before a consequential action is taken. Where to place it depends on the worst outcome if the step runs without a check: before a destructive tool call, after a planning step, or on unexpected output.

distractor_explanations.B: A human-in-the-loop step involves a person. The model does not rewrite its own instructions.
distractor_explanations.C: The loop still runs. The person reviews or approves at chosen points.
distractor_explanations.D: Logging is a separate control. A human-in-the-loop check comes before the consequential action.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: A team ships a Claude Managed Agents integration to production. A later release refines how one endpoint behaves, and their application breaks. What should they have had in place?

options.text: Nothing beyond the beta header, since sending it freezes endpoint behavior for the whole life of the integration.
A fresh agent resource created for each session, since an agent definition changes whenever the beta is refined.
A migration plan from the outset, since the surface is in public beta and behaviors may change between releases.
A Zero Data Retention agreement, as only ZDR customers are insulated from changes to the behavior of beta endpoints.

explanation: Claude Managed Agents is in public beta: every endpoint requires the `managed-agents-2026-04-01` beta header, and behaviors may be refined between releases, so the guidance is to build with a migration plan in place. Treating the surface as fixed leaves the application exposed when a release changes an endpoint. Analogy: if you set up a stall at a market whose organizers may rearrange the layout each season, you keep the stall on wheels. The wheels are the migration plan.

distractor_explanations.A: The header is required on every endpoint, but it does not freeze behavior; the guidance expects refinements between releases.
distractor_explanations.B: An agent is defined once as a versioned API resource and referenced by ID across sessions. Recreating it per session does not address changing behavior.
distractor_explanations.D: Managed Agents sessions are stored server-side and are not currently eligible for Zero Data Retention, and such an agreement would not stop behavior changes.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: An engineering team needs an agent that works for hours, with no loop, sandbox, or tool-execution layer for the team to build or secure. Which wiring path fits?

options.text: Claude Managed Agents, where Anthropic runs the loop and a managed sandbox for long work lasting hours.
A stateless workflow of single API calls, which keeps a long task alive without any loop to maintain.
A raw Messages API loop, which takes long-running execution and the sandbox off the team's hands by default.
The Agent SDK, which runs the loop in the team's process and also provisions a sandbox for each tool call.

explanation: Claude Managed Agents fits long-running execution measured in minutes or hours, a managed sandbox, and teams that would rather not build the loop, the sandbox, and the tool-execution layer at all. Anthropic runs the loop and the sandbox, and the application defines the agent once as an API resource. Analogy: a team that does not want to build, staff, and secure a kitchen hires a catering service for a long event. The raw loop and the Agent SDK are the cases where the team keeps its own kitchen, and the tempting wrong options hand the work off without a loop.

distractor_explanations.B: A workflow of single calls does not keep a task running for hours. An agent loop does.
distractor_explanations.C: A raw loop leaves the loop, the sandbox, and the tool-execution layer with the team.
distractor_explanations.D: The Agent SDK runs inside the team's own process, and the team's code still executes the tools.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: A document-formatting agent runs stateless: each job is independent. Users now start asking follow-ups such as `redo yesterday's file with the same settings`, and the agent has no answer. What does this show?

options.text: Summarized memory has to be adopted first, as a summary has to exist before anything can be written to external storage.
A stateless agent has no way to reach earlier sessions, so follow-ups that depend on them need state kept in external storage.
In-context memory would fix it, as the conversation window carries state across sessions once the window is large enough.
The agent should resend the full transcripts of every earlier job in each request, which keeps stateless agents consistent.

explanation: Memory scope should match the shape of the work. A stateless agent suits independent jobs because nothing has to be stored or retrieved, but the cost is that all prior context is lost, and a follow-up that depends on an earlier session has no way to reach it. Once such follow-ups are required, state has to be written to external storage and read back. In-context memory does not survive the end of a session.

distractor_explanations.A: External storage can hold the state directly. A summary is an option for long conversations, not a prerequisite for persistence.
distractor_explanations.C: In-context state is wiped when the session ends, so a larger window does not carry anything into the next session.
distractor_explanations.D: Replaying every transcript is the in-context approach that inflates every call until the window closes, and it is no longer stateless.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
