prompt: A team is deciding where each set of instructions should live in Claude Code. Which TWO placements match the guidance? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Instructions for a one-off exploratory task confined to a single conversation can simply stay in-context for that session.
Constraints that must hold across all tasks belong in a Skill, which loads only when the request matches its description.
A specialized review checklist that applies to a subset of tasks belongs in CLAUDE.md so it is always available to Claude.
Instructions that must still apply next week can stay in-context, since the conversation window holds them across sessions.
Team-standard coding conventions that apply to everything in the codebase go in CLAUDE.md, which loads in every session.

explanation: Each mechanism has its own loading behavior. CLAUDE.md loads every session unconditionally, which suits always-on standards. A Skill's name and description load at startup and the full instructions load only when the request matches, which suits task-specific expertise. In-context instructions are present each turn of one session but grow with its length and vanish when it ends, which suits one-off work. Analogy: house rules are posted on the fridge for everyone to see every day, a recipe card is pulled from the drawer only when you cook that dish, and a sticky note on the counter is for tonight only.

distractor_explanations.B: A Skill loads on a description match, so it is not guaranteed to be present. Always-on constraints belong in CLAUDE.md.
distractor_explanations.C: Always-loaded content adds fixed overhead to sessions that never need it. A Skill loads only when its description matches the request.
distractor_explanations.D: In-context instructions do not survive session end. A clear command or a new session wipes them.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: An agent has bugs planted in four layers: schema, streaming, context structure, and memory. Which TWO findings are accurate? (Select TWO.)

options.text: The loop sets `stop_seen` on `message_stop` but appends the assistant turn regardless, so a dropped stream commits a partial turn.
Appending tool results in a user turn is a schema-layer bug, as results belong in the tool definition rather than in a turn.
The memory layer concatenates every prior session transcript into live context, so the history grows until the window fills.
Dropping thinking blocks from history is a memory-layer bug, as it removes state that should persist between separate sessions.
The tool description `Gets data.` is a streaming-layer bug, as a short description changes how deltas are assembled in the handler.

explanation: The cumulative task plants one bug per layer. In the streaming layer the loop records that `message_stop` arrived but never checks it, so an interrupted stream commits a half-built turn to history. In the memory layer the agent keeps concatenating every prior session transcript in-context, so the history grows each session until the window fills. Analogy: a restaurant ticket printer that prints orders whether or not the cook has finished writing them leaves half-orders on the rail, and a pile of every past night's receipts on the counter eventually leaves no room to work. Each fault belongs to its own layer, and the wrong options misfile them.

distractor_explanations.B: Tool results belong in a user turn as tool_result blocks. That is how the API expects them.
distractor_explanations.D: Filtering thinking blocks breaks the context structure the API validates. It is not a memory problem.
distractor_explanations.E: A vague description is a schema-layer bug. It leaves Claude without a basis for choosing the tool.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: A team wants a built-in subagent to follow skill-backed behavior. What is the correct path?

options.text: Mention the skill in CLAUDE.md, as a skill named there is loaded into each built-in subagent when it starts.
Rename the skill file to match the built-in agent, as built-in agents load skills by matching file names.
Load the skill in the parent session, as built-in subagents inherit the skills that the parent has loaded.
Create a custom subagent that lists the skill, because built-in agents have no preloaded skills of any kind.

explanation: Subagents start from a clean context. They do not inherit conversation history or skills from the parent, though they do inherit its permission context. Built-in agents do not have preloaded skills, so if skill-backed behavior is needed the correct path is a custom subagent with those skills listed explicitly in its configuration.

distractor_explanations.A: A mention in CLAUDE.md does not load a skill. Built-in agents have no preloaded skills, and Explore and Plan skip that file.
distractor_explanations.B: Built-in agents do not load skills by file name. A custom subagent has to list the skill explicitly.
distractor_explanations.C: Subagents do not inherit skills from the parent. They start with a clean context.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: A team is explaining retrieval-augmented generation to a colleague who assumes it works like loading every document into the prompt. Which TWO statements about how retrieval behaves are accurate? (Select TWO.)

options.text: If retrieval misses the document holding the answer, the model never sees it, so how the sources are organized matters.
Retrieval removes the need to put anything in the context window, because the model queries the database as it generates.
Agentic search needs an embedding index to be built and kept in sync before the first question can be answered at all.
Per-request cost stays roughly flat as the corpus grows, because only the retrieved slice reaches the model each time.
A semantic similarity match reliably returns the chunk that holds a specific identifier, so keyword matching is not needed.

explanation: Retrieval stores material outside the context window, finds the parts most relevant to a request, and supplies only those parts to the model. That is why per-request cost stays flat as the source grows, and also why the model is only as good as what retrieval finds. Analogy: a librarian who hands you three relevant pages never needs a bigger desk when the library doubles, but if she pulls the wrong shelf you never see the right book, and a file named notes_final_v3 is harder to find than one with a descriptive title. Real retrieval still depends on well-organized sources.

distractor_explanations.B: The retrieved slice is supplied to the model in its request, and the model generates from that slice.
distractor_explanations.C: Agentic search skips upfront indexing. The model searches live sources at the moment of need.
distractor_explanations.E: A query for a specific identifier can miss the relevant chunk if a more semantically similar result outranks it, which is why a lexical match is sometimes run alongside.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: A RAG assistant splits its handbook into single sentences. Retrieval returns the right sentences, but answers are often incomplete. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: The embedding match is returning sentences that are semantically close to the question but not relevant to it.
The chunks are too small, so a single chunk lacks the surrounding context needed to be useful on its own.
The assembly step is missing, so the retrieved sentences never reach the model in the structure the prompt expects.
The chunks are too large, so each one dilutes the match with unrelated text from neighboring sentences.

explanation: Chunking decides what a unit of retrievable context is. Split too small and a single chunk lacks the surrounding context to be useful, split too large and one chunk dilutes the match with unrelated text. Sentence- or section-based chunking with a little overlap is a reasonable default. Analogy: handing someone single sentences torn out of a handbook gives them correct words with no page around them, while handing them whole chapters buries the answer. The right size is a section with some overlap, and the tempting wrong options blame other parts of the path.

distractor_explanations.A: The scenario says retrieval returns the right sentences. The gap is that each one is too small to stand alone.
distractor_explanations.C: Missing assembly makes the model answer from memory. Here the answers are incomplete, not ignoring the text.
distractor_explanations.D: Single sentences are the opposite problem. Too-large chunks come from splitting by whole chapters.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: Each turn of an agent's task is small, yet turns get slower and costlier as a long session grows. What best explains this?

options.text: Latency depends on the number of tools registered, so a long session slows down only when new tools are added.
Every token in the window costs input money and adds latency, and a long session compounds both as history builds up.
The model re-reads only the newest turns, so older turns add cost to the invoice without adding any latency.
Output tokens are billed at a higher rate on each later turn, so the cost climbs even when the input stays the same size.

explanation: The context window is not a free resource. Every token in it costs money on input and adds latency to the response, and a long session compounds both, because the accumulated history is processed again on each turn. Analogy: a taxi meter that charges for every passenger's luggage already in the trunk will tick faster each stop, even if the new luggage is one small bag. The trunk is the window, the luggage is the history, and the wrong options blame price changes, partial reading, or the tool list.

distractor_explanations.A: Tool definitions add to the window, but a growing history is what compounds the cost and latency over a session.
distractor_explanations.C: The whole window is processed on each call, so older content adds both cost and latency.
distractor_explanations.D: Pricing does not rise per turn. The history that is re-read on each call keeps growing.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: A prompt says `Return only JSON`. It holds on every test case but slips on an unusual input in production. A colleague proposes passing a schema through `output_config.format` instead. Why is that more reliable?

options.text: A schema makes the model reason more carefully about field names and types, which a plain instruction cannot trigger.
The API validates the finished response against the schema and regenerates it until it matches, so violations never reach your code.
A schema guarantees success on every call, including refusals and responses cut off at `max_tokens`, so no checks are needed.
The API constrains generation token by token, so a violating output cannot be produced; a prompt is only a request.

explanation: A prompt instruction is a request, and it holds on the cases you tried and then slips on one you did not. Structured outputs use constrained decoding: as each token is generated, the API allows only tokens that keep the output valid against the schema, so a violating response cannot be produced. That moves correctness from something checked after the fact to something ruled out beforehand. A refusal or a `max_tokens` truncation can still occur, so `stop_reason` is still checked.

distractor_explanations.A: Structured outputs constrain which tokens are allowed. They do not change how carefully the model reasons.
distractor_explanations.B: The constraint is applied while tokens are generated, not by checking and retrying afterwards.
distractor_explanations.C: A refusal and a truncation at `max_tokens` can still return output that does not match the schema, so the code must still check `stop_reason`.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: Instead of loading every document into the prompt, what does retrieval-augmented generation do?

options.text: It compresses each document into one summary that is placed at the top of every prompt it sends.
It sends each document to the model in parallel requests and keeps whichever answer appears most often.
It keeps the material outside the context window and supplies only the parts relevant to the request.
It trains the model on the documents so that it no longer needs to see them again at request time.

explanation: A model reads everything in its context window for every request, so the more documents loaded up front, the less room is left for the work. Retrieval-augmented generation resolves this by storing the material outside the window, finding the parts most relevant to the current request, and supplying only those at request time. The model then answers from that retrieved slice.

distractor_explanations.A: Retrieval finds the relevant slice for each request. It does not fold the library into one summary.
distractor_explanations.B: Retrieval narrows what the model reads. It does not poll the model over the whole library.
distractor_explanations.D: Retrieval supplies relevant text to the prompt at request time. It does not train the model.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: A team maps where a RAG path can go wrong. Which list names the three places?

options.text: Chunking, the embedding match, and assembly of the retrieved chunks into the prompt for the model.
Caching, the batch queue, and the retry logic that wraps each retrieval call in the application code.
Indexing, the system prompt, and the stop sequence that ends the generated answer for the caller.
Tokenizing, the sampling step, and the streaming of the final answer back to the user of the system.

explanation: A RAG path can break in three places. Chunking decides what a retrievable unit is, the embedding match decides which chunks come back, and assembly decides whether the retrieved chunks reach the model in the structure the prompt expects. A fault in any of the three shows up as a wrong or incomplete answer.

distractor_explanations.B: Those are cost and reliability mechanisms. The retrieval path breaks in chunking, matching, and assembly.
distractor_explanations.C: These are not the three places a path breaks, which are chunking, the embedding match, and assembly.
distractor_explanations.D: Those are general generation steps, not the three places a retrieval path breaks.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: A tool in an agent loop fails. Which TWO statements about returning the failure are accurate? (Select TWO.)

options.text: With `is_error` set to true, the model can try a different approach, ask for clarification, or simply stop.
The failure message belongs in the result's content, so Claude can read what went wrong with the call.
Raising the exception out of the loop is the standard path, as the model cannot use a failure message.
A failed call needs no `tool_result`, as the model infers the failure when it sees no result for that call.
An empty result is the safest return, as the model treats an empty result as a clear signal that the tool failed.

explanation: When a tool fails, the result should come back to Claude with `is_error` explicitly set to true and a message in its content, not as a silent empty result. With the error visible, the model can try a different approach, ask for clarification, or stop. Without it, the model treats the empty result as valid data and continues on a false premise. Analogy: a waiter who returns from the kitchen with an empty tray and no word lets the guests assume dinner is coming, whereas one who says the kitchen is out of salmon lets them reorder. The wrong options hide the failure.

distractor_explanations.C: The error should come back to Claude explicitly so that it can react instead of the loop being abandoned.
distractor_explanations.D: Every tool_use block must be answered by a matching tool_result, including when the tool failed.
distractor_explanations.E: The model treats an empty result as valid data and continues on a false premise.

topic: What a Visible Tool Failure Gives Claude

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: A team connects both GitHub's MCP server and Linear's MCP server to Claude Code. What differs between the two connections?

options.text: Nothing, as each authenticates with a personal access token and differs only in the URL it uses.
The scope, as GitHub can only be project-scoped while Linear can only be user-scoped for sign-in.
Only the authentication step, as both are remote HTTP servers with the same transport and scope.
The transport, as GitHub's tools are local and use stdio while Linear is remote and uses HTTP.

explanation: GitHub's MCP server and Linear's are both remote HTTP servers, and both follow the same transport and scope logic. The authentication step is what differs. GitHub uses a personal access token passed as a Bearer header from an environment variable, while Linear redirects the client to a sign-in page, and a token is issued and stored automatically. Analogy: two offices in the same building share the same lobby and lifts, but one opens with a keycard you carry and the other has a guard who signs you in. The wrong options change the building instead of the door.

distractor_explanations.A: GitHub uses a personal access token as a Bearer header, while Linear starts a browser sign-in handled by OAuth.
distractor_explanations.B: Scope is a separate choice for each server. Neither authentication method restricts it.
distractor_explanations.D: Both are remote servers over HTTP. The transport is the same.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: After a bug where two dependent calls were issued in the same turn, a team sets `disable_parallel_tool_use` on every request its agent makes. What is the consequence?

options.text: Claude can no longer issue tool calls, as the setting requires parallel use to be on for tool use to work.
Independent calls are still issued together, but their results have to be returned one per message in later turns.
Claude issues one tool call per turn, so independent lookups that could have run together each take their own separate turn.
Claude runs the tools itself in dependency order, so the application no longer has to execute them.

explanation: Current Claude models default to parallel calls when calls are independent, and `disable_parallel_tool_use` forces one call per turn. That is the right fix where a real dependency exists, but applied everywhere it gives up the concurrency that independent calls could have had. The narrower design is to model the dependency as separate turns only where it is real.

distractor_explanations.A: The setting limits Claude to one tool call per turn. Tool use itself keeps working.
distractor_explanations.B: With the setting on, Claude issues only one call per turn, so there is nothing to return together or apart.
distractor_explanations.D: Client-side tools are still executed by the application's own code, and results come back as tool results.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: Which part of a tool schema defines the parameters that the tool function accepts?

options.text: The description, which holds the parameter types in a fixed machine-readable format.
The `input_schema`, which describes the parameters using JSON Schema for the tool.
The `tool_use` ID, which Claude generates to carry the parameters from call to call.
The name, which lists each parameter after the tool's identifier in a fixed order.

explanation: A tool schema has three parts: a name, a description, and an input schema. The input schema defines the parameters the tool function accepts, using JSON Schema, and the required array in it names the inputs that are non-negotiable for a call.

distractor_explanations.A: The description tells Claude when to use the tool. It does not define parameter types.
distractor_explanations.C: The ID links a result to its call. The input schema defines the parameters.
distractor_explanations.D: The name is a short identifier. Parameters are defined in the input schema.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: A team sets `defer_loading` in `mcp_toolset` on an MCP Connector request but leaves out the `mcp-client-2025-11-20` header. What happens?

options.text: The configuration applies as written, as the header selects which transport the connector will use.
The request fails with a 529, as the connector retries overloaded servers when the header is set.
The toolset configuration does not apply as described, because the connector needs that beta header.
Every tool loads upfront, but `enabled` still works, as `defer_loading` is the setting that depends on the header.

explanation: The API MCP Connector controls loading through an `mcp_toolset` object, with `defer_loading` and `enabled` settings. The connector requires the `mcp-client-2025-11-20` beta header on the request, and without it the `mcp_toolset` configuration will not apply as described. Only HTTP-exposed servers are supported through the connector.

distractor_explanations.A: The header is what makes the `mcp_toolset` configuration apply. It does not select a transport.
distractor_explanations.B: A missing header does not produce an overload error. The configuration simply does not apply as described.
distractor_explanations.D: Without the header the `mcp_toolset` configuration does not apply as described, which includes both settings.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: A team attaches a server with 80 tools through the MCP Connector and sets `defer_loading` on all of them. A teammate assumes Claude can no longer call the rarely used ones. What is accurate?

options.text: The teammate is right, as a deferred tool stays switched off until a developer enables it again in a later request to the API.
Deferral changes nothing about context cost, as it only reorders where the tools appear in the list sent to Claude each time.
Deferred tools remain callable because only their definitions load later, cutting upfront cost; `enabled` is what hides one.
The teammate is right, and Claude must be sent the beta header once per tool before it can call any deferred one of them.

explanation: Two settings on the toolset look similar but do different jobs. `defer_loading` delays loading a tool's definition until the model needs it, which reduces upfront context cost, while `enabled` turns tools on or off so the model never sees them. Analogy: a restaurant can keep its rarely ordered dishes off the printed menu and bring out a separate dessert list only when you ask, or it can stop cooking a dish entirely. The dessert list on request is deferral, and no longer cooking the dish is disabling. Deferred tools can still be ordered.

distractor_explanations.A: `defer_loading` delays loading the definition. It does not disable the tool, and `enabled` is the separate setting that does that.
distractor_explanations.B: Deferring a definition until the model needs it is what reduces upfront context cost for a server with a large tool list.
distractor_explanations.D: The beta header is set once on the request so that the toolset configuration applies. It is not sent per tool.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: A security reviewer asks which control enterprise reviewers ask about first, and how it is configured. What is the answer?

options.text: A PostToolUse hook, with its log of every call written to an audit store after each tool has run.
OS-level sandboxing, with filesystem and network isolation configured through Claude Code settings.
A longer system prompt, with the rules of the deployment written out in plain language for the model.
A larger context window, with more room for the agent to hold its protected paths in view.

explanation: OS-level sandboxing isolates the agent at the process level, restricting the filesystem to the working directory and outbound network access to a named set of endpoints. Because the operating system enforces it, it holds even when a hook is missing or misconfigured. It is the control enterprise security reviewers ask about first, and it is configured through Claude Code settings, with full documentation at code.claude.com. Analogy: a fence around the whole property still holds when a door lock was left off. The wrong options offer words, records, or room instead of a fence.

distractor_explanations.A: A PostToolUse hook records calls after they run. It cannot block them, and it is not the control reviewers ask about first.
distractor_explanations.C: A prompt instruction is not a security control. Enforcement lives outside the prompt.
distractor_explanations.D: Window size has nothing to do with isolating the agent from paths and endpoints.

topic: The OS-Level Control Reviewers Ask About

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: A reviewer asks where a Claude integration's data is processed. Which checks answer that question?

options.text: The processing region, whether data leaves the customer's boundary, and whether the deployment surface meets it.
The tokens used per call, the latency of each tool, and the error rate that the dashboards show for the integration.
The identity each call runs under, the audit log that is kept, and whether an administrator has locked the configuration.
The model tier in use, the effort setting on each call, and the temperature the application sets for requests.

explanation: Data residency is about where data is processed and stored. Answering it means knowing which region processes the request, whether any data leaves the customer's boundary, and whether the deployment surface, the direct API or a cloud provider's hosted version, satisfies the constraint. The reviewer's other two questions, about access logging and managed configuration, are separate checks.

distractor_explanations.B: Those are cost and reliability metrics. Residency is about where processing happens.
distractor_explanations.C: Those answer the identity, logging, and configuration-control questions, not where data is processed.
distractor_explanations.D: Tier and reasoning settings do not tell a reviewer where data is processed.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: A team scopes data residency, audit logging, and managed configuration early in a regulated project. Why does that keep the security review from stalling?

options.text: Scoping them early lets an administrator approve the review on the team's behalf before the build starts.
The three capabilities are optional extras, as a review mostly checks the quality of the model's answers.
A regulated review asks to see those capabilities, so an integration scoped for them can show what it has.
Scoping them early lets the team skip the review, as the review repeats checks the team has already passed.

explanation: A financial or healthcare customer asks early about where data is processed, how access is logged, and whether an administrator can control the configuration centrally. A regulated review is in practice a request to see those three capabilities, so an integration scoped with them in mind passes by showing what it already has, while one that ignores them scrambles to add controls under deadline. Analogy: a restaurant that already keeps its fridge logs and cleaning rota can hand them to the inspector, while one that does not has to invent them that morning. The wrong options treat the capabilities as optional or approvals as transferable.

distractor_explanations.A: Scoping does not transfer approval. It prepares the evidence the reviewer will ask to inspect.
distractor_explanations.B: A regulated review is a request to see these capabilities, and their absence reads as a risk.
distractor_explanations.D: The review still happens. Early scoping means the answers already exist when the reviewer asks.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: A claims workflow chains an API endpoint that receives customer submissions, a Claude Code task that reads partner web pages, and an MCP server that updates the claims system. A reviewer maps one control to each seam. Which control belongs at the entry point, where requests arrive from outside?

options.text: Input validation on the requests arriving from outside, together with the identity the call runs under in the app.
Scoping the component to least privilege and logging the system access it holds on the application's behalf.
Treating the content as data rather than as instructions, as the entry point is where fetched pages first arrive.
A PreToolUse hook that blocks the claims system's write tool, since the entry point is where writes are approved.

explanation: A multi-component application has a boundary at every seam, and each seam gets the control that fits it. The entry point faces requests from outside, so its controls are input validation and the identity the call runs under. The Claude Code task's seam is the untrusted content it fetched, so the next component treats that content as data. The MCP server's seam is the system access it holds, so it is scoped to least privilege and logged.

distractor_explanations.B: That is the control for the MCP server, which holds access to the claims system.
distractor_explanations.C: Fetched pages are untrusted at the seam leaving the Claude Code task, not at the entry point.
distractor_explanations.D: The entry point does not approve writes. Its seam is the request arriving from outside the application.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: A team has a `deploy-prod` procedure that should run only when a developer deliberately invokes it, never because Claude decided a task matched. What should they use?

options.text: A rules file with a `paths` glob on the deploy directory, so the procedure loads just when those files are read.
A skill whose frontmatter sets `disable-model-invocation: true`, invoked directly by a developer as `/deploy-prod`.
A note in CLAUDE.md telling Claude to run the procedure just when asked, since that file loads in each session.
A skill with a deliberately vague description, so Claude rarely finds a match between the description and the task.

explanation: Skills are the recommended format for both explicit and automatic invocation: you can call one directly with `/skill-name`, or Claude can load it when the request matches its description. When a workflow should run only on an explicit call, the skill's frontmatter carries `disable-model-invocation: true`. A written instruction elsewhere cannot give the same guarantee.

distractor_explanations.A: A rules file loads automatically when Claude reads a matching file, which is the opposite of explicit-only invocation.
distractor_explanations.C: An instruction in CLAUDE.md is a soft rule that can be followed inconsistently. The frontmatter setting is what makes a workflow explicit-only.
distractor_explanations.D: A vague description makes a skill unreliable to load. It does not guarantee the model will never invoke it.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
prompt: A team's LLM judge already returns strengths, weaknesses, and reasoning before its score. Checked against 100 human-labeled cases, it agrees with the human grade on only about half of them. What should the team do next?

options.text: Replace the judge with exact string matching, as a code grader is more accurate than a model for any kind of output.
Rely on the scores as they are, since requesting reasoning before the score already makes a judge's output defensible here.
Fix the rubric by tightening what each score means and adding a good and a bad example answer, then re-measure agreement.
Average the judge's score over several runs per case, which would make its disagreements with humans cancel out.

explanation: A judge is only as trustworthy as its measured agreement with people. Calibration means running the judge on cases a human has already labeled and checking how often they agree. If agreement is low, the repair is to the rubric: define what each score means, add a good and a bad example, and measure again. Analogy: two teachers marking the same essays with different ideas of what a B means will disagree until they sit down with a marking guide and a pair of sample essays. The teacher is the judge, the marking guide is the rubric, and the sample essays are the anchor examples. Averaging more marking rounds would only repeat the same disagreement.

distractor_explanations.A: Exact match is brittle for open-ended answers, where any acceptable paraphrase fails it. It suits outputs with one correct form.
distractor_explanations.B: Reasoning anchors a score, but a judge that disagrees with humans half the time gives a number that looks rigorous and means little.
distractor_explanations.D: Averaging smooths noise but does not fix a rubric that defines scores in a way the human graders did not.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Exam-Style Tier)
prompt: A gateway calls the first-party API through the Python SDK with default retries plus its own exponential backoff. On the 28th, every request starts returning HTTP 429 with error type `rate_limit_error`. The body carries `details.error_code` set to `enforced_spend_limit_reached`, and there is no `retry-after` header. Security has approved only the first-party API. What should the gateway do?

options.text: Stop retrying, alert the owner, and fail fast until the cap is raised or the month ends
Read the `retry-after` value and pause new requests for that many seconds before resuming
Keep retrying with longer jittered backoff, widening the delay until the 429 clears on its own
Fail over to a Bedrock-hosted copy of the model for the rest of the month

explanation: A 429 does not always mean slow down. Ordinary rate limits use a token bucket that refills continuously, so backoff and `retry-after` work. A monthly spend cap is different: the same `rate_limit_error` type comes back, but with no `retry-after`, and access stays blocked until 00:00 UTC on the first of the next month or until the cap is raised. The `details.error_code` field tells the two apart. Analogy: a prepaid phone plan. A busy signal may clear if you redial in a minute, but the message saying your allowance is used up repeats all day, so you stop dialling and top up. Backoff is the redial, and it fails here because nothing refills until the cap is lifted.

distractor_explanations.B: `retry-after` is how the API reports ordinary rate-limit waits. The spend-cap 429 carries no such header, so there is no number of seconds to wait.
distractor_explanations.C: Backoff suits ordinary rate limits, which refill continuously under the token bucket. A spend cap stays closed until 00:00 UTC on the first of the month or until it is raised, so retries only add load.
distractor_explanations.D: Cross-platform failover is a real resilience pattern, but security approved only the first-party API, and it would not lift the cap on the original account.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Exam-Style Tier)
prompt: An internal assistant sends a 120k-token policy manual, identical for every user, plus a short question on each call. At peak the first-party API returns 429s that name input tokens per minute. A limit increase takes weeks and launch is Friday. Cost and cache behaviour are acceptable. Which change most directly relieves the 429s?

options.text: Shorten the user question text on every call and trim the system prompt wording to cut uncached input
Send the traffic through the Message Batches API and its separate rate limits
Add a `cache_control` breakpoint after the manual so repeat reads stop counting toward ITPM
Lower `max_tokens` on each call to reserve less output against the limit each minute

explanation: For most Claude models, only uncached input counts toward ITPM: `input_tokens` after the last breakpoint and `cache_creation_input_tokens` count, while `cache_read_input_tokens` do not. A manual repeated on every call is the ideal thing to cache, so the bulk of each 120k-token request stops consuming the limit. Analogy: a gym that counts only new sign-ins at the door each hour, not members who already hold a locker key. Give the heavy gear a locker, which is the cache, and the door queue shrinks. Batches do not fit here because they trade away the live answers users are waiting for.

distractor_explanations.A: The short question is a tiny share of each request. The 120k-token manual is the bulk of the input, and it is the part to cache.
distractor_explanations.B: Batches do have separate limits, but results can take up to 24 hours. Users here are waiting on live answers.
distractor_explanations.D: `max_tokens` concerns output, and it is not even counted toward OTPM. The 429s name input tokens, which the manual dominates.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Exam-Style Tier)
prompt: A desktop-automation agent keeps every screenshot as base64 in the conversation and resends the whole history each turn. After about 40 turns, calls fail with HTTP 413 `request_too_large`. The images exist only in the app's memory behind a firewall, and users need live turn-by-turn answers. Which change fits best?

options.text: Set `stream: true` on each call so the large request body is sent to the API in chunks
Upload each screenshot once to the Files API and reference it by `file_id` afterwards
Move the agent loop to the Message Batches API, which accepts requests up to 256 MB
Send the screenshots as `url` sources that point at the app's internal image store on the intranet

explanation: The Messages API caps a request at 32 MB, and resending base64 images on every turn makes the body bigger each time. The Files API lets you upload an image once and keep later payloads small by referencing its `file_id`. Batches raise the size cap to 256 MB but cannot serve live turns, and `url` sources need a publicly reachable address.

distractor_explanations.A: Streaming changes how the response arrives. The 32 MB cap on the Messages request body stays the same.
distractor_explanations.C: Batches do raise the size cap, but they are asynchronous with up to a 24-hour window. They cannot serve live turns.
distractor_explanations.D: URL sources must be public and reachable from Anthropic. An image store behind a firewall cannot be fetched.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Exam-Style Tier)
prompt: A compliance tool sends 30 page scans, each 3000 x 4000 px and under 10 MB, as `image` blocks in one request to a model that accepts 100 images per request. All 30 pages must be read together. The call fails with HTTP 400 `invalid_request_error`, and the message mentions "many-image requests". Which change most directly fixes the problem?

options.text: Downscale each scan so neither side passes 2000 px, then resend all 30 in one call
Split the scans across two requests of 15 images each and merge the answers afterwards
Switch to a model that accepts 600 images per request rather than 100 in each call
Convert the PNG scans to JPEG at lower quality to shrink each file well below 10 MB

explanation: Once a request holds more than 20 `image` blocks, every image in it is held to a stricter per-image size in pixels: keep neither dimension above 2000 px, or stay at 20 images or fewer. The 100 or 600 image count is a separate ceiling, and file size is a separate limit again. Analogy: on a full flight, the overhead bins take only smaller bags; the number of passengers is not the issue, the size of each bag is. Splitting into two flights would work but breaks the travel-together rule, and a bigger plane, the 600-image model, does not change the bag-size rule.

distractor_explanations.B: That would clear the limit, because a request with 20 or fewer images avoids it. It breaks the stated need to read all pages together.
distractor_explanations.C: The image count is not the problem, since 30 is under 100. Going past 20 images triggers a stricter per-image dimension limit.
distractor_explanations.D: The stricter limit applies to pixel dimensions, not bytes. JPEG shrinks the file but leaves each side at 3000 or 4000 px.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Exam-Style Tier)
prompt: A records team uploads scanned invoices to the Files API and plans to use `GET /v1/files/{file_id}/content` as its backup copy. A restore test returns a 400 error, and the file metadata shows `"downloadable": false`. What is the best fix for the backup plan?

options.text: Ask Claude in a `document` block request to return each invoice's full text as the backup
Re-upload each PDF with an `expires_in_seconds` value so the content endpoint accepts it
Keep the original PDFs in the team's own storage and use the `file_id` only for requests
Send the invoices in `container_upload` blocks and fetch them back through the container later

explanation: Files you upload carry `downloadable: false`. Only files created by skills or the code execution tool can be downloaded, and trying to fetch an upload returns a 400. The Files API is a reference store for Messages requests, not a vault, so the originals need their own storage.

distractor_explanations.A: Reading a file costs input tokens, and the reply is a lossy, expensive retyping of the text rather than a copy of the original file.
distractor_explanations.B: `expires_in_seconds` schedules expiry. It does not change `downloadable`, which is true only for files created by skills or code execution.
distractor_explanations.D: `container_upload` hands files to the code execution tool for analysis. It does not make an uploaded file downloadable.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Exam-Style Tier)
prompt: A SaaS app runs all tenants in one workspace. The browser sends a `file_id` from an earlier upload, and the backend places it into a `document` block. A pen test shows tenant A can summarize tenant B's file by submitting B's `file_id`. Which change most directly fixes the flaw?

options.text: Issue each tenant its own API key inside the same workspace and rotate the keys monthly
Keep the user-to-file mapping on the server and ignore any `file_id` the client supplies
Upload every file with a one-hour `expires_in_seconds` value and re-upload on lapse
Add a system prompt line telling Claude to refuse any file that belongs to another tenant

explanation: Uploaded files belong to the workspace, not to a user or a session, so any request in that workspace can read any file in it. File IDs therefore stay server-side references, and your app decides which user may touch which file; for hard isolation you can also give each tenant its own workspace. Analogy: a coat check with numbered tickets. If guests may hand over any number they like, one can collect another's coat, so the attendant must decide whose ticket it is. A system prompt is like asking guests politely to take only their own coat.

distractor_explanations.A: Any key with access to a workspace can use every file in it, so separate keys in one workspace do not isolate tenants.
distractor_explanations.C: Expiry limits how long a file lives. During that hour, any submitted ID still works across tenants.
distractor_explanations.D: Claude cannot tell who owns a file. Access control for file IDs has to be enforced in application code.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Exam-Style Tier)
prompt:
A research helper uses the web search server tool. This loop sometimes returns a half-finished answer:

```python
resp = client.messages.create(
    model=MODEL, max_tokens=2048, tools=[WEB_SEARCH],
    messages=messages,
)
if resp.stop_reason == "tool_use":
    messages += run_client_tools(resp)
else:
    return resp  # treated as final
```

Logs show `stop_reason` is `pause_turn` on those runs. What should the loop do on `pause_turn`?

options.text: Run the search in application code, then return its output as a `tool_result` block in the next user turn
Add `resp.content` to `messages` as an assistant turn and call the API again with the same tools
Treat the partial text as the final answer and show it to the user right away
Raise `max_tokens` and resend the original messages unchanged to get a longer reply

explanation: `pause_turn` means a server-tool loop, such as web search, reached its iteration limit and Claude has more to do. You continue by sending the assistant content back as it is, so the next call picks up where the last stopped. Analogy: a relay race. When a runner finishes a leg the baton must be handed on, or the race ends early. The assistant content is the baton. Returning a `tool_result` does not fit, since that handles client tools whose `stop_reason` is `tool_use`.

distractor_explanations.A: `tool_result` answers client `tool_use` blocks. A server tool runs on Anthropic's side, so there is nothing for the app to execute.
distractor_explanations.C: `pause_turn` means the server-tool loop hit its iteration limit with work unfinished, so the text so far is incomplete.
distractor_explanations.D: A larger `max_tokens` addresses the `max_tokens` stop reason. Resending the same messages restarts the work instead of continuing it.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Exam-Style Tier)

options.text: Append the partial turn and a user message asking Claude to finish the call
Set `tool_choice` to `{"type": "any"}` so the model always finishes the call
Turn on `strict: true` for the tool so each call arrives with its complete required input
Skip the cut-off tool call and retry the request with a higher `max_tokens` value

explanation: When `max_tokens` ends a response in the middle of a `tool_use` block, the input is incomplete, so running it executes a half-written instruction. Detect the pattern, discard that block, and retry the request with a higher limit. Analogy: a delivery note torn off mid-address. A courier does not guess the street; they ask for the full note on a bigger pad. Strict mode is the tempting alternative, but it shapes valid input and cannot stretch a token budget that ran out before the block was finished.

distractor_explanations.A: A user message cannot complete a block that was cut off. The documented handling is to retry with a higher `max_tokens`.
distractor_explanations.B: Forcing a tool call controls whether a tool is used. It does not give the response any extra token budget to finish the block.
distractor_explanations.C: Strict mode keeps generated input matching the schema, but a response that hits `max_tokens` can still be cut off mid-block.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Exam-Style Tier)
prompt: A JSON extractor ends each request with an assistant message containing `{` to force JSON output. After the team adopts a Claude 4.6 or later model, every call fails with HTTP 400 `invalid_request_error`, and the message says the conversation must end with a user message. The team must stay on the newer model. Which change is correct?

options.text: Add a `stop_sequences` entry for the closing brace and keep the prefilled assistant turn
Pin the previous model's dated ID for this one workload and migrate it later
Retry each 400 with exponential backoff until the model finally accepts the request
Drop the prefilled assistant turn and request the JSON shape with `output_config.format`

explanation: Claude 4.6 and later models reject a prefilled last assistant message with a 400. Structured outputs through `output_config.format` with a JSON schema give a reliable JSON shape without the prefill, and they are the supported replacement. A 400 is not transient, so retries cannot help, and stop sequences only end generation.

distractor_explanations.A: Stop sequences end generation at a chosen string. They do not remove the rejected assistant prefill.
distractor_explanations.B: Pinned older IDs still accept prefill, but the team must stay on the newer model.
distractor_explanations.C: A 400 is a terminal client error and does not clear on retry. Backoff suits 429 and 5xx responses.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Exam-Style Tier)
prompt: A production service sees intermittent HTTP 500 `api_error` responses from the first-party API. The team wants to file a support ticket that lets Anthropic find each failed call. The SDK retries these calls, and the logs currently keep only the final exception text. What should the team log for every failed call?

options.text: The `anthropic-workspace-id` header returned with each response, plus the call's timestamp
The `anthropic-organization-id` header that the API returns with each response
The message `id` from each failed response body, logged next to the timestamp
The `request-id` header value, also exposed as `_request_id` on SDK response objects

explanation: Every API response, including errors, carries a unique `request-id` header, and the same value appears as `request_id` in error bodies and as `_request_id` on SDK response objects. Support uses it to locate one specific call. Analogy: a parcel tracking number. The sender's address says who shipped, like the organization or workspace ID, but only the tracking number points to the one lost package. A message `id` is like a receipt for a delivered parcel, and failed calls produce none.

distractor_explanations.A: The workspace ID shows which workspace the usage counted toward. Every call from the same key shares it.
distractor_explanations.B: The organization ID names the account and is the same for every call, so it cannot single out one failed request.
distractor_explanations.C: A failed call returns an error body with no message. The identifier to quote is the `request_id` in that error.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Exam-Style Tier)
prompt: Finance wants a nightly job that pulls token usage and cost per workspace for the whole organization from the Usage and Cost API, with `group_by[]=workspace_id`. Only the first-party API is approved. Which credential should the job use?

options.text: A key scoped to the Production workspace that the main application already uses
A per-user key that Claude Code minted in the Claude Code workspace
An Admin API key issued for the finance job and kept in its secret store
Totals computed from the `usage` fields in the application's own response logs

explanation: Usage and Cost reports are organization-level data, and they sit behind the Admin API. That API accepts an Admin API key, an `org:admin` OAuth token, or a personal or service account key that is not scoped to one workspace. prompt:
A dashboard overstates output tokens for long streamed answers:

```python
total_out = 0
for event in stream:
    if event.type == "message_delta":
        total_out += event.usage.output_tokens
```

Short answers look right, but answers with many `message_delta` events show a multiple of the true count. Which change fixes the count?

options.text: Also add the usage reported in the `message_start` event to the running total
Take `output_tokens` from the last `message_delta` instead of adding each one
Call the token counting endpoint on the final text once each stream has ended
Count one token for each `content_block_delta` event received during the stream

explanation: The usage numbers in a `message_delta` event are cumulative, so each one already includes everything before it. Adding them up counts the early tokens again and again, which is why longer answers show a larger multiple. The last `message_delta` holds the final total. Analogy: a car's odometer. Each reading is the distance since the car was built, so summing every reading from a trip gives nonsense, and the last reading is the answer. Fetching a separate count after the stream repeats work the stream already did.

distractor_explanations.A: `message_start` carries the opening usage. Adding it to a sum that already overcounts makes the total larger, not correct.
distractor_explanations.C: That adds a call per stream, and the stream already reports its final usage.
distractor_explanations.D: A delta is a chunk of text or JSON, not a token. Chunk sizes vary, so the count would still be wrong.

prompt: A Python service shares one `Anthropic` client across many code paths that rely on the SDK's default retry behaviour. One nightly enrichment job should tolerate longer bursts of 429 and 529 errors, up to five retries. No other code path may change. Which approach fits best?

options.text: Call `client.with_options(max_retries=5).messages.create(...)` in that job only
Pass `timeout=300` to give each attempt more time to succeed
Wrap the job's call in a loop that catches `RateLimitError` and retries five times
Construct the shared client with `max_retries=5` for the whole service

explanation: The SDK retries connection errors, 408, 409, 429 and 5xx responses twice by default, with exponential backoff. `max_retries` can be set on the client or per request through `with_options`, so one call path can differ without touching the rest. A hand-written loop duplicates the SDK's retries, and a timeout is a different setting.

distractor_explanations.B: A timeout controls how long one attempt may run. It does not change how many times a failed call is retried.
distractor_explanations.C: The SDK already retries, so a manual loop stacks a second layer on top and multiplies the attempts.
distractor_explanations.D: That changes the retry count for every code path that uses the shared client, which breaks the stated constraint.

prompt:
A chat backend must show users an error within about 30 seconds if the model is unresponsive. It is configured like this, and users still wait about a minute before seeing the error:

```python
client = anthropic.Anthropic(timeout=20.0)

resp = client.messages.create(
    model=MODEL, max_tokens=1024, messages=msgs,
)
```

Which change most directly fixes the wait?

options.text: Set `max_retries=0` on the client or call, so a timed-out attempt is not repeated
Switch to `stream=True` for this call and keep the retry settings unchanged
Pass a granular `Timeout` object that sets a short `connect` value of 2 seconds
Raise `timeout` to 60.0 and leave the retry settings at the SDK defaults for the client

explanation: Requests that time out are retried twice by default. With `timeout=20.0` that is up to three attempts of 20 seconds each plus backoff, which matches the minute users see. Setting `max_retries=0` leaves a single 20-second attempt. Analogy: calling a friend and letting it ring 20 seconds, then redialling twice by habit; you listen to a minute of ringing before giving up. Making the ring longer, as a larger timeout does, only lengthens the wait. A short connect timeout covers only the dialling step.

distractor_explanations.B: Streaming suits long generations and leaves retries alone. A timed-out attempt is still retried twice.
distractor_explanations.C: `connect` bounds only the connection phase. The wait here comes from a slow response being retried.
distractor_explanations.D: A longer timeout lengthens the wait for an unresponsive model instead of shortening it.

prompt: A team runs nightly Message Batches on the first-party API, sometimes cancels one that is still processing, and a separate report job fetches results days later. Which TWO statements describe how batches behave? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Results stay available for download from `results_url` for 29 days after the batch is created
Results come back in submission order, so `custom_id` is needed only when retrying a request
A request still queued at the 24-hour mark is retried automatically in a follow-up batch
Requests canceled before reaching the model are still billed at the discounted batch rate
Canceling a running batch moves it to `canceling` and then `ended`, keeping finished results

explanation: A running batch can be canceled. It moves to `canceling` and then `ended`, and the requests that finished beforehand keep their results. Results are downloadable from `results_url` for 29 days after creation, after which the batch can still be viewed but its results are gone. Analogy: a dry cleaner you cancel mid-run. Garments already finished are returned to you, the rest are not charged, and the tickets are kept for a month. Nothing is resubmitted for you, and the garments need not come back in the order you dropped them off.

distractor_explanations.B: Results can arrive in any order, and `custom_id` is how each result is matched to its request.
distractor_explanations.C: Such a request ends as `expired` and is not billed. Re-submitting it is up to the application.

prompt: A streaming client on a Claude 4.6 or later model loses its connection partway through a response. The response had a finished `text` block, then a `tool_use` block that was still arriving. Which TWO statements describe a correct recovery? (Select TWO.)

options.text: The saved text goes in a user message that tells the model to continue from where it stopped
The `partial_json` fragments received so far are parsed and the tool runs with the keys that arrived
The interrupted turn is appended to the history as complete, then the next turn is sent
The unfinished `tool_use` block is dropped, and the retry resumes from the last complete text block
The saved text goes in as the last assistant message, resuming the response as on older models

explanation: To resume, capture what arrived, then send a new request. On Claude 4.6 and later the partial text goes in a user message with an instruction to continue, since prefilling an assistant message is rejected. Tool use and thinking blocks cannot be partially recovered, so you resume from the most recent complete text block. Analogy: a torn recipe card. You can copy the finished steps onto a new card and tell the cook to carry on from there, but a half-written measurement is worthless, so you restart that step. Marking the card as finished ignores that the page is torn.

distractor_explanations.B: Fragments are partial JSON strings. A tool block cut off mid-stream has no complete input to run.
distractor_explanations.C: A turn is committed only after `message_stop`. A turn cut off by a dropped connection is partial and is discarded or resumed.
distractor_explanations.E: Claude 4.6 and later reject a prefilled last assistant message with a 400, so the older recovery pattern no longer works.

prompt: A product page sends 12 parallel requests the instant a user opens it, each repeating the same 30,000-token catalog prefix that ends at one caching breakpoint. Usage shows 12 cache writes and no cache reads. What should the page do?

options.text: Switch to automatic caching with a top-level `cache_control` field on each request.
Send one request first and start the other 11 once its response begins.
Raise the `ttl` on the shared breakpoint from 5 minutes to `1h`.
Add a second breakpoint after the system prompt.

explanation: A cache entry becomes readable only after the first response has begun, so requests fired at the same instant each miss and each pay for a write. Sending one request, waiting until its response starts, and then releasing the rest lets the other 11 read the entry. Analogy: twelve people walk into a copy shop together, each wanting the same 30-page handout. If the clerk has not made a master copy yet, all twelve are charged for a full first copy; if one customer goes first and the master is on the shelf, the other eleven take cheap duplicates. The master is the cache entry and the first customer is the first request. A longer `ttl` is the shelf staying open later, which cannot help people who all arrive before the master exists.

distractor_explanations.A: Automatic caching only moves the breakpoint to the last cacheable block. The timing problem between simultaneous requests stays the same.
distractor_explanations.C: The 1-hour lifetime keeps an existing entry alive longer. It does nothing for requests that all start before any entry has been written.
distractor_explanations.D: Extra breakpoints mark more prefix boundaries. Requests launched at the same instant still find nothing to read.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Exam-Style Tier)
prompt: A team pre-warms a 20,000-token prefix by sending a request with `max_tokens: 0` and a `cache_control` breakpoint when a chat panel opens. Which TWO statements describe how this pre-warm request behaves? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Returns an empty `content` array, `stop_reason: "max_tokens"` and full `usage`.
It can be sent as one of the requests inside a Message Batches submission.
A pre-warm request incurs no cache write charge even when the prefix was not cached before.
It is rejected with `invalid_request_error` when `stream: true` is also set.
It is accepted only when `thinking.type` is `enabled` on the request.

explanation: A pre-warm request reads the prompt, writes the cache at each breakpoint, and returns immediately, so the response has empty `content`, `stop_reason` of `max_tokens`, and full `usage`. Because no output can be produced, streaming, enabled thinking, structured outputs and forced tool choice are rejected, and the request cannot sit inside a batch. The write itself is still billed. Analogy: preheating an oven before guests arrive. You pay for the electricity (the cache write), nothing comes out of the oven (no content), and you cannot ask it to serve a dish while it preheats (stream or think). The tempting claim of a free pre-warm fails because the write charge still applies.

distractor_explanations.B: `max_tokens: 0` is rejected inside a batch. A cache entry written during batch processing would likely expire before the follow-up request runs.
distractor_explanations.C: The request is billed as a cache write when it writes the prefix. Only output tokens are zero, because nothing is generated.
distractor_explanations.E: Enabled extended thinking is one of the settings that make a zero-token request fail. A pre-warm needs no reasoning because no output is produced.

prompt: A chat service on a model that supports forced tool choice caches its tool definitions, system prompt and conversation history with three breakpoints. On the turn where it first changes `tool_choice` from `auto` to a forced tool, the team expects a miss on everything. What does usage show for that request?

options.text: Every breakpoint still hits, and only the new user message is uncached.
Every breakpoint misses and the whole prefix is written again.
