Analogy: a manager who has started handing every sticky note to an assistant. Removing the assistant stops useful delegation, and a cheaper assistant still costs a handoff each time. A house rule saying when to delegate fixes the habit. A nesting limit only stops assistants from hiring their own assistants.

distractor_explanations.A: That blocks the parallel work the team still wants. The problem is when it delegates, not that it can.
distractor_explanations.B: It stops subagents from spawning their own subagents. The main agent can still delegate every trivial edit.
distractor_explanations.D: Cheaper subagents lower the price of each delegation but leave the needless delegations in place.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Exam-Style Tier)
prompt: A research agent runs for tens of minutes per task. Deploys keep killing in-flight runs, and a tool failure late in a run forces the whole task to start over. Which TWO practices from Anthropic's multi-agent research write-up address these problems? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Run three to five subagents in parallel for each research query.
Roll new versions out gradually with rainbow deployments.
Grade each final report with a single rubric-based LLM judge call per run.
Begin with short, broad queries and then narrow them step by step.
Resume a failed run from where it stopped instead of restarting it.

explanation: Long-running agents are stateful, so a deploy can cut them off and a late failure can waste everything before it. Rainbow deployments move traffic gradually so running agents finish on the old version, and checkpoints let a run resume where it stopped. Analogy: a long video game. Rainbow deployments are like letting players finish their current level before the servers update, and checkpoints are the save points that stop a crash from sending you back to the start. Parallel subagents and broad-first searches make the game faster or smarter, not safer to interrupt.

distractor_explanations.A: Parallel subagents cut research time. They do nothing for runs that are killed by deploys or lost to failures.
distractor_explanations.C: That is an evaluation method for output quality, not a way to keep long runs alive.
distractor_explanations.D: This is a search-strategy lesson about query specificity. It does not protect runs against deploys or failures.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Exam-Style Tier)
prompt: A coding agent works across many sessions and must recall progress after each context reset. The security policy says the progress notes may be stored only in the company's own infrastructure. Which approach satisfies the policy?

options.text: Add the memory tool and run its file commands against the company's own storage.
Extend the cache `ttl` to `1h` and rely on the cached notes between sessions.
Enable context editing and retrieve the cleared tool results from the API later.
Turn on adaptive thinking and pass the earlier thinking blocks into each new session.

explanation: The memory tool is client-side: Claude asks for file operations under `/memories`, and the application runs them against whatever storage it chooses. That lets the company keep the notes inside its own infrastructure and read them back in later sessions. Context editing and caching manage what sits in the prompt, not where durable notes live.

distractor_explanations.B: The cache keeps a prompt prefix alive for a limited time. It is neither durable storage nor under the company's control.
distractor_explanations.C: Context editing removes old tool results from the conversation. It does not keep them anywhere for later retrieval.
distractor_explanations.D: Thinking blocks belong to one conversation's history. They are not a store that survives a context reset.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Exam-Style Tier)
prompt: A custom `endpoint-finder` subagent, defined in `agents` with `Read`, `Grep` and `Glob`, finished its first pass. A follow-up must continue from its earlier tool calls and findings without re-reading the files. How should the follow-up run?

options.text: Switch to the built-in `Explore` agent, which keeps a transcript for resuming.
Set `background` to `true` on the definition and then call the same agent again.
Start a fresh query and paste the subagent's final report into the new prompt text.
Resume the first session with `resume`, pass the same `agents` definition and name the subagent's `agentId`.

explanation: A resumed subagent keeps its full conversation history, including its tool calls, results and reasoning. To resume, capture the `session_id` from the first query, read the `agentId` from the Agent tool result, resume that session with the same `agents` definitions, and refer to the agent by id. Analogy: a tutor with a notebook. Calling the same tutor back with last week's notebook lets her continue mid-lesson, while a new tutor handed a one-page summary has to start over. The built-in one-shot agents are tutors who throw the notebook away each visit.

distractor_explanations.A: `Explore` and `Plan` are one-shot and return no `agentId`, so they cannot be resumed.
distractor_explanations.B: `background` only makes the subagent run without blocking. It does not restore any history.
distractor_explanations.C: A new subagent would have only the pasted summary. Its earlier tool calls and reasoning are gone.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Exam-Style Tier)
prompt: An Agent SDK application defines subagents with `AgentDefinition` and runs the parent session in `default` permission mode. Which TWO statements describe how a subagent's tools and permissions behave? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Tools in the parent's `allowed_tools` are added to every subagent's `tools` list.
A `permissionMode` of `bypassPermissions` on a definition takes effect under a `default` parent.
A definition with no `tools` field inherits every tool available to subagents.
A tool left out of `tools` is absent from the subagent's session, with no prompt or error.
A subagent receives the parent's conversation history and tool results as context.

explanation: The `tools` field is an allow-list for the subagent. Omit it and the subagent inherits every available tool; list tools and everything else is simply missing from its session. Permissions are separate: a subagent runs under the parent's mode, and a bypass value on the definition is never applied unless the parent already bypasses. Analogy: building badges. No badge list means access to every room; a listed badge opens only those doors, and the other doors do not even appear on the map. The tempting idea that a definition can grant itself bypass is like an employee printing a master key.

distractor_explanations.A: `allowed_tools` pre-approves tools for calls that need approval. It does not change which tools a subagent has.
distractor_explanations.B: A subagent runs in bypass mode only when the parent session does. The value on the definition is never applied.
distractor_explanations.E: Its context starts fresh. The only thing the parent passes in is the prompt string of the Agent tool call.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Exam-Style Tier)
prompt: A prompt asks a model to compare five 20,000-token contracts. It begins with the question and formatting instructions, then pastes the contracts as five plain text blocks separated by dashes. Answers often cite the wrong contract. Which change is most likely to help?

options.text: Repeat the question after each contract and keep the dash separators.
Shrink each contract to a 500-token summary before the comparison starts.
Raise `effort` to `max` and keep the current prompt layout and separators as they are.
Put the contracts first, each in `<document>` tags with `<source>` and `<document_content>`, and the question last.

explanation: For long inputs, place the documents near the top, wrap each in `<document>` tags with `<source>` and `<document_content>` subtags, and put the question at the end. Queries at the end improved quality by up to 30 percent in tests, especially with several documents. Analogy: an open-book exam. You lay the labelled books on the desk first and read the question last, so you know which book to open. Handing over the question first and an unlabelled pile of pages makes it easy to quote the wrong book.

distractor_explanations.A: It adds clutter without labelling the sources. Dashes still do not say which contract is which.
distractor_explanations.B: Summaries drop the clause-level detail the comparison depends on. The layout problem would remain.
distractor_explanations.C: More effort adds reasoning but does not tell the model where one contract ends and the next begins.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Exam-Style Tier)
prompt: An agent's `lookup_policy` tool returns policy text, and the developer appends the line `Cite the policy section number in your reply` to the end of that tool result. The agent ignores it in most turns. Where should the instruction go?

options.text: Inside the tool result, repeated in capital letters on a line of its own.
Inside the tool result, wrapped in `<instructions>` tags at the end of the text.
In the `description` of every other tool in the request.
In the system prompt, or in a user turn placed after the `tool_result` block.

explanation: Claude treats tool-result content as untrusted data, so instructions placed there may be ignored or even flagged as a possible injection. Standing rules belong in the system prompt, and per-turn instructions can go in a user turn that follows the `tool_result` block.

distractor_explanations.A: Forceful wording does not change how the content is treated. Instructions in a tool result may be ignored or flagged.
distractor_explanations.B: Tags are only delimiters. Content inside a tool result is still treated as data, so the instruction may be ignored.
distractor_explanations.C: Descriptions explain what each tool does and when to use it. They are the wrong place for a rule about the reply.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Exam-Style Tier)

options.text: The 4 oldest tool results are cleared and the 2 newest are kept.
Nothing is cleared yet; clearing starts once input passes 30,000 tokens.
All 6 tool results are cleared and `keep` applies from the next turn.
The request fails with a 400 error until `clear_at_least` is added to the edit.

explanation: The `trigger` decides when clearing activates; here that is when input passes 30,000 tokens. At 24,000 the strategy sits idle. Once it fires, `keep` decides how many of the most recent tool uses survive. Analogy: a thermostat set to 30 degrees. Below the setpoint the heating stays off however many rooms there are, and once it switches on, the rule about which rooms stay warm applies. Clearing four results at 24,000 tokens would be heating the house while it is still cool.

distractor_explanations.A: This ignores the trigger. `keep` only applies once clearing is activated by the trigger.
distractor_explanations.C: Nothing is cleared below the trigger, and `keep` governs which results survive a clear on the very turn it runs.
distractor_explanations.D: `clear_at_least` is optional. The configuration is valid and simply waits for the trigger.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Exam-Style Tier)

options.text: List `clear_thinking_20251015` before `clear_tool_uses_20250919` in `edits`.
Add `clear_tool_inputs: true` to the tool-use edit and keep the order as it is.
Set `keep` on the thinking edit to the string `"all"` instead of a number of turns.
Change the thinking `keep` object to use `"type": "tool_uses"`.

explanation: When both strategies are combined, `clear_thinking_20251015` must come first in the `edits` array. Both edits here are valid on their own, so the only fault is the order they are listed in. Analogy: a form whose rules say the privacy-redaction page must be the first page in the stack. Each page is filled in correctly, but the stack is invalid until that page moves to the front. The thinking edit is the redaction page. Changing `keep` to a different unit only swaps one valid setting for another and leaves the stack in the wrong order.

distractor_explanations.B: That option also clears the call parameters of cleared tool uses. It has no bearing on how strategies are combined.
distractor_explanations.C: `"all"` is a valid value that preserves every thinking block. It does not address the order of the two strategies.
distractor_explanations.D: `tool_uses` is the unit for the tool-result strategy. Thinking is kept by `thinking_turns` or `"all"`.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Exam-Style Tier)
prompt: A coding assistant with file-reading tools answers questions about a repository. Reviews show it sometimes describes functions in files it never opened, with confident but wrong details. The team wants a prompt-level fix that keeps answers grounded. Which change fits best?

options.text: Tell it to read every referenced file before answering and to make no claims about unread code.
Add a few-shot example that shows a well-formatted, polite answer.
Ask for the answer in JSON with a `confidence` field between 0 and 1 for each claim.
Sample five answers per question and return the answer that most runs agree on.

explanation: The grounded fix is to instruct the model to investigate before answering: open any referenced file first and avoid claims about code it has not read. Analogy: a student asked about chapter 4 who must open the book before answering, instead of guessing from the title. Asking five students and taking the majority just collects five confident guesses. A confidence score is the student rating his own guess, and a formatting example only teaches how the answer should look.

distractor_explanations.B: Examples fix format and tone. They do not make the model open files before describing them.
distractor_explanations.C: A self-reported score is not grounding. The model can be confidently wrong about code it never read.
distractor_explanations.D: Agreement between ungrounded answers does not prove they are correct, and it costs several times as many tokens.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Exam-Style Tier)
prompt: A compliance team asks Claude to answer questions from a 90,000-token policy set pasted into the prompt. A reviewer must be able to check each claim against the source text from the answer alone. Which TWO techniques fit? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Have it find a supporting quote for each claim and retract any claim without one.
Run the question five times and compare the answers for any inconsistencies between them.
Ask for word-for-word quotes first, then answer using only those quotes.
Review the summarized thinking blocks when an answer looks wrong.
Allow the answer `I don't know` when the policies are silent.

explanation: For long documents, extracting word-for-word quotes first grounds the answer in the actual text, and asking Claude to find a supporting quote for each claim and retract unsupported ones makes the answer auditable. Analogy: footnotes in an essay. Every statement points to a page, and a statement with no footnote gets deleted. Running the question five times is like asking five students and comparing, which spots disagreement but gives the marker no page numbers. Allowing `I don't know` is good manners, but it adds no footnotes.

distractor_explanations.B: Best-of-N flags unstable answers, but the final answer still carries no link from claims to source text.
distractor_explanations.D: Thinking review helps debug faulty logic. It sits outside the answer, so a reviewer holding only the answer cannot trace claims.
distractor_explanations.E: This reduces invented answers when the text lacks information. It does not tie each stated claim to a quote.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Exam-Style Tier)
prompt: On a model that supports forced tool choice, a triage service forces `tool_choice` to `{"type": "tool", "name": "log_ticket"}` so every request ends in that call. Product now wants a one-sentence plain-text explanation before the tool call. Adding that request to the system prompt changes nothing. What should the team do?

options.text: Add `input_examples` to `log_ticket` that include a sentence of explanatory text.
Switch `tool_choice` to `any` and keep the system prompt request.
Switch `tool_choice` to `auto` and request the explanation in the user message.
Set `strict` to `true` on the `log_ticket` tool definition.

explanation: With `tool_choice` set to `any` or `tool`, the API prefills the assistant turn to force a tool call, so the model emits no text before the `tool_use` block even when asked. Using `auto` and telling Claude in the user message to explain and then call the tool restores the explanation.

distractor_explanations.A: Examples show valid inputs for the tool. They do not make Claude write a sentence ahead of the call.
distractor_explanations.B: `any` also prefills the assistant turn with a tool call, so no natural language comes first.
distractor_explanations.D: Strict mode makes tool inputs match the schema. It has no effect on text before the call.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Exam-Style Tier)
prompt:
A request that uses tool search returns a 400 error, and `get_invoice` must stay deferred. One tool in the `tools` array looks like this:

```json
{
  "name": "get_invoice",
  "description": "Fetch one invoice by number ...",
  "input_schema": {"type": "object",
    "properties": {"number": {"type": "string"}}},
  "defer_loading": true,
  "cache_control": {"type": "ephemeral"}
}
```

Which change is correct?

options.text: Remove `cache_control` here and put the breakpoint on a non-deferred tool.
Set `defer_loading` to `true` on the tool search tool as well.
Drop `get_invoice` from `tools` and describe it in the system prompt text instead.
Remove `defer_loading` from every tool so the breakpoint is allowed.

explanation: A tool marked `defer_loading: true` cannot also carry `cache_control`, so the breakpoint has to sit on a non-deferred tool. The deferred definitions are still sent in `tools` on every request. Analogy: a library with closed stacks and an open shelf. You can clip a bookmark onto a book on the open shelf, but not onto a book that is still in storage. Removing every deferral would put all the books on the shelf and defeat the point. Making the search tool deferred too would lock the catalogue itself in the stacks.

distractor_explanations.B: At least one tool, normally the search tool, must stay non-deferred. Deferring all tools is itself a 400.
distractor_explanations.C: Tool search needs every definition in `tools`. A prompt description gives Claude no callable tool.
distractor_explanations.D: That removes the context savings tool search exists for. Only the conflicting field needs to move.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Exam-Style Tier)
prompt: A platform has 600 internal tools. Claude must find the right ones with the company's own embedding search instead of the built-in regex or BM25 variants, and the lookup has to run inside the normal tool-use loop with the cached tool prefix staying valid. Which design works?

options.text: Use `tool_search_tool_bm25_20251119` and write the embedding scores into the tool descriptions.
Send only the five matches in `tools` on each turn and drop the rest.
Return the matching tools' full JSON schemas as plain text in a `tool_result`.
Defer-load all tools and add a client search tool that returns `tool_reference` blocks.

explanation: A custom search tool is an ordinary client tool whose `tool_result` contains `tool_reference` blocks, and the API expands each into the full definition. Every referenced tool must still be defined in `tools`, normally with `defer_loading: true`. Analogy: a library with its own card catalogue. The catalogue returns call numbers, not the books themselves, and the librarian fetches each book from the stacks. Photocopying book contents into the reply, or shelving only five books per visit, breaks the system.

distractor_explanations.A: The BM25 variant runs its own lexical search on names and descriptions. It never calls the company's embeddings.
distractor_explanations.B: Changing the `tools` array between requests modifies tool definitions, which invalidates the whole prompt cache. Deferred loading keeps the array fixed.
distractor_explanations.C: Text in a result is not a tool definition. Claude cannot call a tool that is not registered.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Exam-Style Tier)
prompt:
An agent turn contains three independent `tool_use` blocks. The loop below runs them in order and stops at the first failure. When the second call raises, the next request is rejected.

```python
results = []
for block in tool_uses:
    try:
        out = run_tool(block)
    except ToolError as err:
        results.append(error_result(block.id, str(err)))
        break
    results.append(ok_result(block.id, out))
messages.append({"role": "user", "content": results})
```

Which change is correct?

options.text: Drop the third `tool_use` block from the stored assistant turn before the next request.
Return a `tool_result` for the unrun third call too, with `is_error` set to `true` and a short note.
Send the third call's result in a separate user message after this one.
Retry the failed second call in a loop until it finally succeeds, then continue.

explanation: Every `tool_use` block needs a `tool_result` with a matching id, all together in the next user message. If you decide not to run a call, you still return a result for it with `is_error: true` and a brief explanation. Analogy: a restaurant with three order tickets on one table. The waiter must bring back a line for every ticket, marking the cancelled dish as cancelled, or the cashier refuses to close the bill. Moving the third line to a later bill, or tearing the ticket up, leaves the bill unbalanced.

distractor_explanations.A: The assistant turn is Claude's own output and should be passed back as it was. Each call in it needs a matching result.
distractor_explanations.C: All results for one assistant turn must come together in the single user message that follows it.
distractor_explanations.D: Retrying may never succeed and still leaves the third call without a result.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Exam-Style Tier)

Each example must validate against the `input_schema`, and examples add some tokens. Other flags change loading, forcing or cost, not the model's formatting.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Exam-Style Tier)
prompt: A healthcare app marks its tools `strict: true` to avoid malformed tool calls. A compliance reviewer asks what that setting does and what to watch for in the tool definitions. Which TWO statements are accurate? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Tool inputs follow the `input_schema` exactly, for example `2` rather than `"2"`.
It guarantees that Claude calls a tool on every request, even with no `tool_choice` set.
It verifies that argument values are right for the business, such as the correct customer ID.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Exam-Style Tier)
prompt:

```python
    permission_mode="bypassPermissions",

)
```

distractor_explanations.A: `dontAsk` plus an allow list is a valid locked-down setup, but it changes the mode the job has to keep.

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Exam-Style Tier)

source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Exam-Style Tier)

Add `--effort low` to the command to lower reasoning effort on every call
Add `--max-budget-usd 5.00` to the command to stop the run at that spend
Add `--max-turns 8` to the command to limit the number of agentic turns

explanation: In print mode, `--max-budget-usd` sets a dollar ceiling for the run, and spend from subagents counts toward it. Once the cap is reached the run stops, which is the per-run guard the team needs. Analogy: a taxi with a fare cap set before the ride. The meter, not the number of turns the driver takes, decides when you stop. `--max-turns` is like limiting the number of street corners, which says nothing about the fare, and a monthly workspace limit is the cab company's annual budget.

distractor_explanations.A: That limit is monthly and changes organization-level settings, which the team ruled out. It cannot stop one run at $5.
distractor_explanations.B: Effort tunes how deeply the model thinks. It lowers typical cost but sets no ceiling on spend.
distractor_explanations.D: `--max-turns` caps turns, not dollars. Turns vary widely in cost, so eight turns can still exceed or fall far under $5.

prompt: A team has 20 carefully written test cases for a support-reply generator, all typical requests, each graded by an engineer who reads the output. After launch, failures come from empty messages, very long pastes and ambiguous requests. What is the best change to the eval?

options.text: Have two experts grade each of the 20 cases to raise the quality of every individual score
Add many more real-traffic cases, edge cases included, with every case graded by automated checks
Replace the 20 cases with a public benchmark published for the model family in use
Revise the prompt until all 20 cases pass, then ship the new version to users

explanation: Evals should be task-specific, so they should include the awkward inputs production actually sees, such as empty, overly long and ambiguous ones. They should be automated where possible, and more cases with slightly noisier automated grading beat fewer cases graded carefully by hand. The 20 typical cases are blind to the failures users report.

distractor_explanations.A: Human grading is slow and costly, and the guidance prefers more cases with automated grading over fewer carefully hand-graded ones.
distractor_explanations.C: Evals should mirror the task's own input distribution, edge cases included. A public benchmark does not.
distractor_explanations.D: Passing 20 typical cases says nothing about empty, long or ambiguous inputs, and tuning to them risks overfitting.
